World.title: Costa Rica’s Whale and Dolphin Festival Returns This Weekend
World.content:
If you have been waiting for the right weekend to see humpback whales in Costa Rica, this is it. The 16th Whale and Dolphin Festival takes place this weekend, September 4, 5 and 6 in Costa Ballena in the South Pacific, timed to the peak of the season when humpbacks fill the warm water off Uvita.

The whales are the reason the festival exists. Adults reach nearly 16 meters (52 feet) and weigh up to 36 metric tons (about 40 short tons), and they arrive here after one of the longest migrations any mammal makes. Whales reaching Costa Rican waters can cover between 5,000 and 8,000 kilometers (3,100 to 5,000 miles) from cold-water feeding grounds, some as far south as the waters near the Antarctic Peninsula.

They come to breed, give birth, and raise their calves where the water is warm and sheltered. Mothers spend these weeks teaching their young to feed, socialize, and move through open ocean. Bahía Ballena, next to Marino Ballena National Park, is one of the best-documented breeding areas in the country. It is also home to the tombolo that gives the park its nickname, a sandbar that takes the shape of a whale’s tail when the tide drops and you see it from above.

Festival organizer Karol Monge said Bahía Ballena belongs on every Costa Rican’s list, describing it as a destination known not only for whale watching but for its beaches, mountains, rivers and waterfalls. Programming runs across all three days and mixes cultural, sporting and nature activities with whale-watching tours sold at special rates for Costa Ricans.

You will also find kite-making workshops, free surf lessons, a food court, a craft fair built around nature themes, concerts, and a communal ceviche event. A whale sculpture several meters tall, built from recycled material including plastic bottles, is on display. To check schedules and prices or reserve a tour, organizers are directing people to the festival’s Facebook page, Festival de Ballenas y Delfines Costa Rica, and to the phone number 8729-3624. Tours book out fast during festival weekend, so calling ahead matters more than usual.

Marcos V. Borges, executive president of the Costa Rican Tourism Institute, said whale watching in the southern Pacific during breeding and calving season is one of the experiences that sets Costa Rica apart. He encouraged domestic travelers to come for the weekend and to choose sustainable tour operators.

That last point is worth taking seriously as Costa Rica regulates how close boats may approach whales and how long they can stay near mothers with calves, and those rules exist because a boat that crowds a nursing calf can separate it from its mother. Ask an operator whether they are licensed and whether a naturalist guide is aboard. Smaller boats carrying eight to twelve passengers generally give you a better view than large catamarans, and morning departures usually mean calmer water and more active animals.

Book a morning tour if you can since most run three to four hours and leave by boat from Bahía Uvita inside the park. If you are driving from San José, you have two routes. Route 34, the Costanera Sur, runs down the coast. The alternative is Route 2 south to San Isidro, then Route 234 toward Dominical. Either way, allow more time than a map suggests on a festival weekend.

The land section of Marino Ballena National Park is open daily and charges a small entrance fee, lower for nationals and residents than for foreign visitors. There are no shops or facilities inside, and the beach at the Uvita sector has almost no shade, so bring water and sun cover. Walking out onto the whale’s tail only works at low tide, so check a tide table before you plan the day around it.

The southern humpback season runs roughly from July into November and peaks between August and October, which means the whales will still be here after the festival packs up. What the weekend adds is the rest of it, the crowds and the music and the ceviche, and the reminder that in Uvita and Bahía Ballena the arrival of these animals is not just an ecological event but the thing that keeps hotels, restaurants, guides and small businesses running through the green season.

World.title: Guanacaste Bakes While the Caribbean Floods in Costa Rica’s Split August
World.content:
August gave us two very different versions of Costa Rica’s rainy season, with unusually little rain falling around Liberia while parts of the Caribbean recorded some of their wettest conditions in decades. Liberia, the capital of Guanacaste and a major gateway for tourists visiting the northwestern Pacific coast, received just 26.2 millimeters of rain during the entire month, or a little more than 1 inch.

At the other end of the spectrum, Canta Gallo in the northern Caribbean recorded 1,781 millimeters, or about 70 inches, during August. The Canta Gallo total made August 2026 the wettest month recorded there during the station’s 30 years of data, according to figures from Costa Rica’s National Meteorological Institute, known as the IMN and Canta Gallo was not alone.

Limón recorded 1,031 millimeters, or about 40.6 inches, making it the wettest August there in 27 years of records. Farther south, Manzanillo received 769 millimeters, or about 30.3 inches, its wettest August in 28 years. The Manzanillo total was roughly double the previous record for the month.

The Caribbean’s unusually wet month was driven by a combination of tropical waves, the position of the Intertropical Convergence Zone and moisture carried into Costa Rica by Caribbean trade winds. This combination repeatedly produced heavy rain over the Caribbean and northern area in August and some of the most intense weather came in the middle of the month.

For example, on August 15 and 16, the IMN counted 20 records for maximum rainfall over a 24-hour period. Mountainous areas of the Caribbean received between 200 and 360 millimeters, roughly 8 to 14 inches, in just 48 hours. Nine weather stations in the northern and southern Caribbean also registered their wettest August 16 on record, with the IMN reporting that the affected stations had at least 10 years of historical data.

By August 17, some stations had already received more rain than they would normally expect during the entire month. In some locations, accumulated rainfall had reached between 100% and 170% of the normal August amount before the month was even two-thirds finished. The situation in Liberia could hardly have been more different.

Only 26.2 millimeters (about 1 inch) fell there during August, showing how sharply rainfall can vary across Costa Rica even during the same weather systems. The northwestern area of Guanacaste and the Caribbean coast often experience very different weather patterns because of the country’s mountains and the direction from which moisture arrives.

The contrast is especially notable for anyone traveling here on vacation since someone spending August along Costa Rica’s Caribbean coast could have experienced days of intense tropical rainfall, while someone staying around Liberia and parts of northern Guanacaste may have encountered considerably drier conditions.

The August numbers also show why broad descriptions such as “rainy season” can be misleading in Costa Rica. Weather can vary dramatically between the Pacific, Central Valley, northern region and Caribbean, sometimes over relatively short distances.

The IMN continued to report unstable conditions in the Caribbean toward the end of August. On August 28, for example, Canta Gallo recorded as much as 110 millimeters of rain in a matter of hours, while forecasters warned that the Intertropical Convergence Zone remained close to Costa Rica and that trade winds were continuing to push moisture toward the country.

August 2026 will therefore go into Costa Rica’s weather records not because everything was exceptionally wet or dry, but because opposite extremes were occurring at the same time.

World.title: Costa Rica Court Orders Protection Plan for Playa Blanca After 32-Year Delay
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Constitutional Court has ordered environmental authorities to create a long-delayed management plan for the protected marine wetland at Playa Blanca, adding a new chapter to the controversy surrounding one of the Central Pacific’s most popular beaches. The court gave the Ministry of Environment and Energy (MINAE), and the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC), a maximum of 12 months to complete the General Management Plan for the Humedal Marino Playa Blanca, located near Punta Leona in Garabito, Puntarenas.

The ruling is notable because the wetland was established in April 1994 and has operated for more than 32 years without an approved management plan. The court decision comes as Playa Blanca is already at the center of a separate fight over public access. In June, the Municipality of Garabito removed barriers at the entrance to Punta Leona after arguing that the road leading toward Playa Blanca is public. The move opened vehicle access through the resort area and led to a sharp increase in attention from visitors wanting to reach the beach. Punta Leona disputes the municipality’s interpretation and has continued challenging the matter in court.

The latest Constitutional Court ruling does not settle that access dispute. Instead, it focuses on how the protected marine area itself is being managed. The Humedal Marino Playa Blanca was created by executive decree on April 7, 1994, and is administered by SINAC through the Central Pacific Conservation Area. Despite its protected status, authorities never completed the management document normally used to determine how an environmentally sensitive area should be protected and used.

A management plan can establish which activities are appropriate in different parts of the protected area, identify environmental threats and set out programs for monitoring, restoration and enforcement. It also allows authorities to update scientific information about the area’s marine environment and surrounding ecosystem. The case was brought by environmental attorney Wálter Brenes Soto, who argued that leaving the wetland without such a plan made it difficult for authorities to properly protect the area.

Environmental officials told the court they had tried at least twice to begin preparing the plan but lacked sufficient financing and institutional resources. SINAC had proposed gathering information during 2026 and 2027, preparing contracting documents in August 2027 and seeking money for the project in its 2028 budget. Once contracted, preparing the plan was expected to take another 12 to 15 months.

The Constitutional Court rejected that timeline.The judges concluded that after more than three decades, a continuing lack of funding did not justify leaving the protected area without the required environmental planning. The court said the situation affects Costa Rica’s constitutional right to a healthy and ecologically balanced environment.

The ruling was issued August 27 and the 12-month deadline begins once authorities are formally notified.The timing adds another layer to the debate surrounding Playa Blanca. When Garabito removed the entrance barriers in June, Mayor Francisco González said the municipality was enforcing a determination dating back more than two decades that the road was public. Punta Leona has argued that the entrance and road cross privately registered property and says the dispute should ultimately be resolved by the courts.

Since then, anyone going there has been able to travel through the Punta Leona entrance toward Playa Blanca, although parking has become an issue. Authorities have warned drivers that public access to the beach does not allow them to park along the roadway. Private parking is available in the area, including parking operated by Punta Leona.

During a July 22 inspection, SINAC personnel reported relatively little tourist activity inside the actual boundaries of the marine wetland and said nearby development lies outside the officially protected area. Authorities acknowledged, however, that a management plan would allow them to better evaluate possible indirect effects from activity surrounding the wetland.

Brenes has linked the court case to what he describes as increased visitation since the Playa Blanca entrance was opened. He argues that the additional traffic makes proper environmental management more urgent. For those that go there, the important point is that the ruling does not close Playa Blanca and does not reverse the opening of the access road. It requires Costa Rican environmental authorities to finally establish a formal plan for managing the protected marine area alongside the beach.

What that plan ultimately contains remains to be seen. But after 32 years without one, the Constitutional Court has now put a firm deadline on the government to produce it.

World.title: Mayor Earl Trapp: Santa Elena to inaugurate 1st ever synthetic field
World.content:
Mayor Earl Trapp: Santa Elena to inaugurate 1st ever synthetic field

By Zoila Palma: The San Ignacio and Santa Elena Town Council is continuing its infrastructure development efforts across the municipality, Mayor Earl Trapp said.

The Mayor says that Requena Street in Santa Elena, behind the Complex, is currently undergoing upgrading works as part of the council’s ongoing efforts to improve local infrastructure.

In addition, the Joseph Andrews Park and Santa Elena’s own synthetic turf are nearing inauguration, providing an improved sporting facility aimed at encouraging children and youths to participate in sports and other activities.

Mayor Trapp said the council remains committed to improving the quality of life for residents while promoting a cleaner, healthier and more developed municipality.

World.title: Investing in healthcare: $2.5 million scholarship program supports 67 Belizeans
World.content:
Investing in healthcare: $2.5 million scholarship program supports 67 Belizeans

By Zoila Palma: Sixty-seven Belizeans pursuing higher education in health-related fields have been awarded scholarships through a collaboration between the Ministry of Health and Wellness, Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology, the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) and several tertiary-level institutions.

The scholarship recipients, who have signed bonds with the Government of Belize, will receive financial support throughout their programs, allowing them to focus on their studies. Areas of study include nursing, medicine, mental health and biomedical engineering.

The initiative is aimed at strengthening Belize’s public healthcare system by developing and retaining highly skilled professionals.

The program also seeks to empower scholarship recipients to expand their expertise and contribute to improving the health and well-being of Belizeans.

With a BZ$2.5 million investment this year, the scholarship program represents a significant commitment to building a stronger healthcare workforce and preparing the next generation of professionals to meet Belize’s evolving health needs.

World.title: International News: France records hottest summer ever as heatwaves, drought and wildfires intensify
World.content:
International News: France records hottest summer ever as heatwaves, drought and wildfires intensify

By Zoila Palma: France experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, with extreme heat, drought and widespread wildfires affecting the country, Environment Minister Monique Barbut said today.

The record was set during the June-to-August meteorological summer, France 24 reports.

France endured multiple severe heatwaves, including one in late June that set a new intensity record and another that lasted 23 days, tying the country’s longest heatwave record previously established in 1983.

Meteo-France reported 53 days of heatwave conditions during the summer, describing the figure as unprecedented.

The extreme weather also fueled a major wildfire season, with forests suffering extensive damage. Barbut said that by the end of August, fires had burned six times more land than the average recorded over the previous 20 years.

Heatwaves across Europe also contributed to thousands of excess deaths in France, while schools were closed and residents struggled to cope with soaring temperatures.

World.title: International News: Canada ready for US trade deal to benefit both countries
World.content:
International News: Canada ready for US trade deal to benefit both countries

By Zoila Palma: Today, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada is prepared to sign a trade agreement with the United States, provided it delivers benefits to both countries and offers stability and credibility for workers, families and businesses.

Speaking in Thunder Bay, Ontario, Carney said Canada is ready to return to negotiations when Washington is prepared to do so.

Carney rejected claims by US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that Canada abandoned trade talks because of domestic political considerations.

He also said the US position appears to have softened on several issues since negotiations broke down last month, including concerns over Canadian language and culture.

The latest developments come as tensions remain between the two countries over trade.

Shortly after Carney’s remarks, US President Donald Trump criticized the Canadian prime minister in a Truth Social post, accusing Carney of portraying him as an enemy and warning that such an approach could have severe consequences for Canada’s economy.

World.title: Can Belize take Sports to the next level? Leaders discuss future at historic summit
World.content:
Can Belize take Sports to the next level? Leaders discuss future at historic summit

By Zoila Palma: Key leaders and decision-makers in Belize’s sporting and education sectors gathered on Wednesday for the opening panel of the Belize Sports Summit 2026, the first event of its kind aimed at examining the current state and future direction of sports in Belize.

The panel, titled “The State of Sports in Belize,” was moderated by CEO Nicole Usher of the Ministry of Tourism, Youth, Sports and Diaspora Relations.

The discussion brought together Devin Daly, Minister of State in the Ministry, Kervin Jean of SYNEK Consultant and UWI, Jimena Saldaña, Secretary General of Panam Sports, Allan Sharp, President of the Belize Olympic and Commonwealth Games Association, and Dian Maheia, CEO of the Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology.

The panel provided an opportunity for stakeholders to examine key issues affecting sports development in Belize, including governance, education, athlete development and the role of national and international sporting organizations.

The participation of representatives from government, education and international sporting bodies highlighted the importance of collaboration in strengthening the country’s sports sector.

World.title: National Meteorological Service warns of drier conditions, drought risk as El Niño impacts Belize
World.content:
National Meteorological Service warns of drier conditions, drought risk as El Niño impacts Belize

By Zoila Palma: The National Meteorological Service of Belize is warning that Belize could experience drier-than-normal conditions during the 2026 wet season as the country continues to feel the influence of El Niño.

The outlook indicates reduced rainfall between June and September, along with potentially prolonged dry spells, although periods of intense rainfall remain possible.

Forecasters note that Belize could also experience short bursts of heavy rainfall capable of causing flash flooding, despite the overall trend toward drier conditions.

The National Met Service says northern Belize is already under a Drought Watch, with the risk that drought conditions could worsen as the country approaches the next dry season.

The projected conditions could have significant implications across several sectors.

In the energy sector, reduced rainfall could lower hydropower generation while higher temperatures increase electricity demand.

In health, prolonged heat may contribute to dehydration, heat exhaustion and other health impacts, while warmer and drier conditions could increase risks associated with vector-borne diseases such as dengue.

The outlook also highlights concerns for food security and agriculture, including reduced crop and livestock productivity, increased pest and disease pressures and potential impacts on fisheries. These conditions could contribute to higher food prices, greater pressure on households and increased reliance on imports.

The National Met Service is encouraging Belizeans to conserve water, prepare for changing weather conditions and remain informed.

In addition, while El Niño increases the likelihood of drier conditions, heavy downpours can still occur highlighting the need for communities to prepare for both drought and flash-flood risks.

World.title: International News: Former Colombia President and Mexican President discuss shifting political landscape across Americas
World.content:
International News: Former Colombia President and Mexican President discuss shifting political landscape across Americas

By Zoila Palma: Former Colombian President Gustavo Petro met with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on Wednesday during his visit to Mexico, where the two discussed what Petro described as a “new political reality” emerging across the Americas.

Petro raised concerns about potential interference by the United States in electoral processes across Latin America. He said Mexico should pay close attention to political developments in countries including Brazil, as well as the growing influence of right-wing political forces ahead of Mexico’s 2027 midterm elections and 2030 presidential election.

Following the meeting at Mexico’s National Palace, Petro said discussions focused on what he called an “artificial political reality” linked to operations originating outside the countries where elections are held.

He said investigations in Bolivia had revealed what he described as a broader phenomenon affecting countries throughout the Americas.

Petro, who has been in Mexico since Monday, is also scheduled to deliver a keynote lecture at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM).

World.title: National Disability Commission holds inaugural working session
World.content:
National Disability Commission holds inaugural working session

By Zoila Palma: Members of Belize’s newly established National Commission for Persons with Disabilities held their inaugural working session this morning.

The session marks the beginning of the Commission’s work to advance issues affecting persons with disabilities and strengthen efforts toward greater inclusion and support.

The Ministry of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs said the Commission will be officially introduced to the nation later today.

World.title: Crisis in the classrooms
World.content:
The 2026 Global School-Based Student Health Survey has painted an alarming picture of the state of Jamaican children surveyed with the data showing “an increase in suicidal ideation and attempts” by students in grades nine to 11 with girls outstripping boys in both thinking about the act and attempting it.

According to researchers, in comparing the 2010, 2017 and 2026 survey results, “mental health indicators have worsened over time with more students reporting suicidal thoughts, suicidal planning, suicide attempts, anxiety and depression”.

With a sample size of 3,058 students between grades 7 and 12 the survey administered questionnaires where the children were quizzed on their behaviours over the past seven days, the past 30 days, and the past 12 months.

The study, which was officially released on Wednesday morning by Health Minister Dr Christopher Tufton in collaboration with representatives of the National Council on Drug Abuse, found that suicidal thoughts were highest among grade 11 students with 36.6 per cent of girls saying they had thought about killing themselves as against 23.1 per cent of boys.

Chillingly it said, 32.4 per cent of grade nine girls, 21.8 per cent of grade eight boys, and 21.5 per cent of grade ten boys reported that they attempted to end their lives since this year.

In the meantime anxiety was highest among grade 10 girls with 46.2 per cent experiencing this, and 16.8 per cent of their grade 11 male peers.

Girls again led the way in reporting depression, with the highest numbers being among grade 11 students where 47.8 per cent of girls and 23.8 per cent of boys said they experienced this.

According to the experts, “If current trends persist, several critical challenges threaten adolescent well-being” across three primary areas.

“First, rising adolescent mental health crises involve escalating rates of emotional distress, feelings of hopelessness and self-harm risk indicating that early action matters,” the experts said.

Secondly they said, “Untreated distress negatively affects school engagement, interpersonal relationships, and substance use risks, demonstrating that untreated problems today lead to greater harm tomorrow”.

“Third, stigma and limited services delay professional help-seeking due to barriers like social judgement, restricted access and long wait times emphasising that early support saves lives” the experts said.

According to researchers, to address the issues several questions must be raised including about the extent to which school-based mental health initiatives address early screening and timely referrals, the clarity of suicide prevention pathways between home, school and community and the impact and scope of the expansion of access to adolescent mental health services.

In the meantime an assessment of social media use and screen time found that “most students have a mobile phone and use it for online activities”. According to the data 87.4 per cent of students surveyed have a mobile phone, 77.5 per cent use their devices for social media/online communication or Internet browsing, while 67. 2 per cent spend three-plus hours of screen time on an average school day. Interestingly, only 39 per cent said their parents or guardians have rules about social media use.

The researchers, in noting that the “high levels of screen time highlight the importance of digital balance and supportive rules” said this was so as “excessive screen time can impact physical, social and mental health”.

In addition they warned that excessive social media use can affect relationships and in-person interactions, and also “increases exposure to risky content and online pressures”.

“If current trends persist, several digital-related challenges emerge across multiple areas. First, there is reduced sleep, activity and family engagement as screen time displaces healthy habits,” the canvasser said, while noting that individuals experience greater exposure to online harms and social pressures, including negative comments, fake news and unrealistic comparisons.

“Thirdly, widening gaps in parental digital supervision appear between technologically confident families who maintain open conversations, privacy settings and screen time limits and parents lacking knowledge or time who are unfamiliar with risks, unclear about settings or have little time to monitor,” the experts declared.

They said to guide future efforts the extent to which health digital habits are promoted in schools must be determined.

In addition the experts said the parenting initiatives in existence for social media provision and monitoring must be known as well as the way in which cyberbullying, online exploitation and harmful content are built into adolescent mental health services.

The GSHS is an international gold-standard survey developed by World Health Organization, in collaboration with United Nations Children’s Fund; United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization; United States Agency for International Development; and the United States-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

It measures self-reported health behaviours and protective factors among youth 13-17 years old in the area of alcohol, tobacco and drug use, dietary behaviour, physical activity, sexual behaviours, violence and unintentional injury and protective factors.

It also establishes trends, and facilitates international comparison, develops priorities, establishes programmes, facilitates resource advocacy for school and youth health programmes/policies.

World.title: Minister cites importance of review process in school repairs
World.content:
The entrance to Ferris Primary School in Westmoreland showing buildings to the left and back that received new roofs. Repair work is left to be carried out on the administrative block to the right. (Photo: Anthony Lewis)

FERRIS, Westmoreland — The importance of speed and having a review process are among the lessons education minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon is taking from the less-than-smooth process of repairing more than 300 schools damaged by last year’s Hurricane Melissa.

“With our contractors, you have to have multiple entities that are reviewing. There are multiple stages of review. I think we’ve also learned how to do it quicker. Because, remember, it’s 300 contracts with 300 different scopes of work. And you’re going to need to have the quantity surveyors doing their work for 300 different contracts. It’s a lot, but I do think that going through this, it will make it much easier as we’re doing projects going forward because we’re not going to be in a position to do this many [schools] again. And so we’ve really built that muscle memory to be able to do this better going forward,” stated Morris Dixon, who also spoke about steps taken to ensure buildings can cope better with future storms.

The minister was responding to queries from the Jamaica Observer while fielding questions from the media at Ferris Primary School in Westmoreland following a tour of schools in the parish on Wednesday. The other institutions visited were Maud McLeod High and Beaufort Primary schools, both located in Darliston.

Describing the undertaking as unprecedented, Morris Dixon again conceded that fixing the damage left by last October’s Hurricane Melissa had been a challenge.

“It was a big undertaking; it’s something that we’ve never done in our history, you know, this kind of scale of repair of our schools and then doing it in terms of resilience. That is a big task, a very difficult task, under very difficult conditions. There were areas that didn’t work as well as we wanted, and then some things went really smoothly,” she said.

“It was a mixed bag but the team at NET (National Education Trust) has been very focused on reviewing what’s out there, the contracts, and making sure things are happening. The regions have also been very much a part of it. With all of us working together, I think we’ve been able to iron out a lot of kinks. There were a lot of kinks in the beginning, as you would have in any kind of emergency situation like this, but I think we’ve been able to iron them out,” the minister added.

Meanwhile, as the nation anticipates the reopening of schools for the new term, Morris Dixon assured that all institutions will open next week.

“Based on the report from the regions, every school will be open on Monday. As I said, not all the repairs will be done, but they’ve put in contingency plans. There are some schools that may be on rotation, which is like a shift system. Others will be using tents, some will be using timber structures,” she explained.

While she could not immediately provide the exact number of schools still utilising tents and board structures, she indicated that the targeted time frame to get them off these temporary settings is varied.

“I have schools that need a complete rebuild of some parts of the school. That’s not going to finish this year in some cases; it goes into next year. I have schools where the contractor said, ‘September, end of September, we’ll be finished completely.’ Others, it’s mid-October. So it really depends on the scope of work for the schools. And the schools have been given the timelines within which the work will be finished,” stated Morris Dixon.

At Ferris Primary, Principal Tracie Campbell told the Observer that repair work started in February and they are now 98 per cent ready for orientation on September 7, with classes commencing two days later.

Repairs were completed on the roofs of two buildings and a multi-purpose container. However, work remains to be done on the administrative block, even though the roof remains intact.

“I think we could have finished a while ago. However, since I’m not particularly in that field, I’m not privy to some of the information as to why it would have taken so long. What I do know though is that some of the repairs were not done. They were explaining that it was not in their contract to have it done. Nonetheless, the building officer came, I think it was about last Friday, and so they had other plans as to how to go ahead with fixing or doing the repairs on the remainder of the school,” stated Campbell.

Despite the delays, she expressed satisfaction with the progress.

“I remember when I came first after Melissa and I cried, Minister, because I would have said to myself, ‘It’s like no home, no school’. And to see that we are here and we are coming back… to see my teachers taking pride in fixing up, it’s like a new beginning. It’s a new spark for us. And parents would come in — even last week, parents came — to repaint, to help with the painting,” said Campbell.

World.title: Plié toasts a decade of dance
World.content:
Mercy performed by Complextions Contemporary Ballet, choreographed by Dwight Rhoden with music by Phil Kline, Michael Murray, Mendelssohn & Hans Zimmer, was among the highlights at Plie for the Arts’ Amalgamation Global Gala at The Little Theatre on Saturday, August 29, 2026. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

It was an evening of elegance, artistry, and celebration inside The Little Theatre on Saturday as Plié for the Arts marked its 10th anniversary with the Jamaican leg of its Amalgamation Global Gala.

The formal affair, held on August 29, brought together an impressive roster of international and Caribbean dancers for the first of two nights of performances, culminating a regional tour that had already made stops in Trinidad and Tobago and Barbados.

Among the night’s major highlights was the Caribbean premiere of Love Rocks, performed by members of the internationally acclaimed Complexions Contemporary Ballet. Choreographed by Dwight Rhoden and Desmond Richardson to the music of rock star Lenny Kravitz, the piece added another memorable moment to a programme packed with world-class dance.

The evening also featured Christopher Grant of New York City Ballet; Ashley Green of Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater; Adji Cissoko and Shuaib Elhassan of Alonzo King LINES Ballet; dancers from Parsons Dance; and the Plié Caribbean Collective, which placed regional talent alongside some of the world’s leading dance professionals.

Richardson, a celebrated dancer, choreographer, and co-founder of Complexions Contemporary Ballet, was the night’s honoree and received the Icon Award, while renowned ballerina Misty Copeland served as patron of the 10th anniversary celebration.

For Richardson, whose mother is Barbadian, being recognised in the Caribbean made the occasion particularly poignant.

“This is an incredible evening. I’m just honoured and so very blessed to be here. My mother is Bajan, and I grew up with this idea of ‘Caribbean-ness’, and experiencing it really feels quite like homecoming,” he said.

Richardson also used the moment to urge Caribbean audiences to continue investing in the region’s young dancers. “Thank you all for helping to support your young talent because they are amazing. We don’t see this type of talent all the time living in the city. So those of you who have these incredible beings in your midst, please continue to support them. They need you,” he said.

That support took tangible form during the evening when three dancers — Kato Austin, Matthew Johnson, and Lauryn Rickman — were awarded scholarships to attend Complexions.

For Plié for the Arts founder and Artistic Director Marisa Benain, Saturday’s packed house was an emotional validation of a vision she has spent a decade building.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer following the first night’s performances, Benain said she was overwhelmed by how far the organisation had come.

“Just having a vision and seeing the same vision evolve and get bigger and bigger and bigger, and you can’t stop it! Plié is from my soul. There is nothing better that I want to do than do Plié,” she said.

The Kingston engagement followed successful stops on Plié’s 10th anniversary Caribbean tour. The celebrations opened in Trinidad and Tobago on August 23 at the National Academy for the Performing Arts, where the production featured the National Philharmonic Orchestra of Trinidad and Tobago. The tour then moved to Barbados for performances at Frank Collymore Hall on August 25 and 26, presented alongside the National Cultural Foundation.

Benain described the reception across the region as spectacular, but said returning home to a full house carried special significance.

“It’s been wonderful. I mean, you’re talking about going to Trinidad and then you go to Barbados and you see the reception and how they loved it. It really warmed my heart, and to come home and get a full house is very special to me. Jamaica is my home and I want that support here,” she said.

Among her personal favourites from Saturday’s programme were Caught, Ave Maria, Bolero, and Carmina. She also reserved high praise for the Plié Caribbean Collective, whose dancers she said demonstrated the world-class calibre of talent that exists within the region.

World.title: Failing families
World.content:
The data shows that “protective family factors have weakened over time” with only three in 10 students reporting that their parents understood their problems.

A growing disconnect between students and parents who are increasingly taking a more hands-off approach has triggered alarm among analysts who warn of long-term repercussions in the just-released 2026 Global School-Based Student Health Survey.

The data shows that “protective family factors have weakened over time” with only three in 10 students reporting that their parents understood their problems and just four out of 10 saying their parents know what they do in their free time, provide guidance or spend quality time with them.

The survey results were officially released Wednesday morning by Health Minister Dr Christopher Tufton in collaboration with representatives of the National Council and Drug Abuse. It showed that of the 3,058 students between grades seven to 12 who were surveyed, only 25.9 per cent felt their parents understood their issues, 39.2 per cent said their parents knew what they were doing in their free time, 42.7 per cent got guidance or advice from their parents while 40.7 per cent said their parents spent quality time with them.

The researchers in comparing the findings across 2010, 2017 and 2026 for Jamaica said fewer parents understand the problems faced by their children today than they did 16 years ago. The data showed a slide from 31.9 per cent in 2010 to 31.3 per cent in 2017 with the numbers falling even further to 25.9 per cent this year. According to researchers, in 2010, 40.4 per cent of students surveyed said their parents knew what they were doing in their free time compared to 39.7 per cent in 2017 and 39.2 per cent this year.

However, a comparison of the data gathered for parents giving advice or guidance to their children showed an 8.5 per cent decrease between 2017 and 2026. No data was gathered for 2010 for that survey question. In terms of parents spending quality time with their children, there was a two per cent decrease from 2017 to 2026 (from with 42.7 per cent to 40.7 per cent. There was no data gathered for 2010.

The surveyors have in the meantime warned that, if current trends persist, “several systemic pressures and behavioural risks will emerge across multiple areas” which will include “a greater reliance on peers and online influences meaning guidance is shaped increasingly beyond the family”. Furthermore they said “adolescents face increased vulnerability to risky behaviours including substance use, unsafe relationships, violence and exploitation and school disengagement leading to higher risks to health, safety and well-being”. According to researchers there will also be growing pressure on schools and support services as increasing cases place more demands on institutions and systems.

According to the analysts, action in the future should be guided by determining the scope of parenting initiatives to strengthen parent-child communication and help parents remain influential sources of guidance. Furthermore they said the question of how effectively parents are being equipped to recognise, prevent and respond to risks affecting the health, safety and well-being of adolescents must also be answered. Additionally, the canvassers said, it must also be established what strategies exist to strengthen parental engagement with schools to reduce reliance on educational institutions and support services.

World.title: BAILEY’S GREEK ODYSSEY
World.content:
Reggae Boyz winger Leon Bailey signing his contact with Greek giants Olympiakos FC on Wednesday, September 2, 2026, after signing from Aston Villa. .

With Reggae Boyz winger Leon Bailey moving to multiple-time Greek champions Olympiacos FC, Greece-based sports writer Nikos Kotsis says his pedigree makes him a needed addition to the squad.

Bailey, who successfully completed his medical, was presented by Olympiacos on Wednesday. He moves to Super League Greece on a permanent deal, signing a three-year contract which ends a five-year stint with reigning Europa League champions Aston Villa.

“I’m very happy to wear the red and white shirt and I can’t wait to experience the atmosphere at the Karaiskakis Stadium,” he said in a video on the club’s social media.

Olympiacos have won the Greek top flight 48 times in their history, although they finished runners-up to AEK Athens last season. The club, who will compete in the UEFA Europa League season, made the knockout phase play-offs of the UEFA Champions League last season and won the UEFA Conference League title in 2024.

Olympiacos have been busy this transfer window, signing close to 20 players. Kotsis, who writes for several Greek outlets, including Sports 24, says Bailey’s arrival is among the top and believes he can make a real impact.

“Bailey’s arrival in Greece is a move that improves the attacking midfield of Piraeus,” Kotsis said. “If the Jamaican is healthy and has no problems, he will be a player who can make a difference. A winger with rich performances at the top level and a career full of brilliance.

“At 29 years old, the absolute leader of the Jamaican national team, Bailey is in the most mature phase of his career. Olympiacos adds to its roster a pure-blooded killer of the wings, capable of breaking down any defense in one-on-one. And now we are counting down to his arrival in Athens.”

Greek Sports Journalist Kostas Lianos reported that the deal is worth £2million ($427 million) and Bailey is set to earn £1.6 million ($342 million) per year until 2029.

Bailey was thought to be staying in the English Premier League with newly promoted Hull City on the verge of securing his signature. However, the move ultimately broke down with manager Sergej Jakirovic calling it “a mess” while Bailey’s representative Craig Butler told the Jamaica Observer that they were weighing up their options with several clubs interested.

Bailey failed to secure a move before the close of the English transfer deadline on Tuesday, with reports saying that he could be off to Saudi Arabia with Al Diriyah and Al Ittihad among the clubs interested given their transfer window closes on Saturday.

Although he had another year left on his contract with Aston Villa, Bailey was told by manager Unai Emery that he wouldn’t be part of his plans for the season, despite being an active part of their preseason.

Bailey joined Serie A club AS Roma on loan last summer but cut his loan deal short after limited game time and injuries and rejoined Villa in January where he went on to make 19 appearances. He won the Europa League title and saw Villa finish fourth in the league to secure a spot in this season’s Champions League.

Bailey, who joined from German club Bayer Leverkusen for £30 million in 2021, made 163 appearances and scored 23 times in all competitions.

His best season came in the 2023-24 campaign where he registered 10 goals and 10 assists in the Premier League, one of the few players to hit double digits in both categories.

Bailey’s departure means only four Jamaican internationals will be in the Premier League this season. They are Coventry City’s trio of Ethan Pinnock, Joel Latibeaudiere and Ephron Mason-Clark, and Brentford left back Rico Henry.

World.title: Class Act: Smart Lunches for Back-to-School with Reggae Jammin
World.content:
Eleven-year-old Zachary Walker gets ready to take a bite of his mini pizza bagel. First-former or not, a fun homemade lunch like this one makes him the coolest kid in class, no contest! (Photo: Travis Muschett)

Four easy recipes and real tips for keeping lunchboxes exciting once the term settles in.

The first week of school runs on adrenaline and good intentions. By week three, though, that fades, and most parents are staring into an open fridge at 6:00 am wondering what can possibly go into a lunchbox that isn’t a repeat of Monday’s sandwich.

That’s the season Reggae Jammin was created for. The range, snappy chicken franks and juicy burgers, is designed to go from freezer to table fast; the deeply seasoned Reggae Jammin Rotisserie Chicken is ready whenever you need it, which means most of the lunch-planning work is done well before the school-week rush even starts.

“Back to school is really about routine, and routine is where a lot of parents lose steam by week two,” says Navron Henry, brand manager at The Best Dressed Chicken. “We created Reggae Jammin around the idea that a good lunch shouldn’t take a good hour to make. If the hardest part of the morning is choosing what to pack rather than cooking it, that’s a win for everybody.”

Here are four recipes that pack well, reheat well and don’t fall apart by lunchtime, plus a few habits worth building into the school-week routine now, while there’s still time before the term gets away from everyone.

Real Tips For Packing Smarter Lunches

Start the night before. Set an 8:00 pm cut-off for lunch prep. Washing grapes, slicing cucumber and portioning dry snacks into containers the night before saves 10 minutes the next morning, and keeps knifework out of a groggy 6:00 am kitchen.

Cook once, pack three times. Franks are made for batch cooking, and the rotisserie chicken pulls double duty too. Buy it for Sunday dinner and there’s enough left for lunches through the week. Grill a full pack of franks on Sunday night alongside that Sunday chicken, and half the week’s protein is already handled.

Compartments beat one hot dish. Kids eat with their eyes, so skip the single hot dish in favour of a compartmented container. Keep starches, fruit and protein in their own sections and there’s no chance for anything to go soggy against anything else.

Let them dip. Kids love dipping. Instead of dressing a wrap or saucing a protein ahead of time, pack a small container of BBQ sauce, honey mustard or ranch on the side. It keeps the texture of the main dish intact and turns lunch into something closer to an activity.

Pack hot food hot and keep it that way. Anything with rice, pasta or chicken needs to go in steaming hot, not just warm, since it won’t be eaten for another four to six hours. Preheat the container first with a minute of boiling water, tip it out, then fill it right to the top. Packed that way, it stays safely hot until the lunch bell.

Freeze a juice box. A juice box straight from the freezer works as a natural ice pack and is thawed and ready by lunchtime. Bread doesn’t freeze well once it’s already been made into a sandwich, so keep those fresh each morning.

Let them choose. Handing over a little control makes all the difference. Kenya Walker, mother of nine-year-old Kennedy, sees it every day at home. “She loves picking out what goes into her lunchbox,” Kenya says. “Once she’s had some part in choosing it, the box comes back empty. I also try to keep at least one thing in there that’s familiar, because a new lunch and a new school day at the same time is a lot to ask of a child.”

Four Lunches Worth Repeating

BBQ Frank Mac & Cheese

Slice Reggae Jammin Chicken Franks into coins and toss them into a hot pan with a spoonful of smoky BBQ sauce until the edges turn crisp and caramelised. Fold them into a pot of macaroni and cheese, then pack it hot into a preheated insulated container. The franks keep their bite far better than most add-ins, so lunch still feels worth eating by midday.

Sunday Roast Fried Rice

Turn Sunday’s dinner into Monday’s lunch. Shred the leftover Reggae Jammin Rotisserie Chicken and fry it in a hot pan with day-old rice, scrambled egg, spring onion and peas. A splash of soy sauce and sesame oil ties it together, and nobody will guess it’s a repeat.

The Waffle Breakfast Burger

Grill a Reggae Jammin Burger and tuck it between two toasted frozen waffles, with a slice of cheese melted over the hot patty. It sounds unusual until the first bite, and it quickly becomes a regular request. Wrapped tightly in foil, it holds its shape all the way through the school run.

Mini Pizza Bagels

Split a bagel, spread each half with tomato sauce, and pile on sliced Reggae Jammin Chicken Franks or crumbled Reggae Jammin Burger before topping with cheese. Broil until bubbling and golden. These travel well cold or warm, making them the easiest fix for a morning with no time to spare.

In the end, between the batch cooking, the compartments and a rotisserie chicken that’s already done half the work, the goal is a rhythm that works for your household: A lunch that gets packed without a fight, eaten without complaint, and doesn’t need reinventing every single morning. That’s how you get through, and actually enjoy, the school year.

World.title: ‘Wake The Town And Tell The People’: U Roy celebration set for Sep 19
World.content:
U-Roy

Five years after pioneer deejay U Roy’s death, his family has taken steps to ensure the songs that made him famous are in the right hands. His daughter, Dionne Beckford, made this clear in a recent interview with the Jamaica Observer.

U Roy (given name Ewart Beckford) died in February 2021 at age 78, leaving a solid catalogue of songs and albums that are still in demand, especially in Europe where he had a lasting following.

“As far as his catalogue being secure and his music being properly distributed, we’re working with a team of lawyers to get things in place. He had 13 to 15 children, and there are about nine to 10 who are alive, and we should keep his legacy going,” said Beckford.

A dance dubbed ‘Wake The Town And Tell The People’ is one of the ways to salute U Roy’s role as an artiste, sound system kingpin and mentor. It takes place on September 19 at Cling Cling Oval in Olympic Gardens, Kingston, and features his Stur Gav sound system.

Some of the artistes who helped make Stur Gav dominant during the 1980s will perform. They include Josey Wales, Little John, Little Twitch and Lone Ranger.

At the peak of its popularity in the 1980s, Stur Gav fielded the biggest names in dancehall music. Among them were Sugar Minott, Charlie Chaplin, Super Cat, Tenor Saw, Tiger and Early B.

Wake The Town And Tell The People is U Roy’s signature phrase. It is also the title of his most famous song, released in 1970 by producer Duke Reid’s Treasure Isle label.

It marked the toaster’s transition from sound system selector to recording artiste. Wake The Town And Tell The People hears him deejaying to Girl I’ve Got Date, a hit for Reid and singer Ellis four years earlier.

U Roy had similar success toasting The Wailers’ Soul Rebel (as Natty Rebel) and The Paragons’ Wear You To The Ball.

Dionne Beckford, who lives in New York City, says she has been aware of his musical influence since childhood.

“I travelled with him on tours, so I got a bird’s-eye view of what’s going on the international scene with dad. That proved to me that our father was a legend.”

World.title: Leon Bailey to move to Olympiacos — reports
World.content:
In this file photo Reggae Boyz winger Leon Bailey attempts a cross in his AS Roma debut against Inter Milan in the Serie A on Saturday October 18, 2025 at the Stadio Olimpico. .

Reggae Boy Leon Bailey is expected to leave Aston Villa for Greek Club Olympiacos, according to international reports.

The move from the English Premier League club is said to be permanent, with a contract until June 2029. It follows Bailey’s loans from Villa to various clubs, including Roma.

Bailey had several rough, injury-plagued seasons with Villa and did not feature at all for the club this season.

An £8 million Hull City move had been in the works but fell through before the close of the EPL transfer window. Several other clubs had shown interest in the 29-year-old, including Saudi-based Al Ittihad and Diriyah Club.

With over 100 titles across national, regional and youth competitions, Olympiacos is the most successful Greek Club on record and consistently dominates its league.

The club’s home ground is the 33,000-capacity Karaiskakis Stadium, in Piraeus near Athens.

Reports are that Bailey is travelling to Athens for medical testing.

World.title: Farage pledges to slash UK energy bills
World.content:
The cost of energy “represents a national crisis,” Tice said. A cap on energy costs, expressed as the average household's bill and set every quarter by the Ofgem regulator, is set to jump 4 percent next month. The hike is principally driven by the impact of the Middle East conflict on global gas markets.

In a statement, Reform said it will remove charges levied on gas generators, including through the U.K. Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS). The ETS is designed to force down harmful greenhouse gas emissions by the most energy-intensive manufacturers.

The Labour government has made attempts to link emissions trading systems in London and Brussels central to ongoing “reset” talks between the U.K. and EU, arguing that will cut industrial costs and ease trade barriers. Both sides are targeting a deal at the next EU- U.K. summit, expected this fall.

Tice will also pledge to scrap Carbon Price Support (CPS), a tax on power generators introduced by former Conservative Prime Minister David Cameron. The Labour government under Keir Starmer had already pledged to remove CPS costs from bills from 2028.

The party said removing those two levies would shave £90 per year from energy bills.

Reform pledged to scrap other policy costs currently added to household bills, including the remainder of the Renewables Obligation scheme, used to fund legacy net-zero projects. The majority of levies associated with the scheme were shifted into general taxation by former Chancellor Rachel Reeves last year.

World.title: Meta blocks dozens of accounts protesting Kushner-linked Albanian resort project
World.content:
Social media has played a crucial role in the protest, allowing citizens and journalists to report in real time from their own accounts, mobilize protesters, and document scuffles with police. But in the last few weeks, they have found themselves hit with copyright infringement notices, content takedowns, and account suspensions and closures.

Those affected insist they have not violated any of Instagram’s rules, yet received copyright infringement notices for content they filmed or created themselves. Digital rights NGO Repro Uncensored said it has reviewed hundreds of instances and observed no violations of Instagram’s community standards.

“Most cases follow the same pattern: accounts are targeted through repeat copyright infringement reports, and platforms restrict or disable them before establishing whether the claims are legitimate,” says Martha Dimitratou, founder of Repro Uncensored. “Some accounts have been repeatedly targeted, while replacement accounts created after suspension have also been deactivated.”

A Meta spokesperson said in emailed comments that they are reviewing the actions taken against the accounts but have already restored some that were removed by mistake. The parent company of Instagram and Facebook added: “We are sorry for the inconvenience caused,” and noted that Instagram has an appeals process in cases where people think their accounts have been erroneously blocked.

While some users’ access has been restored, others face limits on going live and collaborating with other creators, or experience “shadow bans,” in which their content’s distribution is limited to others, usually without notice.

Agron Shehaj, a member of the Albanian Parliament and the leader of the opposition Mundësia party, had his account disabled on Wednesday evening. “If the rules governing account suspensions and removals are not clear and transparent, the government has every opportunity to extend its censorship into social media, causing potentially irreversible damage to society,” he told POLITICO.

World.title: Germany’s far right gains off VW troubles
World.content:
The far-right Alternative for Germany is blaming the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the EU for VW’s difficulties.

BRUSSELS — Volkswagen’s growing crisis — with the company on Thursday approving factory closures and thousands of layoffs — is turning into political rocket fuel for the far-right Alternative for Germany party ahead of Sunday’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt.

“The end of traditional German car plants is the result of a failed economic and energy policy,” Tino Chrupalla, AfD’s federal spokesperson, said in a statement, putting the blame on the coalition government led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

VW's supervisory board on Thursday approved cost-cutting measures proposed by CEO Oliver Blume, agreeing to cut 50,000 jobs by 2030, to trim the company's product line and to shutter four German factories, the company's most radical domestic cutbacks.

World.title: SpaceX, Blue Origin ditch Macron’s space summit after White House pressure
World.content:
But the event comes at a time of strained relations between Europe and the U.S., including over space policy. Washington has lobbied against the European Commission’s EU Space Act, a proposed rulebook for space activities the U.S. sees as targeting American companies by imposing EU rules on them.

A Franco-German push to allocate more mobile-satellite frequencies to European companies, including the EU’s IRIS² satellite network, is also angering the U.S.

Brussels, Paris and Berlin do not want Europe’s satellite connectivity to depend entirely on Starlink or other U.S. providers. For Washington, however, it looks like another example of the EU using regulation and market access to build European champions at the expense of American companies.

French authorities first tried to downplay the Trump administration’s summit threat, arguing U.S. companies were still welcome.

Despite that effort, six French and space industry officials told POLITICO they were not surprised by what they describe as a classic Trump move. The U.S. administration has repeatedly tried to torpedo multilateral initiatives, ranging from global climate measures to quitting the World Health Organization, while also trying to block any European effort to reduce reliance on U.S. companies.



“This is so typical of Trump,” said a space company official who will be participating in the summit. Like others in this story, they were granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Trump likes to belittle Europeans … and even more Macron, who somehow embodies European ‘leadership.’”



Lackluster attendance by U.S. companies is a short-term blow to the summit and Macron. But several space and French officials stressed it will also energize European efforts to reduce reliance on the U.S.

“The silver lining is we’re diversifying our partnerships around the world, investing in our own space industry. It’s not about uncoupling but looking at what we can do with other partners,” said a space official.



Two space industry officials also told POLITICO that Trump’s boycott will have a limited impact. Even if the four companies skip next week’s summit, the World Space Business Week taking place a week later in Paris is set, for now, to include major American space companies like Starlink and Blue Origin.

World.title: Slovakia rejects EU’s plan to lock in Russia sanctions for 12 months
World.content:
The bloc’s ambassadors could not find common ground on the proposal on Wednesday, with Slovakia being the sole holdout.

“Apparently, they have some objections. I think we have heard them before,” one EU diplomat said. They were granted anonymity to comment freely on the closed-door negotiations.

A spokesperson for the Slovak government declined to comment and shared a statement from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs: “Discussions on the regular six-month review of the sanctions regime … are ongoing and are expected to be concluded by 15 September 2026.”

Talks also touched on adding a further 27 individuals and companies to the sanctions list, freezing their EU assets. Technical experts on sanctions policy will now discuss the changes and extension again.

The law is one of the EU’s two main sanctions frameworks: individual and economic sanctions. Originally, both had to be renewed every six months, but the economic sanctions were extended for 12 months in June, after Orbán left office, and will now remain in force until July 2027.

Nicholas Vinocur contributed to this report.

World.title: ChatGPT soumis à de nouvelles règles européennes aux multiples angles morts
World.content:
Un espace hybride

La législation actuelle sur les services numériques, adoptée en 2022, n’avait pas prévu l’essor des chatbots. João Pedro Quintais, maître de conférences en droit à l’université d’Amsterdam, décrit ChatGPT comme une technologie “hybride” qui combine les fonctions d’un moteur de recherche et d’une plateforme en ligne, ainsi que d’autres fonctions plus proches de celles d’un éditeur de ses propres contenus.

La qualification de “moteur de recherche” pourrait limiter la capacité de la Commission à contrôler la manière dont ChatGPT gère les risques liés non seulement à la santé mentale des adolescents, mais aussi à l’intégrité des élections ou aux contenus illicites.

Demander à ChatGPT de citer les noms des candidats à une élection locale devrait désormais relever du champ d’application du DSA. En revanche, une conversation entre un utilisateur et un chatbot sur le choix du candidat pour lequel voter, au cours de laquelle des informations erronées pourraient être diffusées, pourrait ne pas être concernée.

Il a fallu un peu moins d’un an à la Commission pour finaliser la classification de ce chatbot, ses équipes s’étant heurtées à des difficultés pour déterminer dans quelle catégorie le classer. Selon les experts, sans avoir consulté le texte intégral actant cette classification annoncée cette semaine, il est difficile de savoir exactement quelles seront les obligations d’OpenAI.

La qualification de “plateforme” aurait imposé à OpenAI des obligations supplémentaires en matière de modération des contenus au titre du règlement sur les services numériques, mais elle aurait aussi permis à l’entreprise d’échapper à une part importante de ses responsabilités. Le DSA, comme d’autres législations dans le monde relatives aux plateformes, s’articule autour du principe du “safe harbor”, en vertu duquel les entreprises ne sont pas responsables des contenus présents sur leurs plateformes, ceux-ci étant mis en ligne par les utilisateurs. Mais l’avènement des chatbots soulève la question de savoir si une conversation entre une personne et une machine peut être considérée comme un “contenu généré par les utilisateurs”.

Modèles et risques

Si l’attention portée par les autorités de régulation à ChatGPT en tant qu’application grand public est récente, la Commission surveille de près les modèles d’intelligence artificielle qui la sous-tendent via son règlement sur l’IA (AI Act).

World.title: Document: EU Parliament wants tighter fossil fuel exclusions under sustainable finance rules
World.content:
Parliament and member countries disagree on oil and gas exemptions under the revamped Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation.



BRUSSELS — The European Parliament will push for stricter limits on allowing oil and gas companies to be classed as green investments under the EU’s updated sustainable finance rules, according to a document obtained by POLITICO,

The position will set up a fight with member countries, which want to loosen restrictions on fossil fuel companies under the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation — an EU law that aims to prevent greenwashing to support sustainable investment decisions.

Under the SFDR’s new “transition” category — which covers companies that are switching from dirtier to cleaner business models — lawmakers state that fossil fuel companies should only be included if they invest more in green activities than in new fossil fuel projects over a three-year period.
