According to the TradeReport Telegram channel, Laos’ economy grew by around 4.8% in 2025. Kazakhstan imported $428,000 worth of goods from Laos in January-June 2026, while annual imports have never exceeded $1.4 million.

Logistics emerge as a key area of cooperation

Transport and logistics could offer another avenue to expand bilateral economic ties, with Tokayev highlighting Laos’ transformation from a landlocked country into a potential regional transit link.

“Kazakhstan has the largest transport network in Central Asia and is actively developing the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, which connects China and Europe. Our country handles around 85% of continental freight traffic between China and Europe,” Tokayev said.

He noted that Kazakh terminals operate at the ports of Batumi in Georgia and Lianyungang in China, while Kazakhstan has also launched a logistics hub in Xi’an, China, whose platform could be used by Lao freight carriers.

“We see an opportunity to use our transport corridors to facilitate access for Lao products to Central Asian and European markets. Kazakhstan is interested in expanding its exports to Southeast Asian markets through Laos,” he said.

Tokayev also highlighted the role of the Laos-China railway in strengthening Laos’ transit potential and creating new opportunities to connect ASEAN with China and Europe.

“I propose that our governments work toward concluding relevant intergovernmental and interagency agreements in transport and logistics,” he said.

The Laos-China railway, which began full operations in 2021, has strengthened Laos’ position along regional trade routes and could create opportunities for Kazakhstan to use the country as a gateway to Southeast Asian markets.

Tokayev also invited Lao companies to make greater use of the opportunities offered by the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC).

“The AIFC has become an international platform for doing business and attracting investment. It brings together more than 6,300 registered companies from more than 90 countries, creating a dynamic business environment. Through the AIFC platform, $27 billion in investment has been attracted to Kazakhstan,” Tokayev said.

“For Lao companies, the AIFC can serve as an effective tool for entering the Kazakh market and expanding their presence across Central Asia,” he said.

Longstanding ties

Sisoulith said he had seen firsthand Kazakhstan’s development and the scale of the transformations taking place under Tokayev’s leadership.

“It is a great honor for me to make this official visit to Kazakhstan as president and to meet with you today. I sincerely believe that my visit will make a significant contribution to strengthening bilateral relations. I am confident that during our talks we will be able to discuss a wide range of issues and identify promising areas for cooperation and further joint work,” Sisoulith said.

He highlighted that Kazakhstan has consistently maintained good and stable relations with Laos and has supported the country since its national liberation struggle.

“Regardless of how circumstances have changed, relations between Kazakhstan and Laos, as well as our fraternal ties and mutual goodwill, have remained unchanged. I believe that this visit will contribute to further strengthening and expanding friendly relations between our two countries,” Sisoulith said.

He also emphasized Kazakhstan’s contribution to training specialists for Laos.

“Hundreds of Lao citizens have received their education and graduated from educational institutions in Kazakhstan. Today, many of them work in public service, run businesses or hold senior positions at the national and local levels. They all remember Kazakhstan warmly for the support and assistance they received during their studies,” Sisoulith said.

Tokayev and Sisoulith also discussed cooperation in culture, humanitarian affairs and tourism, as well as opportunities to strengthen ties between higher education institutions.

The two countries also exchanged several intergovernmental documents in the presence of the two heads of state, covering political consultations, law enforcement, digital development and cooperation between their capitals.

World.title: Kazakhstan Signs Contract For Construction Of First Nuclear Power Plant
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has signed a contract to design, supply and build its first nuclear power plant, moving the long-planned project into a new practical phase as the country seeks to strengthen energy security and prepare for growing electricity demand.

The contract was signed between Kazakhstan Nuclear Power Plants and Atomstroyexport, a subsidiary of Russia’s Rosatom state nuclear corporation, on the sidelines of the 11th Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.

The signing was attended by Chairman of Kazakhstan’s Atomic Energy Agency Almasadam Satkaliyev and Rosatom Director General Alexei Likhachev.

The agreement marks a significant step in Kazakhstan’s plans to introduce nuclear generation into its energy mix. However, the project has not yet reached the final implementation stage. Under the intergovernmental agreement signed on May 28, 2026, the parties will continue the required procedures, including the necessary approval by the Kazakh government.

From political decision to construction project

The contract moves the first nuclear power plant project beyond early site selection and political decision-making toward detailed implementation. Kazakhstan approved the construction of a nuclear power plant through a national referendum in October 2024. The project is planned for the Zhambyl district of the Almaty Region, with construction expected to take about eight years.

Rosatom was selected from a shortlist that also included China National Nuclear Corporation, France’s EDF and Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power.

Rising electricity demand puts energy security at the center

The government sees nuclear power as a response to a structural increase in electricity demand. Kazakhstan’s economy, industrial production and infrastructure are expanding, while digitalization and the development of artificial intelligence are creating additional demand for stable electricity supplies. Unlike intermittent renewable sources, nuclear power is designed to provide continuous baseload generation.

Globally, nuclear energy supplies nearly 10% of electricity generation and around 20% in advanced economies, according to the International Energy Agency. With global nuclear capacity approaching 413 gigawatts across 32 countries, nuclear power remains a major source of low-carbon electricity.

The IEA estimates that nuclear power currently prevents around 1.5 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide emissions and 180 billion cubic meters of gas demand each year. For Kazakhstan, the attraction of nuclear generation is therefore twofold: it could provide additional stable capacity while supporting the country’s longer-term efforts to reduce the carbon intensity of its power sector.

At the same time, nuclear power is not a substitute for renewable energy. The IEA has emphasized that nuclear and renewable generation can complement each other as countries seek to decarbonize their electricity systems. For Kazakhstan, which has significant wind and solar potential, the final energy model will likely depend on how nuclear generation is integrated with existing thermal plants and the expanding renewable sector.

The bigger opportunity may be industrial

The economic significance of the project could extend beyond electricity generation. The Atomic Energy Agency has emphasized localization as a priority, aiming to involve Kazakh companies, specialists, goods, works and services as extensively as possible in the construction process.

This is particularly important because a nuclear power plant is a highly complex industrial project. Its supply chain requires specialized equipment, engineering expertise, safety systems and technical standards. Building those capabilities domestically could give Kazakhstan an industrial base for future nuclear projects and related activities. The government has said the first plant should help create national competencies and a personnel reserve for the further development of the nuclear sector.

Uranium producer seeks a larger role in nuclear energy

Kazakhstan enters the nuclear era from an unusual position: it is the world’s leading uranium producer but does not currently generate electricity from nuclear power. That creates an opportunity to connect the country’s existing position in the global uranium industry with a domestic nuclear energy value chain.

The first power plant could become the foundation for a broader nuclear-energy cluster, particularly if Kazakhstan proceeds with its stated plans to build three nuclear power plants.

The government has described the project as part of Kazakhstan’s efforts to strengthen energy independence and technological sovereignty. Those goals will ultimately be measured not only by the plant’s completion but by what Kazakhstan can build around it.

A successful project could provide reliable baseload electricity, support industrial growth, create specialized jobs and help establish domestic nuclear competencies. It could also give Kazakhstan greater flexibility as it balances rising electricity demand with decarbonization goals.

For a country already in a leading position in the global uranium industry, the first nuclear power plant could mark a shift from primarily supplying nuclear raw materials to producing nuclear energy.

World.title: Kazakhstan Forms New Government With Majority Of Ministers Retaining Posts
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has formed a new government, with most ministers retaining their positions while several key ministries received new heads, according to presidential decrees and orders.

Mukhtar Tileuberdi was appointed Minister of Foreign Affairs, returning to the position he held from 2019 to 2023. Before the appointment, he served as Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Austria and Permanent Representative of Kazakhstan to International Organizations in Vienna. He replaced Yermek Kosherbayev, who had headed the Foreign Ministry since September 2025.

Several ministries have received new leadership

Murat Mukhanov was appointed Minister of Emergency Situations, replacing Chingiz Arinov. Mukhanov previously headed the Mangystau Region Department of Emergency Situations and later served as chief of staff of the Ministry of Emergency Situations.

Alibek Kuantyrov was appointed Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources, replacing Yerlan Nyssanbayev. Since 2024, Kuantyrov had served as Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs. He previously headed the Ministry of National Economy.

Arman Kyrykbayev was appointed Minister of Culture and Information, replacing Aida Balayeva.

Several members of the government retained their positions

Dauren Kosanov was reappointed Minister of Defense, while Yerzhan Sadenov was reappointed Minister of Internal Affairs. Madi Takiyev will continue as Minister of Finance, Nurlan Sauranbayev as Minister of Transport, Yerlan Akkenzhenov as Minister of Energy, and Yersaiyn Nagaspayev as Minister of Industry and Construction.

Arman Shakkaliyev was reappointed Minister of Trade and Integration, while Yerlan Sarsembayev will continue to head the Ministry of Justice. Zhuldyz Suleimenova retained the post of Minister of Education, Akmaral Alnazarova will continue as Minister of Health, and Nurzhan Nurzhigitov will remain Minister of Water Resources and Irrigation.

Askarbek Yertayev was reappointed Minister of Labor and Social Protection of the Population, Aydarbek Saparov will continue as Minister of Agriculture, Yerbol Myrzabosynov as Minister of Tourism and Sports, and Sayasat Nurbek as Minister of Science and Higher Education.

Galymzhan Koishybayev was appointed Deputy Prime Minister and Chief of Staff of the government. Serik Zhumangarin was appointed Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy, while Zhaslan Madiyev was appointed Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development. Nurlybek Naliyev was reappointed First Deputy Prime Minister, while Kanat Bozumbayev was appointed Deputy Prime Minister.

Tokayev also made several appointments outside the ministerial posts. Yermek Abdramanov was appointed Deputy Head of the Presidential Administration. Murat Kaiyrbek was appointed Head of the Presidential Representative Office in the Kurultai of Kazakhstan.

World.title: Experts: Productivity, Not GDP Rankings, Will Define Kazakhstan as GDP Nears $469 Billion
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s nominal gross domestic product could reach $468.8 billion by 2030, potentially placing the country among the world’s 45 largest economies. But economists say the more important question is whether the expansion reflects stronger productivity, diversification and investment rather than simply larger nominal output.

The projection, based on International Monetary Fund (IMF) data, puts Kazakhstan’s economy within reach of a new group of economies approaching or exceeding $500 billion in annual output.

Economist Ruslan Sultanov, author of the Tengenomika Telegram channel, said that the ranking itself should not be treated as the main measure of economic success.

“The main indicator of success should be the quality of this growth. Productivity, real incomes and well-being are more important than a place in the ranking: economic scale acquires meaning when the standard of living rises alongside it,” Sultanov wrote.

A separate long-term projection by Goldman Sachs places Kazakhstan among the world’s 30 largest economies by 2075, with a projected GDP of about $2.1 trillion. Almas Issayev, an oil and gas industry professional with more than a decade of project management experience at Tengizchevroil, said in his LinkedIn post that a $2–3 trillion economy by 2075 could be within Kazakhstan’s reach, supported by population growth, continued energy revenues, reinvestment, innovation and the country’s position as a Eurasian transport hub.

Kazakhstan enters a new economic bracket

The IMF-based projection estimates Kazakhstan’s nominal GDP at $468.8 billion in 2030, roughly $100 billion more than its current level. At that size, Kazakhstan would rank around 45th globally and would be close to economies approaching the $500 billion threshold.

Nigeria is projected at $464.8 billion, while Portugal is estimated at $444.9 billion, Peru at $437.1 billion and Finland at $388.6 billion. The next group is already close to the half-trillion mark. Chile is projected at $496.8 billion, while the Czech Republic could reach $506.8 billion.

The comparison illustrates Kazakhstan’s potential movement into a larger economic category. But the country would not be moving into a static ranking: other emerging markets are also expected to expand significantly over the same period.

A larger world economy raises the bar

The global economy is projected to exceed $150 trillion in nominal GDP by 2030. The United States is expected to remain the world’s largest economy, with GDP of about $37.7 trillion, equivalent to around 25.1% of global output. China is projected at $26 trillion, while Germany and India are expected to be almost equal at approximately $6.18 trillion and $6.17 trillion, respectively.

The United Kingdom is projected at $5.14 trillion, Japan at $5 trillion, France at $4 trillion, Brazil at $3.2 trillion, Italy at $3.04 trillion, and Canada at $3 trillion.

At the same time, several emerging economies are expected to gain weight. Indonesia could surpass $2 trillion, while Türkiye is projected to approach that level. The Philippines, Bangladesh, Malaysia and Vietnam are also expected to enter the group of the world’s 35 largest economies.

For Kazakhstan, this means that growing in absolute terms will not necessarily translate into gaining economic influence relative to other countries. The country will have to boost productivity and competitiveness while competing with economies undergoing their own rapid expansion.

The bigger question is the quality of growth

A larger nominal GDP can expand the domestic market, increase investment capacity and strengthen a country’s economic weight. But GDP rankings say relatively little about how the benefits of growth are distributed or whether living standards are improving. Sultanov therefore places greater emphasis on the composition of future growth.

For Kazakhstan, the critical indicators will include productivity, the development of domestic production, the emergence of more sophisticated industries and the growth of private investment. Another consideration is how much additional domestic demand the domestic economy captures.

“Pursuing growth solely through quantitative measures can increase nominal GDP, but it will have a significantly smaller impact on the economy if the additional demand is directed towards imports, prices, or investments with low returns,” Sultanov wrote.

This makes the transition from resource-driven growth to productivity-driven growth particularly important.

The 2075 question

Goldman Sachs’ The Path to 2075 projection places Kazakhstan among the world’s top 30 economies by 2075, with GDP of about $2.1 trillion. Reaching that level would require a much longer time horizon than the expansion projected for 2030.

Issayev notes that several structural factors could support such growth, beginning with demographics. According to him, Kazakhstan’s energy sector could bridge the resource-based economy of today and a more diversified economy in the future.

For Kazakhstan, the central challenge will be to use its resource revenues, demographic potential and geographic position to build productive capacity that remains competitive as the global economy changes.

“Economic scale acquires meaning when the standard of living rises alongside it,” Sultanov wrote.

In this sense, reaching half a trillion dollars would be a significant milestone, but not an endpoint. The more consequential question is whether each additional dollar of GDP represents greater domestic value creation, higher productivity, stronger private investment and rising real incomes.

World.title: Kazakhstan Set to Join Digital Cooperation Organization as Membership Expands to 24 Countries
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is set to join the Digital Cooperation Organization (DCO) as a new Member State, opening opportunities for greater cooperation in digital technologies, AI, innovation and digital trade.

The DCO, the world’s first standalone international organization dedicated to accelerating the inclusive and sustainable growth of the digital economy, announced on Aug. 28 that its Council had approved Kazakhstan’s candidature alongside seven other countries.

The move could expand the DCO’s membership from 16 to 24 countries, representing approximately 980 million people, or around 12% of the global population, according to the DCO.

Alongside Kazakhstan, the approved candidate countries are Albania, Azerbaijan, Kenya, Lebanon, Palestine, Syria and Zambia. Tajikistan will join the organization as an Associate Member.

Kazakhstan’s prospective accession would mark the DCO’s first expansion into Central Asia and create a new regional axis for digital cooperation. The organization said the move reflects growing international interest in cooperation on digital policy, artificial intelligence, cross-border data flows, digital public infrastructure and digital skills.

“The rules of the digital economy on data, artificial intelligence, and cross-border trade are being written now, and rules written without you are rules you inherit rather than shape,” said DCO Secretary-General Deemah AlYahya.

The approval of candidature begins the formal accession process. Kazakhstan’s membership will take effect after it completes its internal accession procedures and deposits its instrument of accession in line with the DCO’s founding documents.

The DCO was established in 2020 and currently brings together 16 countries, representing more than 800 million people. Its agenda focuses on promoting digital inclusion, innovation, entrepreneurship and cooperation in the digital economy.

World.title: Kazakhstan Expands Mineral Exploration, But Experts Say Discovery – Only First Step
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is expanding geological exploration, increasing geological knowledge and identifying new mineral resources, but experts say the key challenge is no longer simply discovering what lies beneath the country’s vast territory. It is turning geological potential into economically viable projects, investment, production and higher-value exports.

The government is increasing the detail of geological surveys, digitizing decades of accumulated geological information and introducing Big Data and artificial intelligence tools. But geological discovery is only the first step in a much longer process.

“An identified resource is primarily confirmation of the presence of certain mineralization. But this is not enough for an investor,” said Qanat Qudaibergen, chairman of the board of GWM Capital, in a conversation with the Astana Times.

From geological discovery to an investment decision

Kazakhstan is increasing the scale and detail of geological studies as part of efforts to strengthen the country’s mineral-resource base. Geological and geophysical exploration at a scale of 1:200,000 currently covers about 2.04 million square kilometers. The government plans to increase this figure to 2.2 million square kilometers in 2026.

At the same time, the country has begun 20 projects involving more detailed geological mapping at a scale of 1:50,000. The projects will cover 100,000 square kilometers and focus on areas considered prospective for gold, copper, polymetals, rare and rare-earth metals, lithium, tungsten and molybdenum.

Qudaibergen said that a significant amount of work remains between identifying a resource and making an investment decision. Infrastructure is another critical factor, he said, including electricity, water, roads, railway logistics and access to qualified personnel.

“Only after passing all these stages is it possible to speak about a full-fledged investment decision, financing and construction,” Qudaibergen said, highlighting that this distinction is important when assessing the results of geological exploration.

Askar Ismailov, an oil and gas industry expert, made a similar distinction, noting that geological exploration can produce several different levels of information.

“It is very important not to confuse three completely different things: a geological anomaly, a resource and an economically recoverable reserve,” he said.

According to him, a report that geologists have identified a prospective area or estimated forecast resources in millions of tons does not mean that Kazakhstan has automatically obtained a deposit worth billions of dollars.

New resources expand the base, but do not automatically create new production

Kazakhstan has also recorded an increase in its mineral-resource base following geological exploration. The 54 newly registered deposits over the two years were accompanied by growth in resources and reserves across several commodities.

Kazakhstan currently has around 10,000 deposits of various mineral resources on the state register. Yet the scale of the resource base does not necessarily translate into an equivalent number of new mines or industrial projects.

Qudaibergen said that a more meaningful measure of exploration success would be how many newly identified objects eventually progress from geological discovery to internationally recognized resources and reserves, financing, construction and commercial production.

Critical minerals create a window of opportunity

The growing global demand for critical minerals gives Kazakhstan an additional opportunity to turn its geological potential into a broader industrial role. The country is exploring for lithium, tungsten, molybdenum, rare and rare-earth metals, and other strategic resources. Research has already been completed at 11 sites included in the geological exploration program.

The Kuiraktykol site in the Karagandy Region has been identified as particularly promising, with high forecast concentrations of lanthanum, cerium, neodymium and yttrium. Total forecast resources across the sites amount to 935,400 tons. At the Irgiz area, C2-category reserves have additionally been estimated at 795,800 tons.

Developing these resources could be important for Kazakhstan’s industrial diversification, but Qudaibergen cautioned against equating the presence of critical minerals with a strong position in global value chains.

“Competition today is no longer so much for ore as for control over the entire chain: deposit-beneficiation-metallurgy-chemical processing-materials-components-final products,” he said.

For Kazakhstan, this raises a strategic question: where along these chains can the country create competitive advantages rather than simply export concentrates?

“At the same time, I am not a proponent of the approach that requires us to produce a final product from every mined mineral within Kazakhstan. This is not always economically justified,” he said.

The untapped potential above ground

Qudaibergen also pointed to a less conventional component of Kazakhstan’s mineral potential: resources already accumulated on the surface. These include beneficiation tailings, metallurgical slag, cakes and sludges, ash and slag from power generation and other industrial waste.

Many of these materials accumulated decades ago, when extraction technologies were less efficient, and some rare and rare-earth metals were not considered target products.

“What was historically considered waste can today, with new technologies, prices and the changing structure of global demand, in some cases be regarded as secondary mineral raw material,” he said.

This could create an additional avenue for developing critical-mineral production without opening new mines while also addressing accumulated environmental liabilities.

Oil exploration faces a different question

The challenge of converting geological potential into production is particularly important for oil, where Kazakhstan is simultaneously planning a major expansion of domestic refining capacity. The country is targeting a total oil-processing capacity of about 40 million tons per year through the expansion of the Pavlodar, Shymkent and Atyrau refineries and the construction of another refinery with capacity of around 10 million tons, according to Ismailov.

That creates a different set of requirements for geological exploration: the country needs to understand not only how much oil may exist underground, but how much production can realistically be made available to domestic refineries over the long term.

“Today a significant part of crude oil is exported. With 40 million tons of annual refining, a large guaranteed domestic market for crude emerges, which is currently not fully secured by the resource base,” Ismailov said.

One possible option would be to negotiate additional supplies from large oil projects such as Tengiz and Kashagan. Ismailov, however, considers this approach less promising and argues that greater attention should be given to exploration and the development of new reserves.

For geological exploration, this means linking long-term resource planning with the expected production profile of existing fields and future domestic demand.

Digital geology seeks to connect data with investment

Digitalization is becoming another key part of the transformation. The Unified Subsoil Management Platform now contains a map of Kazakhstan’s subsoil use, with 66,100 first volumes of geological reports linked to 109,500 study contours.

More than 4.8 million units of primary geological information have also been digitized, including about 4.3 million paper sheets, 355,000 graphic attachments, 97,000 magnetic tapes and 62,000 cartridges.

One important step in connecting data with investment is Kazakhstan’s transition toward international standards for reporting mineral resources and reserves. According to Qudaibergen, the KAZRC system is aligned with the CRIRSCO family of international reporting standards. This makes geological information more comparable with projects in major mining jurisdictions and can help investors, banks and mining companies assess the quality and economic potential of Kazakh projects.

“Essentially, we are beginning to speak to the global investment community in one professional language,” Qudaibergen said.

The next test is conversion, not discovery

Kazakhstan is entering a new phase of geological development in which the quantity of information is growing alongside the sophistication of the tools used to analyze it. The country is mapping larger areas, conducting more detailed surveys, expanding its mineral-resource base, digitizing geological archives and exploring the potential of critical minerals and technogenic resources.

For Qudaibergen, Kazakhstan has a strong starting position because of its large territory, established geological expertise and significant underexplored potential. Modern geophysics, remote sensing, large-scale data processing and AI can allow previously studied territories to be examined in new ways.

“If this opportunity is used correctly, Kazakhstan has the potential to become not just a major supplier of mineral resources, but one of the key centers for critical minerals and materials for global industry,” he said.

World.title: Kazakhstan Marks First Kazakh Tazy Day
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is celebrating Kazakh Tazy Day for the first time on Sept. 3, commemorating the anniversary of the breed’s preliminary recognition by the Fédération Cynologique Internationale (FCI) in 2024, reported the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources.

The FCI made the decision in Amsterdam on Sept. 3, 2024, granting preliminary recognition to the Kazakh tazy and officially recognizing Kazakhstan as the breed’s country of origin.

The tazy has lived alongside people in the Great Steppe for centuries, serving as a hunting companion and becoming an important part of Kazakh culture and daily life. Its place in Kazakh tradition is also reflected in the FCI breed standard, which refers to the tazy as one of the Zheti Kazyna (Seven Treasures) of the Kazakh people.

From national heritage to international recognition

Efforts to preserve and promote the breed gained momentum in recent years. In 2022, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev instructed the government to take measures to preserve the national breed and promote it internationally.

A major step came Aug. 22, 2023, when the Union of Cynologists of Kazakhstan became a full member of the FCI at the federation’s General Assembly in Geneva. The membership enabled the country to formally submit the tazy for international recognition. In March 2024, Kazakhstan submitted documentation on the breed to the FCI.

The same year, Astana hosted a specialized breed exhibition where international experts examined 100 Kazakh tazy of various ages, colors, origins and types. The dogs were evaluated for their physical structure, movement and compliance with the breed standard.

In an interview with The Astana Times, FCI President Tamás Jakkel praised Kazakhstan’s progress and said a long-term program is now underway to achieve full recognition.

“We have outlined a program for the next several years to reach final recognition. I offered my support and partnership, and we agreed to continue cooperation,” he said.

Jakkel noted that the issue has broad public relevance given the large number of households that own dogs.

Preserving the breed through science

Preliminary recognition is only one stage of the process. The tazy must undergo a lengthy observation period during which the stability of the breed is assessed across several generations. This includes monitoring pedigree records, health, genetic diversity, breed characteristics and natural and working abilities.

Kazakhstan has also established its first DNA bank for the tazy and tobet, another national dog breed. The initiative follows several years of nationwide genetic research aimed at preserving the breeds’ genetic heritage and preventing genetic loss.

According to Anastasia Perfilyeva, a biology researcher at the Institute of Genetics and Physiology, genetic analysis confirmed that the tazy is an ancient, independent breed.

Researchers also found that the tobet developed at the intersection of Arctic and East Asian dog lineages and is genetically distinct from more than 140 dog breeds worldwide, including other guardian breeds.

Today, nearly 4,000 tazy are registered in the Union of Cynologists of Kazakhstan’s unified pedigree book. The actual population is believed to be higher because many dogs in rural and remote areas have yet to be included in centralized records.

Specialists continue working across the regions to conduct breeding assessments, document pedigrees and monitor the breed’s genetic diversity.

In 2025, The tazy received a patent from National Institute of Intellectual Property Qazpatent.

Tazy gains global visibility

Alongside scientific and breeding work, Kazakhstan has stepped up efforts to promote the tazy internationally.

The breed made its official debut at the World Dog Show in Helsinki in 2025.

In June 2026, Kazakhstan presented 12 tazy at the World Dog Show in Bologna. The breed was also showcased to international judges during the FCI World Judges Congress. A national pavilion introduced visitors to the tazy and Kazakhstan’s traditions and culture.

The breed has also featured in high-profile diplomatic and cultural exchanges. Tokayev has previously gifted Kazakh tazy dogs to French President Emmanuel Macron and renowned Kazakh singer Dimash Qudaibergen, drawing further attention to the breed as a symbol of the country’s national heritage.

The Kazakh tazy was also included for the first time in “Dogs of the World,” a book by U.S. illustrator Lili Chin featuring more than 600 dog breeds.

“I remember seeing a video from Kazakhstan of tazy dogs hunting a wolf. They were incredibly fast and worked as a team. I love that tazy are valued not only as hunters but also as beloved companions and family dogs,” Chin told The Astana Times.

Kazakhstan is also expanding infrastructure for the preservation and development of its national dog breeds. A National Center for Kazakh Dog Breeds is under construction in the Zhetysu Region. The facility will support breeding programs, maintain the national pedigree registry, train cynology specialists and host exhibitions, trials and competitions.

The next stage will be particularly important for the tazy. Full FCI recognition will depend on demonstrating the breed’s stability over several generations while preserving its distinctive characteristics, genetic diversity and working qualities.

World.title: ‘If Russia decides to withdraw its military base, we will not object’ – Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on the withdrawal of Russia’s military base from Armenia.

“If Russia decides to withdraw its military base from Armenia, we will not object. But if they want to stay, we are ready to discuss that too,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said during his regular weekly briefing.

He also said Yerevan does not consider the presence of Russia’s 102nd military base in Armenia vital.

Putin raised the issue after his meeting with Pashinyan in Bishkek, although the Armenian prime minister says they did not discuss the issue either during those talks or before them. Putin said:

“If Armenia believes that Russia’s military base is not needed in Armenia, we will leave tomorrow if necessary. Is Armenia ready for that? Fine, we will not impose anything on anyone. But if the Armenian people want some kind of Russian military ‘wing’ there, we will stay. We will work and cooperate.”

Pashinyan also commented at the briefing on the issues he discussed with Putin in Bishkek. In particular, he once again explained Armenia’s position on its membership in the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union, Russia’s concession to operate Armenia’s railways and the construction of a new nuclear power plant.

Armenia cannot be forced to hold a referendum

“And who said that all EAEU member states swore allegiance and would remain members of the EAEU for their entire existence?”

That was Pashinyan’s answer to a question about Armenia’s membership in the Russian-led EAEU. He gave it among the first answers at the briefing. The issue also dominated the open part of the Pashinyan-Putin talks.

For several months, Russia has been calling at various levels for Armenia to hold a referendum on membership of the EAEU or the European Union. The Russian president also insisted on this at the meeting in Bishkek.

“The adoption of the law to begin Armenia’s accession to another organisation amounts to a declaration that it is leaving ours,”* Putin said.

Pashinyan explained to the Russian president, and repeated at the briefing, that under the union’s charter, a country must give six months’ notice before ending its membership. However, Armenia has no such intention for now.

He said he continues to explain this to his Russian partners, trying to make Armenia’s position “clearer and more acceptable”.

One journalist who raised the issue described Putin’s tone towards Pashinyan as “harsh”. He said Moscow was taking a tough line and forcing Yerevan to choose between the EAEU and the EU. Armenia’s prime minister replied:

“I am also giving the Russian president a tough choice. I say: this cannot continue, the issue of the railway concession must be resolved. Why is there no headline saying ‘Pashinyan gives Russian president a tough choice’?”

Pashinyan himself believes Armenian media do not use such headlines because the country still follows the “logic of subordination to the Central Committee of the USSR”. In his view, that logic produces the following reaction: “They called from Moscow, we urgently need to bring out the cognac.”

At the same time, the prime minister stressed his position: Armenia cannot be forced to hold a referendum.

He said the country’s Constitution requires a referendum before joining a supranational organisation. However, Armenia should hold one only when the issue “is ripe”. This would mean, in particular, when Armenia applies for EU membership or at least sets out its roadmap. Holding a referendum before that, he argued, would mean asking citizens to go to polling stations before anyone has formulated the question or decided what answers they can choose.

Selling the railway concession is the best solution

Pashinyan said he discussed the future of South Caucasus Railway with Putin. This issue is, incidentally, more important to the Armenian side. For a long time, Armenia’s authorities have been telling their Russian partners that the country is losing its competitive advantage in developing regional railway links because Russia controls the Armenian railway.

Since 2008, the company South Caucasus Railway has operated Armenia’s railway under a concession agreement. Russian Railways owns 100% of the company. The agreement grants the concession for 30 years. However, since 2008, freight traffic on Armenia’s railways has halved, some routes have stopped operating, and the investment commitments have remained unfulfilled.

The Armenian prime minister therefore proposed selling the concession to a third country that is friendly to both Armenia and Russia. Russian partners described the proposal as “strange and largely unacceptable”.

However, Pashinyan said the following about the outcome of his meeting with Putin:

“We reached an understanding that the current situation cannot continue for much longer. We need to resolve this issue somehow. Both Armenia and Russia understand that one possible solution would be to sell the concession rights to a third party acceptable to both Armenia and Russia. Frankly, I think this is the best solution. The other options seem unrealistic.”».

Moscow to present proposals for building a new nuclear power plant

According to Pashinyan, Rosatom CEO Alexei Likhachev will visit Armenia in September.

“He will present Armenia with proposals on what Russia can offer today for the construction of a new nuclear power plant. I have already said that we do not see the nuclear power plant as a geopolitical choice. We need the best value for money. We will go with whoever makes the best offer,” the prime minister said.

He said Armenia would consider all possible options, whether a small modular reactor proposed by Western partners or a conventional Russian nuclear power plant:

“We have never said that the Russian proposal cannot be the best one, including in terms of modular reactors. It is not the case that Russia has no proposal for modular reactors. However, there are a number of important factors: the price, the payback period, the construction time and the financing arrangements.”

Nikol Pashinyan said work on the issue had intensified and that Armenia should make a decision within a year.

He said Armenia initially favoured a small modular reactor, but “desire is one thing and reality is another”.

The problem is that experts are concerned about the lack of experience in building modular nuclear power plants and the potential risks.

According to the prime minister, if there are no operating or licensed modular nuclear power plants anywhere in the world when Armenia makes its decision, this will create “uncertainty” and make the decision very difficult.

At the same time, he said work was continuing to extend the operating life of the existing Metsamor nuclear power plant beyond 2036.

No plans to introduce visas for Russian citizens

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said that “if Armenia suddenly introduces visas as well, it will not introduce them against us — it will introduce them against its own citizens”. She also said the move would affect Russian citizens who have relatives in Armenia.

Importantly, no one in Armenia had suggested introducing a visa regime for Russian citizens before her statement.

“We have absolutely no such intention, and never have. It has never even crossed our minds. We are very happy to welcome tourists from Russia. We can see that they have now become very active in promoting Armenia’s tourism attractions. Society also welcomes these people. And they themselves seem to feel quite comfortable in Armenia. We are happy to have them, just as we are happy to welcome tourists from other countries,” the prime minister said.

Pashinyan on the withdrawal of Russia’s military base from Armenia

World.title: Georgian politicians questioned after ex-prime minister’s claims about Lazare Jorbenadze’s death
World.content:
Death of Georgian human rights defender Lazare Jorbenadze

Georgian politicians have been summoned for questioning over public statements by former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili about the death of Lazare Jorbenadze.

According to the Georgian Prosecutor’s Office, investigators have confirmed the suicide theory without ambiguity following investigative work into Jorbenadze’s death on 4 April 2026 and interviews with members of his family.

Nevertheless, because convicted former prime minister Irakli Garibashvili and others have made public statements about the case, investigators will question several political figures further: Irakli Garibashvili himself, Nika Gvaramia, Irma Inashvili, Nanuka Zhorzholiani, Khatia Dekanoidze, Tazo Datunashvili, Gia Khukhashvili, Giorgi Liluashvili, Zaza Davitaia and Ermile Nemsadze.

What happened

On 1 September 2026, former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili published another letter from prison. He called on the authorities to answer questions about the circumstances surrounding the death of Lazare Jorbenadze, a human rights defender who had criticised Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze.

Garibashvili writes that Jorbenadze died by suicide shortly after journalist Dito Chubinidze published an article based on an interview with him.

The newspaper Asaval-Dasavali, which published the interview, questioned the suicide theory. In his letter, Garibashvili stresses that the public should receive an answer about the true cause of Jorbenadze’s death.

The former prime minister says he decided to speak publicly about the issue after comparing the contents of a letter he received from government representatives in February with other circumstances.



Lazare Jorbenadze

According to Garibashvili, on 12 February, officials acting on the instructions of Irakli Kobakhidze and Deputy Prime Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze gave him an article that the newspaper Asaval-Dasavali had published on 2 February 2026.

The article featured a conversation between Dito Chubinidze and Lazare Jorbenadze. Garibashvili says it focused mainly on criticism of Kobakhidze and serious allegations against him.

The former prime minister says the message he received suggested that he was behind the article. “I received a message expressing the suspicion — based on a completely false assumption — that I was behind the article in question,” Garibashvili writes.

Garibashvili says he categorically rejected the accusation and told government representatives that he had never engaged in publishing “commissioned articles”.

What do politicians say?

Khatia Dekanoidze, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, said she would appear in court to testify in the Lazare Jorbenadze case. She said Bidzina Ivanishvili bears responsibility for the system he created, so investigators should question him as well.

“Bidzina Ivanishvili created a system in which people fight for positions and money, testify against each other, fabricate cases and, of course, are deeply involved in corruption. That is why Bidzina Ivanishvili, Kobakhidze, Mdinaradze and everyone who fabricates all sorts of dirt for money should be summoned for questioning. As for the investigation itself, I have made my position clear: I will go to court,” Dekanoidze said.

Political analyst Gia Khukhashvili said he did not understand why authorities had summoned him for questioning in the Lazare Jorbenadze death case, as he had made no specific statements about Jorbenadze and only learned of his existence after his death.

“I only learned of Jorbenadze’s existence after his death. I did not comment specifically on the situation involving Jorbenadze. I spoke more broadly about suicide cases that raise questions. Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze should be here instead of me, because Garibashvili named them, but they are not being summoned — I am. And now this has turned into nothing more than a tragicomedy,” Khukhashvili commented.

According to Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Coalition for Change, investigators did not ask him about any other subjects during his questioning in the Jorbenadze death case. Gvaramia believes the case may serve two purposes: one could be political propaganda, while the other could involve bringing new charges against the former prime minister.

“The next step, I am sure, will be to bring new charges against Garibashvili, under the article concerning illegal wiretapping. As far as I know, investigators are currently questioning him in prison. Mdinaradze and Kobakhidze should themselves be concerned about such allegations if they are true, although Garibashvili should also provide further explanations,” Gvaramia said after the questioning.

Death of Georgian human rights defender Lazare Jorbenadze

World.title: Social assistance is shrinking in Azerbaijan: Is poverty falling, or are low-income people losing support?
World.content:
Targeted social assistance in Azerbaijan

In Azerbaijan, the authorities have raised the income threshold for classifying families as low-income. It would be logical to expect this to increase both the number of people receiving assistance and the amount of support they receive. However, official statistics show the opposite trend: both the number of families receiving targeted state social assistance and the amount paid per person are falling.

According to the State Statistics Committee, as of 1 July, 349,300 people from 78,900 families received targeted social assistance. A year earlier, the system covered 353,300 people from 80,300 families. This means that over the year, the number of families receiving assistance fell by 1,400, while the number of recipients fell by 4,000.

The decline becomes even more striking over the longer term. In mid-2017, 498,400 people received this type of assistance. Over nine years, that figure fell by 149,100, or about 30%. Meanwhile, the country’s population increased during the same period.

These figures raise an important question: have the incomes of low-income families increased enough for them to no longer need social assistance, or has the system stopped reaching some people who still need support?

The income threshold has risen, but social assistance has fallen

Targeted social assistance is not a fixed payment. The authorities calculate it as the difference between the needs-based threshold for all family members and the family’s average monthly income. The calculation takes into account income from the previous 12 months.

In 2025, the needs-based threshold stood at 285 manats (approx. $167.65) per person. In 2026, the authorities raised it to 300 manats (approx. $176.50), an increase of 5.3%. Despite this, the average payment per person fell from 100.37 to 97.94 manats (approx. $59 to $57.70). In nominal terms, the payment fell by 2.43 manats (approx. $1.43), or 2.4%.

Applying the current formula to the average figures suggests that the system calculated recipients’ average monthly income per person at 184.63 manats (approx. $108.60) in 2025 and 202.06 manats (approx. $118.90) in 2026. This represents a nominal increase of 9.4%. Mathematically, the lower payments reflect the fact that, according to the system’s calculations, family incomes grew faster than the needs-based threshold.

However, these figures do not prove that the financial situation of all low-income families has improved. The average for families that remained in the system in mid-2026 is being compared with the average for families that received assistance a year earlier. Families whose payments stopped or whose applications were rejected no longer form part of the new average.

Our calculations, based on official data, show that total monthly payments to recipients fell from about 35.46 million (approx. $20.86 million) to 34.21 million manats (approx. $20.12 million). The government therefore reduced its monthly spending on this group by about 1.25 million manats (approx. $735,300), or 3.5%, in nominal terms.

The assistance has lost even more purchasing power

According to July 2026 data, annual inflation stood at 5.8%, while food inflation reached 7.3%. After taking price rises into account, the purchasing power of the 97.94-manat payment fell by about 7.8% compared with the 100.37-manat payment a year earlier. If we consider only food price increases, the decline approaches 9%.

After receiving assistance, the system brings a family’s calculated income per person up to the needs-based threshold of 300 manats. However, this represents only a 5.3% increase from last year’s level of 285 manats. That increase falls short of overall inflation and especially of food price growth. As a result, even the minimum income of families that remain in the social assistance system has not increased in real terms.

The number of people receiving assistance is not the number of people living in poverty

The State Statistics Committee’s final data for 2025 put the poverty line at 286 manats (approx. $168.20) and the poverty rate at 5.2%. With a population of 10.26 million, this amounts to roughly 534,000 people.

At the end of the same year, 336,000 people received targeted social assistance, or about 3.3% of the population. The authorities use different methodologies and reporting dates to calculate these figures, so we cannot directly compare them. Nevertheless, the gap of about 198,000 people clearly shows that the number of assistance recipients cannot serve as a measure of poverty in the country.

Moreover, earning less than 300 manats does not in itself qualify a person for assistance. Under the rules, a family must show that factors beyond its control have caused its low income. The official criteria allow authorities to reject an application if the family owns or uses a car, has two properties of the same type at different addresses, or has carried out purchase or sale transactions worth more than 12 times the subsistence minimum over the previous 12 months. Authorities can also reject an application if an able-bodied family member has turned down two suitable job offers.

Based on the 2026 subsistence minimum, the threshold for purchase and sale transactions stands at 3,600 manats (approx. $2,118). Authorities can also reject assistance if a family spends 45 manats (approx. $26.50) or more per person each month on utilities and communications. For a family of four, that amounts to 180 manats (approx. $106) in total. The authorities also count money and gifts from relatives, as well as estimated income from a household farm or garden, when calculating family income.

These criteria may help identify hidden income and assets. However, the same rules can exclude a family with a low cash income if it owns an old car, faces high utility bills or mainly survives on financial support from relatives.

The number of pensioners is falling, while more people receive age-related benefits

Another question arises when we examine other social security figures. On 1 July 2025, Azerbaijan had 1,103,300 pensioners. A year later, the figure had fallen to 1.1 million. At the same time, the average pension rose by 10.5% to 594.4 manats (approx. $350). However, the number of pensioners fell by 3,300.

Meanwhile, the number of people who do not qualify for a labour pension but receive a 220-manat age-related benefit (approx. $130) rose from 166,200 to 177,500. We cannot say that the changes in these two groups involve the same people. However, the fall in the number of pensioners as the elderly population grows, alongside the rise in recipients of a lower benefit, requires a separate explanation in terms of access to labour pensions.

What data the government should disclose

To treat a decline in the number of assistance recipients as evidence of falling poverty, we need more than one headline figure. The Ministry of Labour and Social Protection of the Population should report how many families entered the system over the past year, how many stopped receiving assistance, how many applicants faced rejection and why authorities rejected their applications.

The government should also report how many families failed to qualify under each criterion, including car ownership, purchase and sale transactions, utility costs, discrepancies in income data and refusal to accept an offered job. It should also disclose how many decisions authorities reviewed following complaints and what share of assistance recipients are children.

Without this data, we cannot conclude that poverty has fallen. So far, the official statistics show only this: the number of people covered by targeted social assistance has fallen, the average payment has declined in nominal terms, and its purchasing power has fallen even further.

Targeted social assistance in Azerbaijan

World.title: Beslan school siege 22 years on: Where does investigation stand and what did victims achieve?
World.content:
Beslan school siege anniversary

Twenty-two years have passed since the Beslan school siege, one of the most tragic events in the modern history of North Ossetia.

Commemorative events are being held across the republic, but there is still no complete clarity over what exactly happened during the attack.

“Three days in hell”: Timeline of the attack

On 1 September 2004, militants took pupils and teachers at School No 1 in Beslan hostage, including children starting their first year at school, their parents and babies who were with them.

In the first hours of the siege, the militants shot dead the adult male hostages. They held the others in the school’s gymnasium for three days, denying them water and making political demands, including the withdrawal of Russian troops from Chechnya.

The militants also demanded the presence of the then president of North Ossetia, Alexander Dzasokhov, Ingush President Murat Zyazikov, and CIS Executive Secretary and former Russian Security Council Secretary Vladimir Rushailo. None of them complied with the demand.

The North Ossetian authorities attempted to negotiate the release of the hostages, but without success. On 2 September, former Ingush President Ruslan Aushev managed to negotiate with the Ingush members of the militant group. He was allowed into the gymnasium and secured the release of around 20 women with babies.

At noon on the third day, two explosions were heard in the gymnasium.

According to some of the hostages and the official account, one of the explosive devices that the militants had placed along the walls detonated. A fire broke out in the gymnasium and the militants began shooting at the hostages.

An unofficial account, however, maintains that the explosion and subsequent fire were caused by an external strike on the school building using a Shmel rocket launcher.

This account remains disputed, with the North Ossetian and wider Russian authorities rejecting it as unfounded. FSB special forces, who were rehearsing an assault plan in a nearby village when the explosions occurred, were then urgently deployed to Beslan. Fighting with the militants ensued, during which most of the hostages were freed.

However, the death toll was still extremely high. A total of 334 people were killed in the attack, including 314 hostages and 20 members of the FSB special forces, Interior Ministry and Emergencies Ministry. Another 783 hostages were injured.

According to the official account, there were 32 militants. All were killed except Nur-Pashi Kulayev, who was detained and later sentenced to life imprisonment.

However, the criminal investigation launched immediately after the attack has still not been concluded. Relatives of the victims disputed the authorities’ official account and demanded an “objective and fair investigation”. According to some former hostages, there were more than 32 militants and some may have escaped.

There were also claims that the attackers had hidden weapons inside the school in advance and that some of the militants had previously gained access to the building by posing as workers carrying out repairs.

Commemoration ceremony in the gymnasium where the hostages were held

22 года спустя

On 1 September 2026, the Mothers of Beslan public organisation held its annual press conference.

The organisation’s leader, Susanna Dudiyeva, reported some progress in the criminal investigation, which she said had been made possible following a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin two years ago, when he visited Beslan ahead of the 20th anniversary of the attack. According to Dudiyeva, Putin subsequently issued instructions to the head of Russia’s Investigative Committee, Alexander Bastrykin.

Dudiyeva told the press conference that investigators had established that there were in fact more than 32 militants and that the criminal case remained open because not all of those killed had been identified. In particular, investigators have been unable to identify one of them, a Saudi national, as the Saudi authorities have not been cooperating with Russian investigators.

The health of former hostages was one of the main issues discussed at the press conference. The Mothers of Beslan committee has successfully campaigned for victims of the attack and their relatives to receive regular social and medical assistance. A comprehensive rehabilitation programme for those affected by the attack has been extended until 2030, while funding for their medical treatment has been increased.

“I would say that rehabilitation at health resorts is going well. There are some problems and some issues, but they can all be resolved. It is particularly encouraging that the children of former hostages who were born after the attack are now also receiving rehabilitation. Almost no other victims of terrorist attacks in Russia have access to this kind of rehabilitation,” Susanna Dudiyeva said.

The question of granting victims an official legal status remains a pressing issue. The adoption of relevant legislation would open up significant new opportunities to provide support to survivors and even their children.

Elvira Tuayeva, a member of the Mothers of Beslan organisation, said the group would continue campaigning for a law establishing the legal status of victims of terrorist attacks, not only those affected by the Beslan siege but by all terrorist attacks that have taken place in Russia.

World.title: Georgian businessman, animal rights activist Tamaz Elizbarashvili begins prison hunger strike
World.content:
Activist Elizbarashvili on hunger strike

Georgian businessman, animal rights activist and outspoken critic of the Georgian Dream government Tamaz Elizbarashvili, who was detained earlier, has gone on hunger strike.

Tamaz Elizbarashvili was detained at his home after law enforcement officers searched his car and flat. The Interior Ministry said the search of Elizbarashvili’s car was carried out as part of an investigation into alleged threats and the illegal acquisition and possession of weapons.

According to his lawyer, Elizbarashvili is currently being held in administrative detention.

What is known so far?

According to Elizbarashvili’s lawyer, Iako Siranashvili, her client was detained by law enforcement officers as he was attempting to jump from a balcony and take his own life.

Siranashvili said Elizbarashvili attempted to take his own life after seeing law enforcement officers use force against his lawyer and witnessing his children in distress.

“Tamaz Elizbarashvili was going to take his own life when he saw me being pushed into the building and beaten. When he saw his children crying and in distress, he tried to jump from the balcony. Tamaz was detained over this and charged with disobeying police orders,” Siranashvili said.

According to the lawyer, law enforcement officers tried to take her phone away when she began filming the search. She alleges that around 20 officers then used physical force against her.

“They tried to take my phone away to stop me filming the search. Anyone is allowed to film, especially a lawyer. They probably wanted to plant a weapon or some other prohibited item, but I prevented them from doing so because I was filming. Around 20 people then attacked me: they grabbed me and snatched the phone from my hands. When I resisted their attempts to take it, they twisted my arms, threw me to the ground and began kicking me,” Siranashvili said.

The lawyer said she had sustained injuries to various parts of her body and was having difficulty walking. Siranashvili said she had left the clinic of her own accord.

“My injuries are such that I can barely walk. I have difficulty moving around. My left arm is in severe pain. My hearing has also deteriorated and I have swelling around my facial bone. I left the clinic of my own accord because I did not think it was necessary to remain there,” she said.

According to Siranashvili, an investigation has been launched under Article 333 of Georgia’s Criminal Code, which covers abuse of official powers. She said, however, that investigators should also examine whether offences had been committed under Articles 364 and 365, which concern obstruction of a lawyer’s professional activities.

“What angers me most is not the fact that I was beaten, but that I was prevented from carrying out my professional duties. That is what makes me most angry, as does the fact that violence was used against a lawyer. Other articles must also be applied; the investigation cannot be limited to Article 333 alone,” the lawyer said.

She said her health had so far prevented her from attending the investigative authorities for a medical examination.

“I feel very unwell and have not yet been physically able to get to the relevant authorities. Investigators have ordered a medical examination, and I hope it will be carried out,” Siranashvili said.

World.title: Former head of Armenia’s State Revenue Committee arrested after appearing in court on stretcher
World.content:
Former Armenian revenue chief in court on stretcher

In Armenia, the arrest of former State Revenue Committee chairman Gagik Khachatryan has sparked widespread debate. He faces charges of accepting a particularly large bribe and money laundering. The Anti-Corruption Court is also considering cases seeking to confiscate allegedly illicitly acquired property from Khachatryan and people linked to him, including his sons.

However, the video that his lawyers shared on social media, rather than the charges against Khachatryan, has caused the biggest public outcry. The footage shows National Security Service officers carrying the 71-year-old Khachatryan, who is groaning in pain, from a bed onto a stretcher during his arrest. His lawyers said they consider the law enforcement officers’ actions equivalent to torture.

Human rights defenders and civil society representatives have also condemned the actions. They said authorities handled the transport of a person with serious health problems “improperly”, causing him physical suffering.

“No legal procedure or procedural necessity can justify violating human dignity,” experts from the NGO Disability Rights Agenda said.

What is Khachatryan accused of: all known details

The Investigative Committee said the previous day that investigators had carried out searches at the homes of the former head of the State Revenue Committee and his son as part of a case involving particularly large-scale bribery and money laundering. They also searched the offices and branches of more than 20 companies linked to them. Shortly afterwards, reports emerged that authorities had arrested Gagik Khachatryan for two months.

According to the case file, Khachatryan faces charges of:

accepting a particularly large bribe from the directors of Progress Armenia and Local Developers,

misappropriating 174 million 581 thousand drams ($482,000) in state funds during the reconstruction of the Dilijan training centre,

illegally transferring property belonging to a local university, worth 208 million 908 thousand drams ($577,000),

and laundering particularly large sums of money. The charge concerns concealing 151 million 126 thousand drams ($417,000) of illegally obtained funds.

Meanwhile, the Anti-Corruption Court is hearing a case seeking the confiscation of allegedly illicitly acquired property. The Prosecutor General’s Office is seeking to confiscate from Khachatryan and people linked to him:

193 properties, including properties in Yerevan’s most expensive central district,

89 properties in Kotayk Province,

stakes in 29 legal entities,

14 movable assets,

bonds worth $1,451,074,

a bank deposit of $147,210,

claims arising from loans worth approximately $23.1 million, 409.8 million drams (more than $1 million) and €9,800, and

7 billion 761 million drams ($49 million).

Defence lawyers and prosecutors disagree over the defendant’s health

The Prosecutor General’s Office says it conducted a forensic medical examination.

“Khachatryan has no health problems that could prevent him from taking part in any procedural actions as part of the criminal proceedings,” the experts concluded.

However, his defence team takes the opposite view.

Lawyer Yerevan Sargsyan told reporters that in June, authorities also took Khachatryan to the investigative body and then to court on a stretcher. At the time, however, the court found that his detention could pose health risks.

“They waited so long until they got the [forensic medical] conclusion they wanted. How they did it is known to them. And now they have organised the arrest in the same way again,” Sargsyan stressed.

Ombudsman’s office examines the case

On 2 September, a day after the lawyers published the video, the Human Rights Defender’s Office issued a statement. It said that the ombudsman had initiated an urgent examination of the case. A team of experts has already gone to the penitentiary to speak with Khachatryan and monitor respect for his rights.

The ombudsman’s office has also asked the relevant authorities for explanations to establish all the circumstances. After it completes the investigation and reviews its findings, the Human Rights Defender will present its position.

Comments

Human rights defender Zaruhi Hovhannisyan believes that the published photograph of the defendant on a stretcher in the courtroom is “not simply a sad scene”. In her view, the situation raises questions about the state’s attitude towards human rights:

“The photograph shows a 71-year-old man with serious health problems lying on a stretcher, completely covered, in the middle of a courtroom. People involved in the proceedings, tables, microphones and documents surround him. On one side stands the entire institutional machinery of criminal justice, organised by the state. On the other stands a person whom the system completely ignores.

The issue is not to make people feel sorry for the man lying on that stretcher, or to discuss why he ended up in court, what case he faces or how many charges he faces. The issue is that this is an extremely dangerous picture. When the state becomes accustomed to subordinating human dignity to a judicial process, it puts not only one person’s rights at risk but also the boundary that should prevent the state from gaining unlimited power over an individual. Human dignity and the prohibition of torture limit the state’s power over a person.”

Former head of Armenia’s State Revenue Committee in court on a stretcher

The NGO Disability Rights Agenda also issued a statement about the videos that Gagik Khachatryan’s lawyers circulated:

“According to the defence, doctors diagnosed Gagik Khachatryan with spinal stenosis in 2015 and implanted special devices in his cervical spine. The footage also shows him in a semi-conscious state while people were moving him.”

The organisation’s experts believe the authorities should structure the court proceedings in a way that prevents harm to a person’s health or humiliating conditions. Appropriate specialists should accompany people with limited mobility at all times. Medical professionals should supervise their movement and authorities should provide the necessary technical equipment.

“Regardless of the nature of the charges or his former position, humanitarian principles and safeguards for physical integrity must remain unchanged,” the statement says.

The organisation called on law enforcement agencies to take the following steps during further procedural actions:

rely only on impartial professional assessments,

provide the necessary medical care,

prevent any actions that cause a person unnecessary physical pain.

Former Armenian revenue chief in court on stretcher

World.title: Amnesty International: Georgia must not deport Denis Kulanin to Russia
World.content:
Denis Kulanin’s case

Amnesty International is calling on the Georgian authorities to prevent the deportation of Russian citizen Denis Kulanin to Russia, where the organisation says he faces a real risk of imprisonment and torture.

The organisation says Georgia should protect Kulanin from being forcibly returned to Russia because he has publicly opposed Russia’s war in Ukraine and expressed support for opposition leader Alexei Navalny. According to Amnesty International, both positions could lead to criminal prosecution in Russia.

“Denis Kulanin has publicly opposed Russia’s war in Ukraine and expressed support for Alexei Navalny — both actions constitute criminal offences in Russia and can lead to imprisonment. The Georgian authorities must ensure that he is not deported to Russia. Amid the harsh repression of people who oppose the war, he faces a real risk of arbitrary criminal prosecution, imprisonment, torture or other ill-treatment,” said Denis Krivosheev, Amnesty International’s deputy director for Eastern Europe and Central Asia.

He said Georgia must uphold the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning a person to a country where they face a real risk of serious human rights violations.

“The Georgian authorities must also ensure that Denis Kulanin has an effective opportunity to seek international protection, including by allowing him to leave voluntarily for a safe third country,” Krivosheev added.

Who is Denis Kulanin?

Denis Kulanin is a Russian citizen who lived in Georgia and took part in pro-European protests. Police arrested him on 28 March 2025 during a demonstration outside parliament. The authorities accused him of smashing a police car window and sentenced him to two years in prison.

On the Orthodox Christian feast of the Dormition of the Mother of God, President Mikheil Kavelashvili pardoned Kulanin. However, because Kulanin is not a Georgian citizen, the authorities did not release him. Instead, they transferred him to the migration department.

According to his lawyer, deporting Kulanin to Russia would be both unacceptable and dangerous. While in detention, Kulanin sent a letter in which he wished Ukraine glory and peace. His lawyer says that in Russia, authorities can interpret almost any statement about the war in a way that could lead to criminal charges.

Denis Kulanin. Photo: Publica

On 30 August 2026, the Tbilisi City Court ordered Denis Kulanin to be held at the temporary detention centre run by the Georgian Interior Ministry’s Migration Department. He will remain at the centre until the grounds for his detention cease to apply or the authorities enforce the decision to deport him from Georgia, but for no longer than three months.

On 31 August, Kulanin’s lawyer was told that he would not be allowed to leave Georgia voluntarily until the Tbilisi City Court considers his deportation case.

On 1 September, Kulanin’s lawyer said the Migration Department had asked the Tbilisi City Court to deport him to his country of citizenship, the Russian Federation.

Denis Kulanin’s case

World.title: Opinion: ‘An attempt to make Abkhazia’s residents feel part of single political space with Russia’
World.content:
Abkhazia is actively preparing for Russia’s State Duma elections, which will take place on 20 September 2026. Most Abkhazia residents hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship, which gives them the right to vote in the elections.

Russia will open 319 polling stations in 152 countries for citizens voting abroad. 35 of them — more than 10% — will open in Abkhazia.

Many people think this is excessive for a small republic with a population of 250,000.

One of those who objects is Akhra Bzhania, a prominent Abkhaz blogger and public figure. He believes that the “excessive” number of polling stations and the active election campaign aim to create a sense among Abkhazia’s residents that they somehow “belong” to Russia.

Akhra Bzhania: “There is a standard procedure for people with dual citizenship who vote abroad.

Usually, two or three polling stations open, plus a polling station at the consulate or embassy. That’s it.

Abkhazia cannot use its budget to cover the costs of holding a constitutional event of a foreign state. That makes no sense.

If someone argues that the Russian side is paying for the campaign, that is even worse!

Let me explain why. Fifty or 60,000 votes from Abkhazia will have no impact on the overall balance of parties in the State Duma.

This means the election campaign here must serve a different, ideological purpose — to create a sense among Abkhazia’s citizens that they share a single political and administrative space with Russia. And from there, a common state is not far away.”

I have no doubt that some Abkhaz citizens with dual citizenship care deeply about the differences between the programmes of Russian political parties. For them, State Duma elections are therefore not only a civic but also a political act.

But in that case, they can plan ahead and vote in Sochi, Krasnodar or Moscow, as Russians living in Armenia, Kyrgyzstan and elsewhere do.

Yet our entire republic is covered with banners urging people to vote for a government body of another country! We plan to open 35 polling stations, just as we do for our own presidential elections!

It seems strange to me — and not only to me — and out of line with the status of our state and the level of Abkhaz-Russian relations.”
