World.title: Karabakh Revival Fund partners the first Lachin International Film Festival (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. The Karabakh Revival Fund (KRF) served as an official partner of the first Lachin International Film Festival, held in Lachin from 24 to 27 August.

The festival formed part of the ceremonial programme marking Lachin City Day and represents a further step in the cultural revival of Karabakh and East Zangezur.

Held under the banner “Where Film Meets LIFE”, it was organised by the Hoçazfilm studio with the support of the Ministry of Culture of the Republic of Azerbaijan, the Special Representative Office of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan in the Lachin district, the Karabakh Revival Fund, the Film Agency of the Republic of Azerbaijan and Bakı Abadlıq Xidməti.

As the first international film festival ever held in Karabakh and East Zangezur, it showed once again that the reconstruction of the liberated territories is not a matter of infrastructure alone: restoring the cultural and civic life of these lands is no less of a priority.

The festival will be remembered as more than a programme of screenings — it was a cultural event that embodied the idea of revival itself. Its significance works on several levels at once: it brings new creative voices to light, introduces Lachin’s cultural revival to an international audience, and establishes the city as a new creative venue on the map of world cinema.

Among those attending were government officials, prominent figures from culture and the arts, guests from abroad, and residents and visitors of Lachin.

Speaking at the ceremony, Rahman Hajiyev, Chairman of the Executive Board of the Karabakh Revival Fund, said that alongside the large-scale reconstruction under way across the liberated territories, bringing cultural life back to the region remains a particular priority.

The festival, he said, gives filmmakers from Azerbaijan and abroad a rare chance to see Karabakh as it is today. He expressed confidence that the initiative will inspire the international film community with the story of the region — its past and its present revival — and encourage filmmakers to take up Karabakh as a subject in future work.

Close to 300 films from 47 countries were submitted to the festival, of which 20 titles representing 15 countries were selected for screening. Among them was a special Karabakh premiere of the Uzbek film Amir Temur, directed by Jacob Schwartz.

The closing and awards ceremony was held as part of a special event for Lachin City Day, attended by hundreds of residents and visitors. Official Selection certificates were presented to 39 participants, and 17 awards were made in total. The festival’s official prize, the Golden Oak Branch, went to five Azerbaijani and two international directors.

World.title: TURKPA Secretary General meets with OSCE PA President (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. The Secretary General of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Turkic States, Ramil Hasan, held a meeting with the OSCE PA delegation, headed by the President of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly, Pere Joan Pons Sampietro, who is on an official visit to Azerbaijan, at the TURKPA International Secretariat.

The meeting addressed issues of mutual interest, including the effective and active cooperation of TURKPA with the OSCE PA since 2010. The parties also exchanged views on the steps taken to obtain observer status for TURKPA in the OSCE PA, the voting process on this issue at the OSCE PA annual session held in The Hague in July, and the next stage.

The meeting also covered the parliamentary elections held in Kazakhstan, TURKPA's large-scale and productive engagement in recent times, as well as effective cooperation between the OSCE PA and TURKPA in promoting dialogue, peace, stability and mutual understanding. Both the OSCE PA President and the TURKPA Secretary General underscored that more active participation of their respective delegations in future activities would serve the common interests.

Meanwhile, the OSCE PA President thanked for the warm welcome, expressed his satisfaction with the cooperation with TURKPA, and expressed his willingness to provide all possible support to TURKPA’s further activities in the processes related to the development of parliamentary diplomacy, where democratic values ​​serving mutual dialogue are prioritized.

The Secretary General emphasized the importance of joint participation in mutual activities and projects, noting that this is one of the main factors serving common interests.

The meeting was attended by the OSCE PA Vice President and Special Representative for the South Caucasus, Luís Graça, and the Deputy Secretaries General of the TURKPA International Secretariat, Talgat Aduov and Muhammet Alper Hayali, as well as the Secretary of the Commission, Aynura Abutalibova.

World.title: After his Broncos ending, a new beginning looms for Payne Haas
World.content:
A dead rubber game in an empty stadium was no way for Payne Haas's time as a Bronco to come to an end.

To match what he's produced in nine seasons with Brisbane that averaged out to magnificent, Haas's last game would've needed to feel like a life and death struggle where the winners touched the heavens and defeat sent the fallen screaming into hell.

Such contests have been where Haas has enjoyed some of his finest hours and those are the games of 159 appearances for Brisbane that have made him a living legend.

NRL live The Broncos win a final-round contest against the Bulldogs, in a game that doubled as Payne Haas's farewell from Brisbane. Follow live.

But for the last before he heads to South Sydney, he had to settle for purgatory.

Brisbane's 34-20 win against Canterbury on Thursday night felt like so many other games that happen as non-finals teams grimly march to the end of the season.

Tackles were made, tries were scored and whistles were blown on a night that felt flat and lonely, as the citadel of Stadium Australia often can be with nearly 70,000 empty seats.

Brisbane did send Haas out a winner, and that still matters. Josiah Karapani played a blinder and the Broncos found a little of the football that marked that championship season last year.

Haas got in the action early, smashing his way through four defenders to score the opening try of the night and later spent time in the sin bin after being pinged for repeated infringements.

With 152 metres across 71 minutes the numbers were strong, as they always are for Haas, but it's important not to get lost in them.

While the match as a spectacle and a contest was not a fitting finale for Haas's Brisbane career as a whole, it made much more sense as the close for what has been an uneven year in comparison to his other campaigns.

Haas has not played poorly and even if he had, a poor Payne Haas game would be a stand-out performance for many other props.

You could say he's good enough on a bad day but he hasn't had enough truly bad days for us to be sure.

Haas has still averaged 156 run metres and just under 35 tackles a game, marks many players would be proud to call their own.

In 2026, Payne Haas has not quite hit the superhuman form he's become known for. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

He has still had big moments, like his rampaging try against the Bulldogs on his last night, or his similar effort against Canberra two weeks ago that kicked off a rollicking Broncos comeback win.

Australia and Samoa would still both crawl over broken glass to have him in their World Cup sides because he is still the best prop on the planet.

But Haas has not quite been superhuman, and that is what we have become accustomed to during his Bronco years.

We are used to him being closer to a miracle than a man — 156 metres per game, somehow, is the second-lowest average of his career as a starter.

His offloads have plummeted, from 70 last year to just 21 this season. So too his tackle busts, which have fallen from 130 to 64 with the wide-running charges that became such a feature of his game in recent years seemingly hard to find.

In similarly short supply are the inexplicable, gut-busting efforts to cover the defensive mistake of a teammate or clean up a loose ball or just generally be where no prop forward ever should be to do a little extra that no other prop forward can ever really do.

After making the Dally M team of the year four of the past five seasons, Payne Haas will miss out in 2026. (AAP: Jono Searle)

After making the Dally M team of the year four times in the past five seasons — with a 14-match year in 2024 marking his only exclusion — Haas will miss out this year and rightly so.

The Roosters' blunt-force artist Naufahu Whyte and New Zealand's James Fisher-Harris have both enjoyed better seasons.

So too has the old iron Cowboy himself, Jason Taumalolo, and the greatest forward of an age now past got the better of Haas in both of North Queensland's wins over their southern rivals.

Mitch Barnett, Haas's replacement in Brisbane for next year, did the same last month when the Warriors beat the Broncos up like they owed them money.

Even players outside the top eight have got a bit of a turn to put one on the living legend.

Haas barely ever misses tackles — he made 40 without a single miss against Canterbury — but last week against Melbourne Stefano Utoikamanu brushed past him for a try the Storm man can tell the grandkids about because it's not every day you get one on the king.

Haas is not the only player at Brisbane who has struggled to deal with the premiership hangover but he is the only player who seemed above such things. Motivation is fleeting, it comes and it goes and that is why it's for humans, not heroes.

Haas is the player who goes all day, every day, no matter what and he has done it on worse Bronco teams than this.

In the final game of the 2020 season, when Brisbane lost to North Queensland to confirm their first wooden spoon on as low a night as the club has ever had, it was a breakaway try to Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow that confirmed the result.

Chasing Tabuai-Fidow, then or now, is to put in maximum effort for a futile cause at the best of times, let alone in the dying stages of the final game of a nightmare season.

But there going after him, as sure as the sun will rise tomorrow, was Payne Haas. It didn't make a difference, but Haas did it just in case it might.

Last year's premiership was Payne Haas's ultimate reward. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

He kept going like that until it felt like a way of life, until years later when he lifted the premiership trophy and confirmed a legacy that meant he could stand alongside the likes of Glenn Lazarus, Shane Webcke and Petero Civoniceva as the greatest forwards in Brisbane's history.

That journey to greatness is in starker relief given his first Brisbane years began in low-down valleys, making the trail he forged all the way to a premiership his Everest.

His sense of triumph and relief was palpable after that grand final win even amid the throng of family, friends and backslappers that filled the Brisbane sheds as the air felt thick with emotion and cigar smoke.

The player who always found more to do at last had some satisfaction. The seemingly endless appetite for the grind and the fight was satiated.

It was the culmination of Haas's entire footballing life and if anyone had earned the right to look a little more mortal in the aftermath, it was him.

Why Haas's move changes the fate of two NRL giants Payne Haas's decision to leave Brisbane for South Sydney in 2027 didn't just shock the rugby league world, it transformed the futures of two of rugby league's most powerful clubs in an instant.

This version of Payne Haas is still more than good enough to impact the premiership race. If this is the new normal he will still be mighty for South Sydney in a way few players can ever dream of and regardless of what happens next, his greatness is already assured.

But there's every chance the move now creates the chance for another rise, in a new city with new colours and a fresh start amid new challenge that will, from time to time, demand he again pushes himself beyond reasonable limits.

As hyperbolic as we can get about players of Haas's ilk, they are still human. They still need something to chase and last year, after so much effort and so much time, Haas made his ultimate catch.

Perhaps it meant that his farewell season as a Bronco, and particularly his final night, could not match what has come before.

But even if it wasn't a fitting end to what was, it is still an end — which means a new beginning can follow.

World.title: Dockers wilt against masterful Hawthorn in qualifying final
World.content:
So good for so long this year, Fremantle chose an inopportune time to put in — by some distance — their worst shift of the AFL season.

But that assessment is unkind to a Hawthorn side who were nothing short of brilliant in Thursday night's qualifying final at Perth Stadium.

The Hawks dominated on the ground, in the air and particularly down back, holding Fremantle to 40 points, their lowest score of the season.

The victory was built on manic pressure, the visitors forcing the Dockers into turnovers and denying them the chance to get their running game going.

Hawks complete stunning upset over Freo to clinch prelim berth Hawthorn will host an MCG preliminary final after an upset 32-point win over minor premier Fremantle in Perth.

Hawthorn's 32-point win puts them into a home preliminary final, the club now two MCG wins away from its 14th premiership.

Fremantle, meanwhile, toppled from joint-premiership favouritism, and will have to do it the hard way if the club is to bring a first flag to the port city.

The concerning thing for the Dockers was the manner of the defeat.

No Wharfie Time

Other than the first two minutes of the game, the result rarely looked in doubt.

There would be no Wharfie Time comeback against the Hawks this time, as there had been in round nine when the Dockers emerged from a titanic scrap with a 15-point win.

The Hawks came, saw and conquered the Dockers at Perth Stadium. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

Last night Fremantle, who had been unbeaten at home all year, just couldn't get close enough to push the button.

So good was Hawthorn's defence that the Dockers' three-headed forward line leviathan — Josh Treacy, Jye Amiss and Pat Voss — combined for only two goals.

Voss and Treacy managed just one mark between them.

Credit must go to Hawthorn's three-headed beast of its own — backmen James Sicily, Josh Battle and Tom Barrass proving majestic in getting their blend of destruction and creativity just right.

James Sicily was masterful in defence for the Hawks. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

After Fremantle kicked the opening goal of the match, Hawthorn then banged on the next six to take a 33-point lead into the long break.

The Dockers needed to make a move in the third quarter, and they emerged from the sheds with renewed vigour.

But every time Freo struck, the Hawks replied.

The Dockers failed to kick two goals in a row all night, and most of the 59,446 fans who poured through the turnstiles would have been resigned to their fate long before the final siren.

On a night when few Dockers beat their direct opponents, Jordan Clark was outstanding — the All Australian defender notching up 38 disposals and dragging down a spectacular mark.

Sicily was Hawthorn's best with 26 touches, while Jack Gunston, Dylan Moore and Nick Watson kicked two goals apiece.

'Not dead and buried'

Speaking after the match, Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir backed his decision to select Brandon Walker for his first game since round one to curtail the influence of Nick Watson, describing their contest as a "pretty good tussle".

But Walker's rolled ankle ended that tussle early, the dashing defender in tears on the bench after being ruled out of the game.

Watson capitalised on his absence, kicking a goal late in the third quarter and then producing a moment of pure wizardry early in the fourth, handballing to himself before burning off Luke Ryan to set up a goal for Harry Morrison, who extended the lead to 38 points.

Nick Watson prepares to activate the jets to get past Luke Ryan and send Hawthorn inside 50. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

There was no way back for Fremantle, who have now lost three of their past four games.

But Longmuir denied his side was out of form.

"Go back and have a look at the Adelaide game [in round 23], I thought we played a good brand of footy against a really desperate team who had it all to play for," he said.

"We had a couple of away games where we didn't play our best footy, but I've got a lot of faith in this group to bounce back from that."

The coach, who has preached the value of "process" all year, backed his men to get the processes spot on over the next week ahead of a cut-throat home semi-final against either Carlton or Geelong.

"It's not the way we wanted it to go, but we're not dead and buried," he said.

Emotional win

For Hawks coach Sam Mitchell, the overwhelming feeling was one of pride.

Teams like Geelong, Sydney and Adelaide had been able to meet Fremantle's fire for quarters and halves this season, but no one has been able to douse it completely for an entire game at Perth Stadium like the Hawks.

Sam Mitchell was proud of the intensity his players showed. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

"The relentless pressure that we had on them in that game was what we thought would be required," Mitchell said.

" Full credit to the players for being able to produce that level of effort for that long. "

The coach paid tribute to Will Day, the midfielder outstanding in his first final after a dreadful run with injuries.

An emotional Day let the tears flow on the final siren, and Mitchell said he was feeling it too.

"He's so resilient, he's been through so much," Mitchell said.

"He showed it more than I did, but I felt exactly the way he looked after the game."

World.title: Victorian healthcare system is 'fundamentally broken', GP says
World.content:
When Jacqueline Altree went on maternity leave last November, her patients at Terang Medical Clinic had to wait three or four months for a routine appointment for things like a script repeat or blood pressure check.

Even with Dr Altree back at work, patients at the south-west Victorian clinic still have a two-week wait for their preferred GP, and upcoming staff movements are expected to make that even longer in the future.

The regional GP said she was worried patients managing long-term chronic disease would go without care and potentially end up in hospital.

"That's most of what I see, and that's most of what I feel anxious about when I know there is a big waitlist to get in to see me," she said.

"What are we missing, what aren't we caring for, what is going to need to go to hospital because I physically can't see any more patients?

"There's only so many hours in the day — either you cut down on the time you spend with each patient, in which case you might miss stuff, or you see less patients, and you're going to worry about that."

Jacqueline Altree says there are no easy solutions to primary healthcare in regional Victoria. (Supplied: Jacqueline Altree)

She said she believed more people were turning up at emergency departments (EDs) because they were unable to see a doctor promptly.

"People are presenting to ED sicker and later, because they couldn't get appropriate care earlier," she said.

Lack of GPs helping drive ED overload

Insufficient access to GPs is among the key factors blamed for rising pressure on regional Victorian hospital emergency departments.

The ABC previously reported emergency departments at multiple hospitals across regional Victoria have faced high demand and long wait times, with hospital staff saying they are at breaking point.

Hundreds of GPs walked off the job for four hours at the Ballarat and Bendigo emergency departments yesterday to protest poor pay and working conditions.

The latest Rural Workforce Association of Victoria worker census released last month found "critical workforce gaps" for GP roles across the state, except for the Baw Baw area in the state's east.

Meanwhile, the Commonwealth government's most recent data showed there were fewer doctors per capita in rural and remote communities in Victoria, compared to metropolitan and regional centres.

Doctors and GP advocacy groups have told the ABC that unless something is done to fix the GP shortage, the ED crisis will only get worse.

Policy change needed

The far south-west Victorian town of Casterton had no GP for six months in 2024 when their long-standing doctor retired, and a patchwork of locum staff failed to fully plug the gaps.

Patients unable to travel an hour to the nearest clinics in Hamilton or Mount Gambier went without care.

Andrea Cumming, practice manager of the Edgar House Medical in Casterton, said the situation was "absolutely dreadful".

"People's health is at risk when they can't see a doctor," Ms Cumming said.

While the town now has three doctors, she said the problem was going to keep coming up due to a national policy issue.

Andrea Cumming says more doctors should experience the joys of living in the country. (Supplied: Andrea Cumming)

In 2022, the federal government implemented changes to Distribution Priority Area (DPA) policy, which eased the limits on where international medical graduates were allowed to work as GPs.

Under the old policy, doctors who gained their training overseas either had to work in a small rural town for 10 years or in a remote location for five years.

At the time, rural and regional clinics sounded the alarm, saying the change was going to make it harder to recruit doctors.

Last year, the federal government further expanded the areas counted as a DPA, a move criticised by the Royal Australian College of GPs.

Casterton is a small country Victoria town, home to just over 1,600 people. (ABC News: Jean Bell)

Ms Cumming said her former workplace in Hamilton lost three doctors shortly after the 2022 change, and says the policy should be reversed so that doctors are required to do a stint in the country.

"[The government] should bring that back in and give doctors a five or ten-year moratorium … so they have to come to these areas and gain that experience," she said.

"That would help us quite a lot."

Ms Cumming said though the Casterton clinic currently had three doctors, one had recently foreshadowed retirement, which meant the practice would be back to relying on locum staff.

She said it pointed to another ongoing problem that needed solving.

"[Hiring locums] costs a lot of money … sometimes we're in the negative, but we have to have the GP coverage for the patients," Ms Cumming said.

She said a solution would be to pay GPs more if they moved out of the cities.

"Doctors aren't getting paid well enough to come into rural areas; they can make more money working in Melbourne," Ms Cumming said.

"All of the locums tell me that."

'Exceptionally difficult' to hire GP

Birregurra, a small country town less than an hour's drive west of Geelong, is attracting a growing population, but can not get a second GP to go with its population boom.

Despite a promise of free haircuts and coffee from the community, Birregurra Medical Clinic's 18-month search has been fruitless, leaving Jared Kilday as the town's sole GP.

Birregurra is a small town in south-west Victoria. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

"It's just been exceptionally difficult, despite advertising through all the right channels and generating a bit of media interest," Dr Kilday said.

He said he was only taking on new patients who lived directly in the town, meaning he turned away multiple prospective patients from the surrounding area every week.

"If I take on more patients than I can service, then ultimately it's not going to be good for my patients and good for me, my mental health, and job satisfaction," Dr Kilday said.

"Although it's disappointing, especially for the new people that are moving to the area, it's a decision I've made for the time being until we can recruit someone else.

" There's plenty of demand but not enough me. "

He said the answer was to put more funding into primary care to bolster the GP workforce.

Not only would it help lure doctors to places like Birregurra, but it would also ease the pressure on EDs.

"If you come and see the local GP, it's potentially costing the government $80 or $90 to fix a lot of stuff," Dr Kilday said.

"[But] as soon as they land in an emergency department, the bill starts ticking at $500-plus, and then a hospital admission is priced at $1,000-plus per 24-hour period."

Some regional emergency departments are straining under patient demand. (ABC News: Daryl Torpe)

'System is fundamentally broken'

Michael Veal is a country GP in Avoca and Creswick in the state's west, and said many of his patients who need hospital treatment refuse to travel to the EDs in Ballarat or Bendigo.

"No one wants to sit in ED or an ambulance trolley for 12 hours, and the outpatient wait time for many of the clinics, including things like vascular surgery, is stretching to three years," Dr Veal said.

Michael Veal says the healthcare system is "fundamentally broken". (ABC News: Alexander Darling)

"So the pressure is right back on the GPs.

" The system is fundamentally broken — I don't think it's actually repairable. "

Dr Veal said that instead of investing in telehealth, governments should return to the days when GPs were made to work in rural and remote areas.

"I saw a lady yesterday [who] came in with cold and flu symptoms [and] whilst listening to her chest, I noticed a dark melanoma spot on her back," he said.

"So that can't be done over [telehealth]."

Dr Veal says regional infrastructure is breaking down. (ABC News: Alexander Darling)

A multi-decade proposition

Rob Phair is a hospital-based rural generalist doctor in East Gippsland.

He said the pressures in regional emergency departments are felt more acutely because of fewer health resources.

"We have fewer GP options, less access to primary health care, fewer aged care facilities and an aging population," Dr Phair said.

Rob Phair is a hospital-based rural generalist doctor in East Gippsland. (Supplied: Rob Phair)

He said those latter issues meant older patients were clogging up hospitals and EDs because "we don't have safe destinations we can discharge them to, we don't have carers at home to help support, and we don't have enough aged care beds for them to go to either".

Dr Phair said all levels of government needed to look at better solutions for primary healthcare and aged care in the regions, which he said is a multi-decade proposition.

"We have to have a greater commitment to supporting the doctors, the health services that are under most pressure, which are almost all beyond the fringes of outer suburban Melbourne," he said.

"That's where the greatest vulnerabilities are, and those are the health services that need to be prioritised."

More pressure on hospitals

The Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) co-deputy chair Christie Rodda said GPs were a vital link in the healthcare chain.

Christie Rodda says GP access is critical to prevent overloading of emergency departments. (Supplied: Christie Rodda)

"We're seeing far more patients with comorbidities … they have heart disease, lung disease, diabetes, and mental health [issues]," Dr Rodda said.

"If they delay that care through not being able to access GPs who care for those complex needs, they will end up being sicker and presenting to an emergency department when they're more unwell.

"That means they're more likely to be hospitalised."

Dr Rodda said that if GP shortages were not addressed, the ED crisis would worsen, and people would get sicker.

"We're going to see that pressure flow onto the hospital system, so more crowding in emergency departments, more backlog of beds, more demand for residential aged care facility beds that don't exist," she said.

She said there were several solutions to help provide more GP care in regional communities.

These included more government funding in Medicare rebates for longer consultations, along with an exemption from payroll tax to help clinics stay financially viable.

She said practices and supervisors also needed ongoing support to help train students as rural GPs.

In 2026, the RACGP had 363 future GPs in training, with 149 of those in rural and regional Victoria.

"We've got to make sure that both levels of government are supporting training those doctors coming through the pipeline as well," she said.

The federal health department was approached for comment, while the Victorian government said more needed to be done to make GP care more accessible, noting it had established 29 urgent care clinics in the state to help meet demand.

World.title: Imran Khan's sons say former PM's health declining in prison
World.content:
Whenever a call from an unrecognised Pakistani came, no matter what time of day or night, Kasim and Sulaiman Khan scrambled to answer.

It might have been their dad — legendary cricketer and former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan — calling from Rawalpindi's Adiala prison.

But for six months, there have been no calls at all and the brothers are worried. They say an aunt who saw him briefly in a military hospital told them his health was worsening.

"He seemed like he wasn't doing well, in terms of high blood pressure, heart palpitations and general anxiety," Khasim told 7.30.

" He seemed kind of disturbed by the long period of isolation that he's been facing. And as you know, it's very uncharacteristic of him to be anxious. "

Political rise and fall

Imran Khan was an exceptional cricketer who leveraged his immense popularity as the captain of Pakistan's 1992 World Cup-winning side into a successful political career.

Pakistan captain Imran Khan led his team to victory at the 1992 Cricket World Cup final. (Getty Images: Tony Feder)

"He's fearless in a lot more than just kind of sporting sense," Kasim said.

"And I think now so more than ever been, because he kind of found faith and spirituality later in his life, at the tail end of his cricket career."

He won the backing of Pakistan's powerful military and was elected prime minister in 2018.

But by 2022 he had lost the support of the military, the University of Western Australia professor Samina Yasmeen said.

Samina Yasmeen believes some of the charges against Imran Khan were "politically motived". (ABC News: Glyn Jones)

"They then did exactly the opposite of what they had done to bring him to power. So they got the people who had joined his coalition to gradually desert him," she said.

Khan was ousted in a vote of no confidence that sparked huge protests in Pakistan before he was eventually charged with more than 100 offences, including corruption.

He was convicted and jailed for terms totalling more than 30 years.

Imran Khan's supporters believe he has been incarcerated for political reasons. (Reuters: Fayaz Aziz)

Professor Yasmeen says a lot of the charges were "politically motivated", in her view, but some of them stuck.

"One, for example, which is still running, is the anti-terrorism case in which he is accused of mobilising people," she said.

Barely allowed outside

Khan has been in jail for more than three years in conditions that have been criticised by a UN working group and Amnesty International.

His sons say the conditions are tough.

Supporters of Imran Khan protested in February this year amid concerns about his health. (Reuters: Akhtar Soomro)

"He's not allowed reading materials," Sulaiman said.

" He's barely allowed outside of his cell. It's a small, dark cell, extremely hot in the summer, with no kind of air conditioning or anything like that. "

The Supreme Court of Pakistan has ordered that Khan be treated by independent doctors in a private hospital, but his family and independent observers say that has been ignored by authorities.

"We're just trying to raise awareness about the conditions he's being kept in," Sulaiman said.

"There's been a Supreme Court order that he has treatment at a private hospital, he's allowed visits from his family, from his lawyers, that his health is independently reviewed and that he has calls with us.

"That's so far been completely ignored by the government."

Pakistan denies Khan is being mistreated, says he is medically fit and is allowed phone contact with his relatives.

Cricketers speak up for Khan

Former international cricket captains including Australia's Greg Chappell and England's Michael Atherton have written in support of Khan, asking that his conditions and medical treatment be improved.

Australian captain Pat Cummins has tweeted his support:

"I hope the court-ordered medical assessment be allowed to run its course, and that family visits continue. I hope Imran Khan is treated with the dignity anyone deserves," Cummins wrote.

The brothers said they were incredibly grateful to Cummins and the former cricketers.

Current and former cricketers have spoken out about the conditions Khan is facing in prison. (Reuters: Mohsin Raza)

"It's made a huge difference," Suleiman said.

"It's just raised awareness so much more than before, and it had really gone quiet for the 10 months while our father was in isolation.

"Things like that really bring this to the attention of people who otherwise wouldn't know what was going on."

It appears the criticism is having some impact — last week, after an interview with the brothers was recorded at Lord's Cricket Ground, Pakistan threatened to withdraw its players from their Test match against England.

The brothers say Pakistan's leaders clearly see their father as a threat.

Imran Khan during his time in office as Pakistan's prime minister. (Reuters: Akhtar Soomro)

"The intention is clearly to just remove him from politics completely," Suleiman told 7.30.

"I think when he was first imprisoned, if he'd just agreed to live in exile and not be involved in politics for the rest of his life, they would have loved that and they would have accepted it and allowed him to do that.

" I think they fear his popularity and they want to remove him from public life and from politics. "

Professor Yasmeen agrees that Khan could have just quietly left the country before his conviction.

"I think every politician in Pakistan has the opportunity to leave Pakistan and live in exile and all the political leaders have done that," she said.

"Where Imran Khan possibly had that opportunity, but he refused to do that is because he wants to make sure that he's seen as someone different from all those who came before him."

Professor Yasmeen says Khan remains a formidable political force.

Supporters of Khan have previously taken to the streets to demand his release. (Reuters: Akhtar Soomro)

"Imran Khan isn't finished. Imran Khan commands huge support among young people and more than 60 per cent of Pakistan's population," she said.

"Even others who are not so young, who have been disillusioned with the way politics has worked in Pakistan, they also have sympathies for him. So there is a possibility that if he is brought back into the political space, that he might command that support again."

Suleiman says his father has not given up.

"While he's been in prison, I think part of what he's been doing has been strategising and imagining what he would do if he were in power now, what he might have done differently when he was in power," he said.

" I don't think he'd still be in prison if he'd given up hope of getting back into power one day, or at least influencing Pakistani politics in some way. "

World.title: Kiss makes selection gamble for Wallabies-Argentina rematch
World.content:
Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii has been thrust back into the Wallabies' starting side while Ben Donaldson will steer the ship in Mendoza for his first start at fly-half in two years.

After a tight win a week earlier, coach Les Kiss has again tinkered with his side for their Argentina rematch on Sunday morning (AEST).

After a run of six losses, the side is chasing five-straight wins for the first time since 2021.

Carter Gordon, reportedly under an injury cloud during the week, has been shifted to the bench to give perennial back-up Donaldson a rare start in the number 10 jersey.

Ryan Lonergan will remain at scrum half, and Tom Wright will play his 50th Test after being named at fullback.

Billy Pollard and Josh Nasser will share the hooking duties, with Brandon Paenga-Amosa rotated out.

It's otherwise a full-strength pack with Angus Bell, Taniela Tupou, Josh Canham and Jeremy Williams all starting, while Harry Wilson has been recalled at number 8 alongside Fraser McReight and Rob Valetini.

Kiss has switched his centres though, with Isaac Henry benched and Hunter Paisami left out to make room for star pair Len Ikitau and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii.

It will be the first time that pair, who were midfield regulars under Joe Schmidt, start together under Kiss, who is 3-0 as Test coach.

Fililipo Daugunu will earn his first start of the season on the wing, replacing Harry Potter, while Kalani Thomas takes Reds teammate Tate McDermott's spot on the bench as back-up scrum-half.

Prop Aidan Ross and lock Lukhan Salakaia-Loto also come into the side on the bench, with Charlie Cale the back row back-up.

Team to face Argentina: Angus Bell, Billy Pollard, Taniela Tupou; Josh Canham, Jeremy Williams; Rob Valetini, Fraser McReight, Harry Wilson; Ryan Lonergan, Ben Donaldson; Filipo Daugunu, Len Ikitau, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Max Jorgensen; Tom Wright. Bench: Josh Nasser, Aidan Ross, Massimo De Lutiis, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Charlie Cale, Kalani Thomas, Carter Gordon, Isaac Henry.

World.title: Holdout juror preventing verdict in Lindsay Clancy trial, defence says
World.content:
A single juror in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial is preventing the jury from reaching a unanimous verdict, her lawyer has said in court.

Warning: This story contains details that may be distressing for some readers.

The judge declined on Thursday, local time, to remove the juror as deliberations stretched into a sixth day over whether to convict the Massachusetts woman of killing her three young children.

The jury sent a note to Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth, Massachusetts, that prompted him to re-instruct jurors on what would constitute "reasonable doubt". The note was not read aloud in court.

After the jury was sent back to continue deliberating, defence attorney Kevin Reddington moved to have a holdout juror removed.

He said the note from the jury's foreperson indicated "there's one juror who refuses to listen to the law that you've given him or her on reasonable doubt".

Kevin Reddington unsuccessfully sought to have one of the jurors removed. (AP: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/Pool)

"I suggest respectfully that the soft instruction that you gave them saying, at the sidebar, 'can you listen to the law as I instruct you, does not focus on the issue' — the question is not sufficient enough, it does not allow any foundation for a motion to remove the juror who refuses to accept your instructions on the law on a reasonable doubt," he said, as reported by the BBC. "If we come back In a half an hour with a mistrial because of a juror that has just spurned the instructions of this court, that's a shame, that's a real shame. "And that's why I object to the court's ruling, I request that we have further inquiry — my motion is to remove this juror that refuses to listen to your instruction on reasonable doubt."

Judge Sullivan declined to remove the juror before sending the jury home for the day.

"I don't feel that it is proper for me to side with one side or the other of the deliberations. I don't feel it's appropriate for me to say I agree with one juror or the 11," Judge Sullivan said.

The jury sent the judge a note a day earlier that said: "After much deliberation, we are still unable to come to a unanimous decision."

They sent a similar note on Tuesday. But on both days, the judge instructed them to continue deliberating.

Jury in Lindsay Clancy trial remains deadlocked Jurors in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial remain deadlocked on reaching a verdict, prompting the judge to instruct them for a second time to keep deliberating.

If the jury does not reach a verdict and Judge Sullivan declares a mistrial, prosecutors would need to decide whether to retry the case, which has included more than 80 witnesses and more than 300 exhibits.

Asked during a lunch break about his thoughts on the state of the deliberations, Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz told reporters outside the courthouse that "we'll hang on and find out".

On the question of whether prosecutors in his office would retry the case if it ended in a mistrial, Mr Cruz said only: "I'll talk when this is all over."

Mental health struggles

Ms Clancy, 36, faces life in prison without parole if convicted of first-degree murder.

If found not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, or reason of insanity, she could be committed to a state psychiatric hospital for evaluation.

She has admitted to killing her three children on January 24, 2023, in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury.

Her attempt to take her own life afterwards left her paralysed.

A carton of letters from Lindsay Clancy's supporters. (AP: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/Pool)

During the six-week trial, Mr Reddington sought to convince jurors that Ms Clancy was in the midst of a psychotic episode when she killed Cora, five, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan.

Testimony from family members, including Ms Clancy's now ex-husband, Patrick, showed how she had struggled with her mental health in the months after the birth of her third child, repeatedly seeking treatment from healthcare providers who prescribed her a myriad of drugs.

Prosecutors do not dispute that Ms Clancy, a former labour and delivery nurse at Massachusetts General Hospital, had been dealing with mental health issues.

But they argued she was able to appreciate the wrongfulness of killing her children and intentionally chose to do so anyway, opting to kill them because she had decided to kill herself and was convinced they would suffer without her.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: 'Regulars': Hitchhiking birds catch Sydney train commuters by surprise
World.content:
You may have heard of snakes on a plane, but what about birds on a train?

A pair of common myna birds have become regulars on Sydney's inner-city North Shore Line, perching themselves on the back of the seats during quieter hours.

The lively duo went viral after 702 ABC Sydney Drive producer Jackie Dent posted a recording of their morning on social media.

Ms Dent said upon boarding a train at Roseville Station in Sydney's upper north shore on a Sunday morning, she spotted the two birds on the upper level.

"They weren't fluttering around. They were very relaxed, they were very at home," she said.

"I've never seen it, and the older lady on the train said, 'I've never seen this in all my life.'''

Loading...

When she reached Chatswood on the lower north shore, Ms Dent had an interesting conversation with a guard:

"I say, 'Hey, look, there are these two birds trapped on the train,'" she said. "And she [the guard] says, 'They're not trapped. They're regulars. They just commute.' "And so I say, 'Well, what do you mean they're regulars?' "And she said, 'Well, these birds go between Lindfield and Artarmon every day, and then they come back.'''

That is about a seven to 10-minute trip.

"Apparently they [the train staff] think that the birds know when to get off the trains because of the announcements; maybe there's something in the lights," Ms Dent said.

Common mynas not alone

Loading...

The video has now amassed more than 4.6 million views, with many sharing their own interesting bird stories in the comments.

"Quite a few people are saying that this is a thing that they see, including a guy who worked at the Newcastle Interchange who has said that he saw birds get on," Ms Dent said.

"Apparently the birds jump on the train there, they eat the food, and they jump off.

" Once they hear the chimes, they know when to get off. "

She said other users asked whether the Sydney common myna pair had tapped on and off using their transport cards, describing the ordeal as a 'myna situation'.

Ms Dent has also spotted a pigeon getting on and off a train in Sydney, leaving some unsightly evidence of its behind.

Loading...

The guard told her there was another set of birds known to travel via train between North Sydney and Milsons Point, as well as a bird called Archie who was a regular in North Sydney before he died.

'Street kids' of the bird world

Sean Dooley from BirdLife Australia, who originally thought the video was made with artificial intelligence, said birdwatchers "tend to love to hate" the common myna.

"But you have to admire their intelligence," he said.

"That's why they're so common, is because they've worked out how to live alongside humans, both in Asia and now where they've been introduced around the world.

"They're pretty much tied to human habitation, be it the sort of rubbish we throw out or the agriculture we have, and they really know how to work the system."

Mr Dooley says birdwatchers love to hate common myna birds. (ABC News: Jason Katsaras)

Mr Dooley said he had a "grudging admiration" for the bird.

"They essentially are street kids, and they just have a bad PR because what they do, it can be brutal," he said.

"They do turf out parrots, like native parrots, and they will even kill the chicks of the parrots to take over that nesting hollow.

"But it's because it's right in front of us that we see it and we begin to dislike those birds, but this sort of behaviour happens a lot throughout nature."

Western Force five-eighth Ben Donaldson has been placed in the driver’s seat by the Wallabies for the first time in two years after Les Kiss again rang in mass changes for the second Test against Argentina in Mendoza.

World.title: French trio minted as billionaires as the world’s most valuable company swoops
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMergers & acquisitions French trio minted as billionaires as the world’s most valuable company swoops Tara Patel and Dylan Sloan September 4, 2026 — 6:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hugging Face’s three French founders have emerged as billionaires after the artificial intelligence platform agreed to be acquired by Nvidia a decade after they first started the company with a completely different focus. Clement “Clem” Delangue, 38, Julien Chaumond, 42, and Thomas Wolf, 41, will each have a net worth of about $US1.8 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, which is valuing their fortunes for the first time. Nvidia agreed to buy the startup in a transaction valued at roughly $US13 billion. Clem Delangue (pictured), Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf will stay with the company after the deal goes through. Bloomberg A spokesperson for Brooklyn-based Hugging Face, which began in 2016 in Paris, didn’t respond to requests for comment about the founders’ wealth. The deal — expected to close in the first half of 2027 — marks the biggest move yet by Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang to broaden the uptake of AI and extend his customer range. It’s also a big test for Hugging Face, which has long backed keeping the industry open and decentralised, boasting it’s “on a mission to democratise good machine learning” and describing itself as being like an AI library.



“I am honored that Clem came to me as he considered the next chapter of Hugging Face and believed Nvidia would be a great home for the company,” Huang said in a blog post announcing the deal. Related Article Wall Street Apple’s value grew by $1b a day for 15 years under Tim Cook. But he had one big flaw Hugging Face operates a platform for sharing AI models that can be used freely by others. It was at the centre of a cybersecurity incident this year when it was inadvertently hacked by a model being tested by OpenAI. Under the deal unveiled, Nvidia pledged Hugging Face will remain an open platform, with users able to upload and download AI models and datasets of their choosing. The co-founders will remain at the company under a six-year retention agreement, Wolf said in an interview on Bloomberg TV. The three co-founders have made public accessibility to cheaper, open-source AI models their mantra, even organizing a street march in San Francisco earlier this year in support of the principle.



“I think it would be a really great world if we can enable, empower more people to be AI builders because it means that we won’t outsource that to just a couple of labs in Silicon Valley,” Delangue, who is chief executive officer, said earlier this year at a conference. The Hugging Face trio join the three founders of Paris-based Mistral AI as French nationals who have become billionaires through their stakes in AI and computing companies. Also included in the cohort are Olivier Pomel and Alexis Le-Quoc, founders of New York-based Datadog. The company was at the centre of a cybersecurity incident this year when it was inadvertently hacked by a model being tested by OpenAI. Bloomberg Their success has sparked some soul-searching in France because in the case of Datadog and Hugging Face it has come outside the country. French President Emmanuel Macron has made turning the nation into a serious global AI competitor a policy priority. While illustrating prowess in engineering talent, the two companies have also shown the advantages of the US’ extensive capital markets in fueling tech company growth and wealth creation. Despite having headquarters in New York and living in Miami, Delangue has said the company considers itself Franco-American and is “strongly attached to France,” where most of its employees are based.



His first startup experience was with Moodstocks, a developer of machine-learning based on image recognition technology, that was bought by Google, according to his LinkedIn profile. He attended universities in Madrid, Dublin and Bangalore before going to a French business school and taking an online introduction to computer science course at Stanford University, where co-founder Chaumond had completed some of his studies. The deal — expected to close in the first half of 2027 — marks the biggest move yet by Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang to broaden the uptake of AI and extend his customer range. AP Photo/Jeffrey McWhorter They started their company a decade ago, choosing Hugging Face as a “temporary” name, and later joining billionaire Xavier Niel’s startup campus Station F, located in a redeveloped, century-old freight station in Paris. In a post on LinkedIn ahead of the deal announcement, Station F said the three first arrived in 2017 to develop a chatbot for teenagers, then pivoted, began raising money, and were set to become a “titan of an exit.” Singing robot Delangue has said they honed in on the idea of creating a platform for open-source models after co-founder Wolf spent a weekend re-packaging Google’s “Bert” model and then putting it online to great acclaim.



As chief science officer, Netherlands-based Wolf was one of the drivers behind Hugging Face’s release last month of a singing $US400 bipedal robot called Microduck, which he has said is aimed at showing AI is “very accessible” and not expensive or scary. The company’s foray into robotics came after it took over a French developer called Pollen Robotics. Like Chaumond, Wolf attended France’s elite engineering school Ecole Polytechnique. He then completed a PhD in physics and a law degree in Paris before practicing for six years as a European patent lawyer with clients including a roster of machine-learning startups. Related Article Opinion

Wall Street The world is facing a dual threat that could blow up markets Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Chaumond, who is chief technology officer and based in Brooklyn, counts himself among the co-founders of reading startup Glose, which was bought by Medium. On Thursday he posted what he said was a personal take on the deal, saying that AI is “at an inflection point,” where open source can become less relevant if big, closed labs run away with it. “Given Jensen’s stance on open source AI and how he stepped up to defend it when it was under threat, Nvidia was the only partner we truly considered,” Chaumond wrote.

World.title: ASX set to advance as Wall Street climbs; Nvidia rises after sealing $18b deal
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to advance as Wall Street climbs; Nvidia rises after sealing $18b deal Alex Veiga Updated September 4, 2026 — 6:12am ,first published 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Gains in big technology stocks and easing bond yields helped lift Wall Street even as oil prices ticked higher amid an escalation in the US war with Iran. The S&P 500 rose 1.1 per cent, with technology stocks powering much of the gains. The Dow climbed 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rose 1.4 per cent. Gains in big technology and communication services stocks led Wall Street higher. AP The Australian sharemarket is set for gains, with futures at 5.59am AEST pointing to a gain of 28 points, or 0.3 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.5 per cent on Thursday to snap a three-session losing streak. The Australian dollar is stronger at US72.05¢. Gains in big technology and communication services stocks led Wall Street higher. Their large market values tend to give them more influence over the broader market’s direction.



Microsoft rose 2.7 per cent, Apple gained 1 per cent and Meta climbed 3 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Wall Street The world is facing a dual threat that could blow up markets Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Giant chip maker Nvidia, whose high-end chips have emerged as AI’s best building blocks, rose 1.8 per cent after saying it would buy the artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face for $US13 billion ($18 billion). Markets rose in Europe, but ended mixed in Asia. Oil prices ticked higher as the six-month long US war with Iran intensified.



Iran fired at Kuwait on Thursday in retaliation for US bombardments earlier in the week. The fighting between the US and Iran heated up after the US hit Iranian rocket launchers Sunday on an island in the Strait of Hormuz, saying Iran was planning to use them to send mines into the waterway. The renewed fighting has sent US crude prices sharply higher this week, though the momentum cooled Thursday. After rising in the early going, the price of Brent crude, the international standard, was down 0.1 per cent to $US95.55 per barrel. Benchmark US crude rose 0.5 per cent to $US91.51 a barrel. Rising oil prices have added to existing inflationary pressures and exacerbated a bond-market sell-off earlier this week. But bond yields have shown signs of stabilising. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which influences mortgage rates, dropped to 4.76 per cent from 4.79 per cent late on Wednesday. It has been rising steadily throughout the year and was as low as 4.20 per cent at the beginning of 2026.



Related Article Exclusive

Credit cards How a legal loophole lets CBA and Westpac charge their most loyal customers more The yield on the 2-year Treasury, which closely tracks expectations for Federal Reserve moves on interest rates, slid to 4.33 per cent from 4.39 per cent. It remains significantly higher for the year, though, and was as low as 3.50 per cent at the beginning of 2026. Traders had their eye on several companies following their latest quarterly snapshots. Snowflake jumped 16.6 per cent after its quarterly profit and revenue blew past analysts’ estimates. The company noted that artificial intelligence continues to be a strong driver for its business. Other tech companies echoed the theme of strength in AI-related demand, but that wasn’t enough to send their stocks higher.



Broadcom’s results beat Wall Street’s estimates and the chipmaker forecast that its AI chip revenue would double in its fiscal year that ends in 2028. But its stock fell 2.7 per cent after its revenue outlook fell short of expectations. Hewlett Packard Enterprise also raised its guidance for cloud and AI demand strength as it reported quarterly results that topped analysts’ estimates. But the company’s shares slid 0.2 per cent on worries about supply constraints and other concerns. Elsewhere in the market, Tyson Foods fell 7.3 per cent after the meat company lowered its guidance for revenue and operating income for its fiscal year, citing margin compression due to volatile cattle prices amid a severe US cattle shortage. And Victoria’s Secret slumped 13.2 per cent after its latest quarterly earnings beat Wall Street estimates, but its revenue fell short of expectations. In economic news, the Labor Department reported Thursday that more Americans filed for unemployment benefits last week, but layoffs are still rare and jobless claims remain at historically low levels.



On Friday, the crucial US employment report for August is released. The previous report for July showed that the jobs market stalled, with employers cutting positions. Related Article Opinion

On Background ‘I was just weak’: How an avoidant Rupert Murdoch could have warded off family fight Calum Jaspan Media Writer Both inflation and the jobs market have been key focuses for Wall Street and the Federal Reserve. The Fed is trying to balance its tasks of supporting employment and taming inflation. Wall Street expects the central bank to raise interest rates before the year ends in an effort to cool inflation, which remains well above 3 per cent. The Fed has a stated goal of cooling inflation to a target of 2 per cent. The government will release August inflation figures September 11, shortly before the Fed’s policymaking committee’s next meeting, which ends on September 16.

World.title: Trump suggests he would not help UK in another Falklands clash
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeTrump diplomacy Trump suggests he would not help UK in another Falklands clash David Crowe September 4, 2026 — 5:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A casual remark from Donald Trump has heightened concerns in Britain about its military capacity after the US president seemed to dismiss the idea of helping one of America’s closest allies. Trump suggested the UK would not get his help in the event of a clash with Argentina over their rival claims to the Falkland Islands, where the two countries went to war in 1982. Trump has repeatedly linked the island dispute to the UK declining to send ships to help open the Strait of Hormuz. Bloomberg The president linked the issue to the Iran war by noting, as he has in the past, that former British prime minister Keir Starmer turned down his request for military support to help open the Strait of Hormuz. “Your country was not there to help me,” he told broadcaster GB News.



While Trump’s comments were brief and did not constitute a formal shift in foreign policy, they added to the debate in Britain over a potential conflict with Argentina, as its leader is becoming increasingly assertive about the territorial claim. Related Article FIFA World Cup ‘Build up the Royal Navy’: UK brawls over Falklands war after World Cup loss to Argentina Argentine President Javier Milei, one of Trump’s ideological allies and the beneficiary of generous White House support, this week declared the islands were a “sacred” claim for his country. When GB News asked Trump if he would back Britain in any dispute, the US president praised the UK for winning the 1982 war but cast doubt on whether he would help in another conflict. “I was there when they had the first war, that was a long time ago, and I watched it so carefully,” he said.



“And you comported yourselves very well. You took it back pretty strongly. “But it’s a long way away. That’s a big trip. It’s a long way. “So, your country’s not doing well. Don’t forget you get a big percentage of your oil from the Strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me. Your country was not there to help me.” British paratroopers march across East Falkland island during the 1982 war. Hulton Archive Trump made the complaint while also repeating his previous claim that the US did not need help from Britain in the war with Iran. He said he asked Starmer if the UK could send a “couple of ships” and was told the UK had none to spare.



The formal US policy on the conflict is to remain neutral on the rival claims. Under the Monroe Doctrine, declared two centuries ago, US administrations see the Americas as their own sphere of influence, not a domain for European powers. Related Article Middle East at war The US warship that spent too much time at sea finally gets a break Under Trump, the “Donroe Doctrine” dictates that America comes first. And the US president will only help those who give him what he wants – whether it is Greenland or a fleet of ships in the Persian Gulf. While the US said it was neutral in the 1982 war, it leaned toward Britain when Argentina’s military junta ordered an invasion of the islands. US president Ronald Reagan kept up supplies of military material to the UK when British prime minister, Margaret Thatcher, sent a fleet to the South Atlantic to reclaim the formal British territory. The British victory was followed by the crumbling of the Argentine military dictatorship, under which an estimated 30,000 people were murdered, and many others were targeted in human rights abuses over eight years.



The Royal Navy had almost 200 vessels at the time of the Falklands War, while it has about 70 today, including some that are being decommissioned. MPs have warned in a series of reports that the country needs a stronger military. Labour MP Tan Dhesi, the chair of the House of Commons defence committee, this week urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to spend more on defence – and he named concerns about the US as one of the reasons. Trump with Argentine President Javier Milei in January, who is seem as one of his major ideological allies. Bloomberg “The British people should be under no illusion that the nation faces a significantly increased threat level, especially from Russia, but also that we have a US leadership for whom European security is no longer a focus or a priority,” Dhesi told parliament. “That is why it is imperative that we invest in our armed forces in the here and now, rather than being sorry later.”



Related Article Analysis

UK politics Britain’s budget blues will end Burnham’s honeymoon Burnham’s office has issued a statement that repeats the British claim to the Falklands, which have been British territory since 1833 and were first sighted by an English captain in 1592. There were no indigenous inhabitants. The key unknown is whether Milei will seek to provoke Britain rather than merely repeat his rhetoric about Argentina’s claim to the islands. Would he really start a serious fight? That would be utterly irrational. Even so, the war of 1982 illustrates the key risk for Britain: some governments are quite capable of starting stupid wars. World.title: Missing out on Katseye was the best thing to happen to this rising pop star
World.content:
CultureMusicReview Missing out on Katseye was the best thing to happen to this rising pop star Robert Moran and Barry Divola September 4, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Adela’s debut album is essential pop. Adela, Prima ★★★★★ Failure can be a difficult stench to shake for aspiring pop stars. For Adela Jergova, the Slovak singer-songwriter who’s about to become your favourite new pop star, it could’ve proved terminal. Her public debut to most was on Netflix’s Pop Star Academy: Katseye, where she was one of the desperate hopefuls who didn’t make the cut for the global K-pop girl group Katseye. On that series she was an elder mentor of sorts at 18, a favourite among the industry experts for her strong singing and dancing skills but a complete bust among the fan votes. In the end she was the first contestant eliminated, her pop dreams dashed unbearably close to the dangling carrot.



Considering what’s happened to Katseye in their short history – just last month they lost their second member to a “health hiatus” – Jergova’s outcome on the show looks like a blessing. Almost four years on she has built an aesthetic identity on her own Eurotrash terms, and now a debut album that’s the best pop baptism since Addison. The Slovak singer-songwriter leans into her outsider status on Prima. On Prima, the cast-off narrative serves her persona well: she’s the rebellious pop outsider the corporate machine couldn’t control, a lone wolf with something to prove. (Never mind that she’s signed to Capitol Records, an imprint of the behemoth Universal Music Group; illusion is the language of pop.) Raucous opener KGB dives straight into her story, with dirty electro-pop that plays on her ethnic background. She’s the kid in post-communist Eastern Europe, plotting her pop future by studying Disney Channel stars and Y2K-era MTV videos ’til her eyes are “bloody”. “I was like eight, working the night shift to learn English,” she sings over glitchy handbag house – the hip production credits include 100 Gecs’ Dylan Brady and The Dare’s Harrison Patrick Smith – marrying her pop aspirations to the wider immigrant struggle.



Her songs showcase the exacting detail of her pop studies. Stellar lead single Ain’t in LA – with its loser reclamation, “I’d rather be a nobody than be like everyone!” – blends Miley’s We Can’t Stop with Salem’s chopped and screwed wooziness, while Nicole Kidman bizarrely borrows Kanye’s golden-era chiptune soul, a handful of tacky references to Our Nicole (“Moulin Rouge, my corset is so tight/Babygirl in control, I feel like Nicole”) and somehow makes it feel effortlessly fun. Boys and Fantasize, meanwhile, throw back to In the Zone-era Britney, all head voice and coquettish whispers. It’s enough to get you excited for Adela’s inevitable MTV VMAs performance (Jergova has trained in ballet since she was three), once you’re done doing your own hip thrusts and hair-whips in the kitchen. But it’s the personal indulgences that make Prima essential pop. On Therapy, a devastating stream of consciousness that takes Charli XCX’s tilt towards vulnerability to its extreme, she sings raspily about the sacrifices she’s made for her pop aspirations, such as leaving her family behind in Slovakia and not seeing her sister grow up, and the drive behind it all (“I wanna move my mum out here, but I don’t have that kinda money”). It’s definitely not the sort of thing you’d get to make being in a girl group for K-pop conglomerate Hybe. Adela’s infectious attitude on Prima reminds us you can’t spell failure without an “f” and “u”. Robert Moran



Dinosaur Jr’s new album is as consistent as death and taxes. Dinosaur Jr, There Near ★★★ As someone who has interviewed Dinosaur Jr main man J Mascis more than once, I can confidently say the man prefers to speak through his guitar. He has the demeanour of a sloth in conversation, and his wall of Marshall amps makes all the noise he needs to communicate. No wheels are reinvented on the 13th Dinosaur Jr album, which is fair enough, but at times it’s like, “Is this actually the same wheel?” Several Got Away has the familiarly fuzzy guitars, yawning vocals and teeth-rattling solo that have made songs like The Wagon so enduring, even if it is the sonic equivalent of a shrug. Everything is cranked to 11 – so far, so normal – until you get to Take Me With You and realise that Mascis’s amps must actually go to 12.



There’s not much point quoting lyrics. Mascis himself points out in the album bio, “I try not too hard to think about any of it”, and the lyric sheet backs this up. Bass player Lou Barlow gets his obligatory two songs, the mid-paced kiss-off Blowin’ Up and the pointed No One’s Ready, where the recurring line “no one’s ready for your war” leaves little doubt about his target. So yeah, it’s a “not bad” Dinosaur Jr album. Mascis probably wouldn’t say much more than that, so neither will I. Barry Divola

World.title: The critics have spoken: Add these books to the stack
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There are some big forces at work in this week’s new releases: oceans, technology, history, motherhood and the occasional supernatural presence. Our five novels range from a Hawaiian love story shaped by disaster to a wonderfully strange satire in which childbirth produces a rather alarming new mother. In non-fiction, Thomas Mayo considers fathers and sons, George Megalogenis takes Australia’s temperature, and Toby Walsh contemplates a future dominated by AI. Fiction Photo: Everything to the Sea by Alicia Upano (Bloomsbury, $35)

Hawaiian writer Alicia Upano delivers an impressively restrained love story from amid the epic ruin caused by a tsunami. Growing up in Hilo, Hawaii, Jane is an architecture student whose ambitions call her away to university. Summer holidays draw her back to Hilo, where she falls unexpectedly in love with Kenji – a family-oriented friend who works in construction. The summer fling gets serious, and Jane invites Kenji to live with her in Honolulu. Passion will soon turn to grief, when a tsunami devastates Hilo and Kenji rushes back to assist. A traumatised Jane can’t face the life that has been swept away, leading to an estrangement between them. Some of the novel’s most sensitive writing describes how Jane and Kenji tentatively re-establish contact years later and discover their true feelings about a love derailed. Everything to the Sea is a nuanced literary romance, with lively, well-observed characterisation, understated humour, and a narrative that draws force from the conflict of values between the lovers. Reconciliation is a vital theme, and it’s embedded within a piercing portrayal of the pain and struggle of community recovery in the aftermath of a catastrophic event. Photo: Mother Waters by Lisa Nan Joo (Affirm Press, $35)

A subgenre of feminist gothic cli-fi has emerged lately. Books in this vein feature a strong female protagonist (usually a scientist) embarking on a survival adventure; they tend to take place in extreme natural environments, with flickers of the numinous haunting the action. Where Charlotte McConaghy’s Wild Dark Shore did it with subantarctic islands, Lisa Nan Joo descends into the lightless depths of the ocean.



Mother Waters follows Charlie, a bioacoustic specialist who has lost herself in marriage. Walking out on her husband on their fifth wedding anniversary, she rededicates herself to a career exploring the sounds of life beneath the waves, even as she remains haunted by her father’s death. He was lost at sea when she was a girl, and his memory is one ghost lying in wait on a planned deep-sea expedition. Funded by a billionaire’s son, Dexter, who’s battling his own father’s difficult legacy, the mission will descend into the otherworldly refuge of an oceanic trench. It’s an unsettling odyssey, marrying psychological and political obstacles (especially those facing women in science) to the greater problems caused by our war against nature. Photo: The Wild Beneath by Kelly Anderson (Text Publishing, $35)

Another title in this subgeneric surge, Kelly Anderson’s The Wild Beneath makes more of a ripple than a splash – despite using another tsunami as a hook. On the Pacific Northwest coast, 20-year-old Annie MacLeod has always been deeply attuned to the sea, yet it will be the source of a disaster that strikes just as adulthood arrives. When a tsunami washes away her parents and much of her hometown, it leaves Annie and her childhood sweetheart, Evan, as survivors. But when Annie saves a strange, mute young man called Walker from the wrack and wreckage, a visceral bond forms between them. They seem bound by something as ancient as the waves, including a private language: Walker emits a hum that only Annie can hear. A predictable love triangle develops, and it’s the formulaic quality of The Wild Beneath that fails to satisfy. What should be a turbulent coming-of-age romance, awash with trauma and wonder, resorts to uninspired prose and superficial characterisation, and the book’s uneven pacing and tone can make its wildness seem rather tame. Photo: The Perfect Circle by Claudia Petrucci (Wakefield Press, $35)

Italian author Claudia Petrucci’s The Perfect Circle is a pleasingly patterned feminist ghost story. A real estate agent, Irene, is called upon for a hard sell. The “round house” on Via Saterna in Milan is known for its circular staircase and interiors, despite its square facade. It’s also haunted by a woman, Lidia, who’s reputed to have died there. Reports of her death may be exaggerated, and the novel unfolds in dual timelines – one moving towards death, one towards new life – as Irene begins to expose the secrets of the haunted house, and the twisted geometries of space and time combine to disorienting effect. The Perfect Circle creates an escalating sense of unease: the haunted house trope here is a vehicle for exploring gaps between the illusion and reality of women’s experience over everything from romantic love to motherhood. It’s a ghost story that also bears a fascinating resemblance to high-concept detective metafiction – to Borgesian labyrinths, say, or the existential architectural horror of Mark Z. Danielewski’s House of Leaves.



Photo: But Won’t I Miss Me by Tiffany Tsao (HarperVia, $35)

When it comes to satirising the social expectations of women regarding pregnancy and motherhood, no plot device could be too outrageous. Tiffany Tsao hits upon a sensational speculative trick. In the world of But Won’t I Miss Me, new mothers gain superhuman powers in the final stage of delivery – the “Rebirth” – in which they spawn a “fetal mother”. This doppelganger is identical to the mother, rapidly grows to adult size, and promptly cannibalises and replaces them with a new self – indestructible, ideally maternal, and with an endless (and renewable) supply of energy. All perfectly normal, except to Vivi, whose Rebirth goes awry, leaving her weakened by postpartum depression. To save herself and her child, Vivi must flee to an uncle and an underworld that society has left behind. She becomes an electrician to serve people who have gone off-grid, and dystopian answers loom to the question of what happened to Vivi during her pregnancy. Tsao’s idea is a brilliant one. True, the world-building isn’t always as well executed as this speculative feminist parable deserves, but it should attract a wide audience with its unflinching critique of the pressures of motherhood. Non-fiction Photo: Dear Son by Thomas Mayo (Hardie Grant, $35)

In 2021, when the first edition of this book was published, Thomas Mayo was confident that racism was on the wane. Travelling the country to take the Uluru Statement from the Heart to the wider community, he’d been struck by the positivity. Everything changed, however, when the Nationals and the Liberals announced they opposed the Voice referendum. A torrent of hatred was unleashed. Despite this dark event and the shadow of intergenerational trauma, these letters by Indigenous men to their fathers or their sons are suffused with love and compassion. At the same time, the history that shaped them and their fathers is never far from the surface. Stan Grant writes of the “deep well of pain” he saw in his father’s eyes. And how glad he is that life has been easier for his son. “Writing to you,” says Mayo to his son, “has been like an antidote for the vestiges of toxic masculinity learnt from father figures, peers and Western culture. I’m still unlearning.” These soul-searching letters are a soulful reckoning with what it means to be a First Nations father and son.



Photo: Three Shocks by George Megalogenis (Penguin, $37)

Alfred Deakin, our second prime minister, declared that he would “have no traffic with the unclean thing” of “coloured immigration”. When George Megalogenis was growing up in Melbourne in the 1960s and ’70s, this attitude lingered in the playground where he was called “dirty” because of his olive skin. Even as a boy, he sensed that this was an argument about belonging: “Australia’s perpetual agony of identity”. While most of Three Shocks is political and demographic analysis, this brief foray into memoir captures the origins of Megalogenis’ attunement to the changes in the make-up of our society in recent decades and his insights into how our politicians are lagging the electorate. Migrants and their children now constitute the majority of the Australian population – this is the first shock. The second is that professional women now outnumber blue-collar men in the workforce. The third concerns uncertainty in global alliances and Australians’ wariness of the US and China. Having drilled down into the data and surveyed shifts in the body politic, Megalogenis distils powerful trends that politicians would be wise to heed. Photo: Wild Hope by Claire Scobie (NewSouth, $37)

Claire Scobie calls it her “ecophony”. An epiphany of the ecological variety. Ordinary people can wait for governments to “do something” about the urgent crises of our times, she realised, or they can instigate change themselves. As a storyteller, Scobie set out to find the innovators who were showing how things can be done differently. The term that underpins all their stories is “regenerative thinking”. For farmers Dianne and Ian Haggerty, this means taking infertile land and creating a drought-resistant, chemical-free ecosystem for crops and top-grade wool. For Regen Melbourne, it’s about being the “engine” for the community collaboration behind the push to make the Yarra fit for swimming and for the creatures that live in it. Scobie’s own story binds these hopeful stories together as she moves with her husband, Gumbaynggirr man Aden Ridgeway, to his Country on the mid-north coast of NSW, and discovers what regeneration might mean in her own life.
