World.title: A quarter-billion-dollar mistake? Queensland’s diesel bus route slammed
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandElectric vehicles A quarter-billion-dollar mistake? Queensland’s diesel bus route slammed Cameron Atfield September 4, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A leading electric bus company has blasted the Queensland government’s purchase of 630 diesel buses, saying the decision could be a mistake that would eventually cost the state’s taxpayers a quarter of a billion dollars. Queensland Transport Minister Brent Mickelberg launched a procurement process for up to 630 new diesel-fuelled buses on Tuesday, at the same time blasting the former Labor government’s electric bus plan as “buying big, expensive paperweights to block local streets” due to a lack of associated charging infrastructure. Mickelberg defended the move on Thursday, arguing that immediate fleet upgrades were required for local depots that are not yet equipped for electric infrastructure. A Zenobe electric bus-charging system in Sydney. But Zenobe Energy’s Australia and New Zealand country director, Gareth Ridge, told this masthead Queensland’s decision to mandate diesel in its procurement program could prove costly.



The UK-based company entered the Australian market in 2023, on the back of a $1.7 billion capital-raise led by private equity giant KKR, building an electric bus depot at Leichhardt, in Sydney’s inner-west. Zenobe Australia-New Zealand country director Gareth Ridge. Oscar Colman “I would have thought that a tender like this would be technology-agnostic and would allow the market, whatever the technology that comes out, to decide,” Ridge said. “Putting aside the carbon [emissions] and whether it’s zero-emission or not, one thing that everyone should care about is the best value-for-money procurement option, and then that pulls away from the debates around climate. “You would probably see a clear winner on a financial case, and no one needs to debate whether it’s clean or green or not, because I think the winner will be both clean, green, and be cheaper as well.”



Energy Futures Foundation executive director Bruce Hardy said responsible economic management demanded an open tender, where all technologies could bid on an equal footing. Related Article Electric vehicles Soaring EV sales to shield Australia from fuel shortages “Not doing so is a betrayal of Queensland taxpayers and ratepayers, who miss out from seeing the best deals the market has to offer,” he said. Hardy said, at a time of increased fuel costs due to conflict in the Middle East, Queensland taxpayers should be furious that the government was “picking winners without properly comparing bids”. “If the government is so sure about electric bus technology, why wouldn’t they let electric bus companies bid for the tender?” he said.



“They simply don’t want to have to justify their decision to go with a more expensive diesel option in an open process if electric buses powered by Queensland sunshine come back cheaper and more reliable.” Mickelberg said the bus industry found the former Labor government’s electric buses plan “overly ambitious”. The Brisbane Metro bus system runs on electric/battery power. Courtney Kruk “This tender is for buses to be stored at facilities without either recharging or alternative fuelling facilities, but we remain technology-agnostic for future purchases and depot constructions,” he said. Addressing the minister’s concerns about depot infrastructure, Ridge said that while upfront costs for electric buses exceeded those of diesel, they proved far cheaper over the vehicle’s lifespan.



“Definitely, there’s a premium if you’re looking at it just purely on what you are buying today – the buses are maybe around 15 per cent more expensive and you’ve got all the depot upgrades, which for 600 buses would be in the order of $100 million,” he said. “There is a significant upfront premium that you pay, but looking at that in isolation is not quite accurate because you’re going to have all the operating costs that go with it. “You really need to look at this from a whole-of-life or a total-cost-of-ownership perspective to see how it really stacks up.” Ridge said, based on Zenobe’s dealings with governments across the Western world, Queensland was an outlier in its pursuit of diesel. “Sure, we’ve seen some small numbers to plug some gaps, but the scale of this procurement is nothing that we’ve seen,” he said.



The electric vehicle industry has lined up to condemn the Crisafulli government’s diesel policy. Australian Electric Vehicle Association Queensland branch director Nathan Gore-Brown took particular aim at Mickelberg’s “paperweight” comment, which he said was ill-informed. “This is not a risk his interstate counterparts seem worried about,” he said. Electric Vehicle Council chief executive Julie Delvecchio said the policy exposed Queenslanders to health risks. “Queensland communities will be paying for this decision – in asthma treatment, preventable hospitalisations and lung disease – for years to come,” she said.



“These diesel vehicles will still be on the road come the 2032 Olympics, spewing out pollution for decades to come, right when the eyes of the world will fall on the Sunshine State. “We urge the Queensland government to make the tender for these 630 buses open to all fuel types so that they can consider the best solution which is cheaper to run, cleaner electric buses.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Donaldson given rare start as Kiss rings in mass changes for Wallabies
World.content:
Western Force five-eighth Ben Donaldson has been placed in the driver’s seat by the Wallabies for the first time in two years after Les Kiss again rang in mass changes for the second Test against Argentina in Mendoza.

The Wallabies coach has made eight changes to the starting side – and 14 overall – that beat the Pumas in Jujuy last week, with an all-new front-row, Harry Wilson returning as captain in the backrow and big changes in the key spots of the Wallabies’ backline.

Ben Donaldson scoring against Italy in July. Getty Images

As forecast, Donaldson has been given a shot in the No.10 jersey, which will be his first appearance in the starting role since the second Test against Argentina in 2024 in Santa Fe, which the Wallabies lost 67-27. It is the highest score ever conceded by Australia.

The man Donaldson replaced, Carter Gordon, has overcome a minor calf issue and will come off the bench.

World.title: French trio minted as billionaires as the world’s most valuable company swoops
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMergers & acquisitions French trio minted as billionaires as the world’s most valuable company swoops Tara Patel and Dylan Sloan September 4, 2026 — 6:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hugging Face’s three French founders have emerged as billionaires after the artificial intelligence platform agreed to be acquired by Nvidia a decade after they first started the company with a completely different focus. Clement “Clem” Delangue, 38, Julien Chaumond, 42, and Thomas Wolf, 41, will each have a net worth of about $US1.8 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, which is valuing their fortunes for the first time. Nvidia agreed to buy the startup in a transaction valued at roughly $US13 billion. Clem Delangue (pictured), Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf will stay with the company after the deal goes through. Bloomberg A spokesperson for Brooklyn-based Hugging Face, which began in 2016 in Paris, didn’t respond to requests for comment about the founders’ wealth. The deal — expected to close in the first half of 2027 — marks the biggest move yet by Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang to broaden the uptake of AI and extend his customer range. It’s also a big test for Hugging Face, which has long backed keeping the industry open and decentralised, boasting it’s “on a mission to democratise good machine learning” and describing itself as being like an AI library.



“I am honored that Clem came to me as he considered the next chapter of Hugging Face and believed Nvidia would be a great home for the company,” Huang said in a blog post announcing the deal. Related Article Wall Street Apple’s value grew by $1b a day for 15 years under Tim Cook. But he had one big flaw Hugging Face operates a platform for sharing AI models that can be used freely by others. It was at the centre of a cybersecurity incident this year when it was inadvertently hacked by a model being tested by OpenAI. Under the deal unveiled, Nvidia pledged Hugging Face will remain an open platform, with users able to upload and download AI models and datasets of their choosing. The co-founders will remain at the company under a six-year retention agreement, Wolf said in an interview on Bloomberg TV. The three co-founders have made public accessibility to cheaper, open-source AI models their mantra, even organizing a street march in San Francisco earlier this year in support of the principle.



“I think it would be a really great world if we can enable, empower more people to be AI builders because it means that we won’t outsource that to just a couple of labs in Silicon Valley,” Delangue, who is chief executive officer, said earlier this year at a conference. The Hugging Face trio join the three founders of Paris-based Mistral AI as French nationals who have become billionaires through their stakes in AI and computing companies. Also included in the cohort are Olivier Pomel and Alexis Le-Quoc, founders of New York-based Datadog. The company was at the centre of a cybersecurity incident this year when it was inadvertently hacked by a model being tested by OpenAI. Bloomberg Their success has sparked some soul-searching in France because in the case of Datadog and Hugging Face it has come outside the country. French President Emmanuel Macron has made turning the nation into a serious global AI competitor a policy priority. While illustrating prowess in engineering talent, the two companies have also shown the advantages of the US’ extensive capital markets in fueling tech company growth and wealth creation. Despite having headquarters in New York and living in Miami, Delangue has said the company considers itself Franco-American and is “strongly attached to France,” where most of its employees are based.



His first startup experience was with Moodstocks, a developer of machine-learning based on image recognition technology, that was bought by Google, according to his LinkedIn profile. He attended universities in Madrid, Dublin and Bangalore before going to a French business school and taking an online introduction to computer science course at Stanford University, where co-founder Chaumond had completed some of his studies. The deal — expected to close in the first half of 2027 — marks the biggest move yet by Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang to broaden the uptake of AI and extend his customer range. AP Photo/Jeffrey McWhorter They started their company a decade ago, choosing Hugging Face as a “temporary” name, and later joining billionaire Xavier Niel’s startup campus Station F, located in a redeveloped, century-old freight station in Paris. In a post on LinkedIn ahead of the deal announcement, Station F said the three first arrived in 2017 to develop a chatbot for teenagers, then pivoted, began raising money, and were set to become a “titan of an exit.” Singing robot Delangue has said they honed in on the idea of creating a platform for open-source models after co-founder Wolf spent a weekend re-packaging Google’s “Bert” model and then putting it online to great acclaim.



As chief science officer, Netherlands-based Wolf was one of the drivers behind Hugging Face’s release last month of a singing $US400 bipedal robot called Microduck, which he has said is aimed at showing AI is “very accessible” and not expensive or scary. The company’s foray into robotics came after it took over a French developer called Pollen Robotics. Like Chaumond, Wolf attended France’s elite engineering school Ecole Polytechnique. He then completed a PhD in physics and a law degree in Paris before practicing for six years as a European patent lawyer with clients including a roster of machine-learning startups. Related Article Opinion

Wall Street The world is facing a dual threat that could blow up markets Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Chaumond, who is chief technology officer and based in Brooklyn, counts himself among the co-founders of reading startup Glose, which was bought by Medium. On Thursday he posted what he said was a personal take on the deal, saying that AI is “at an inflection point,” where open source can become less relevant if big, closed labs run away with it. “Given Jensen’s stance on open source AI and how he stepped up to defend it when it was under threat, Nvidia was the only partner we truly considered,” Chaumond wrote.

World.title: ASX set to advance as Wall Street climbs; Nvidia rises after sealing $18b deal
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to advance as Wall Street climbs; Nvidia rises after sealing $18b deal Alex Veiga Updated September 4, 2026 — 6:12am ,first published 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Gains in big technology stocks and easing bond yields helped lift Wall Street even as oil prices ticked higher amid an escalation in the US war with Iran. The S&P 500 rose 1.1 per cent, with technology stocks powering much of the gains. The Dow climbed 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rose 1.4 per cent. Gains in big technology and communication services stocks led Wall Street higher. AP The Australian sharemarket is set for gains, with futures at 5.59am AEST pointing to a gain of 28 points, or 0.3 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.5 per cent on Thursday to snap a three-session losing streak. The Australian dollar is stronger at US72.05¢. Gains in big technology and communication services stocks led Wall Street higher. Their large market values tend to give them more influence over the broader market’s direction.



Microsoft rose 2.7 per cent, Apple gained 1 per cent and Meta climbed 3 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Wall Street The world is facing a dual threat that could blow up markets Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Giant chip maker Nvidia, whose high-end chips have emerged as AI’s best building blocks, rose 1.8 per cent after saying it would buy the artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face for $US13 billion ($18 billion). Markets rose in Europe, but ended mixed in Asia. Oil prices ticked higher as the six-month long US war with Iran intensified.



Iran fired at Kuwait on Thursday in retaliation for US bombardments earlier in the week. The fighting between the US and Iran heated up after the US hit Iranian rocket launchers Sunday on an island in the Strait of Hormuz, saying Iran was planning to use them to send mines into the waterway. The renewed fighting has sent US crude prices sharply higher this week, though the momentum cooled Thursday. After rising in the early going, the price of Brent crude, the international standard, was down 0.1 per cent to $US95.55 per barrel. Benchmark US crude rose 0.5 per cent to $US91.51 a barrel. Rising oil prices have added to existing inflationary pressures and exacerbated a bond-market sell-off earlier this week. But bond yields have shown signs of stabilising. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which influences mortgage rates, dropped to 4.76 per cent from 4.79 per cent late on Wednesday. It has been rising steadily throughout the year and was as low as 4.20 per cent at the beginning of 2026.



Related Article Exclusive

Credit cards How a legal loophole lets CBA and Westpac charge their most loyal customers more The yield on the 2-year Treasury, which closely tracks expectations for Federal Reserve moves on interest rates, slid to 4.33 per cent from 4.39 per cent. It remains significantly higher for the year, though, and was as low as 3.50 per cent at the beginning of 2026. Traders had their eye on several companies following their latest quarterly snapshots. Snowflake jumped 16.6 per cent after its quarterly profit and revenue blew past analysts’ estimates. The company noted that artificial intelligence continues to be a strong driver for its business. Other tech companies echoed the theme of strength in AI-related demand, but that wasn’t enough to send their stocks higher.



Broadcom’s results beat Wall Street’s estimates and the chipmaker forecast that its AI chip revenue would double in its fiscal year that ends in 2028. But its stock fell 2.7 per cent after its revenue outlook fell short of expectations. Hewlett Packard Enterprise also raised its guidance for cloud and AI demand strength as it reported quarterly results that topped analysts’ estimates. But the company’s shares slid 0.2 per cent on worries about supply constraints and other concerns. Elsewhere in the market, Tyson Foods fell 7.3 per cent after the meat company lowered its guidance for revenue and operating income for its fiscal year, citing margin compression due to volatile cattle prices amid a severe US cattle shortage. And Victoria’s Secret slumped 13.2 per cent after its latest quarterly earnings beat Wall Street estimates, but its revenue fell short of expectations. In economic news, the Labor Department reported Thursday that more Americans filed for unemployment benefits last week, but layoffs are still rare and jobless claims remain at historically low levels.



On Friday, the crucial US employment report for August is released. The previous report for July showed that the jobs market stalled, with employers cutting positions. Related Article Opinion

On Background ‘I was just weak’: How an avoidant Rupert Murdoch could have warded off family fight Calum Jaspan Media Writer Both inflation and the jobs market have been key focuses for Wall Street and the Federal Reserve. The Fed is trying to balance its tasks of supporting employment and taming inflation. Wall Street expects the central bank to raise interest rates before the year ends in an effort to cool inflation, which remains well above 3 per cent. The Fed has a stated goal of cooling inflation to a target of 2 per cent. The government will release August inflation figures September 11, shortly before the Fed’s policymaking committee’s next meeting, which ends on September 16.

World.title: Trump suggests he would not help UK in another Falklands clash
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeTrump diplomacy Trump suggests he would not help UK in another Falklands clash David Crowe September 4, 2026 — 5:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A casual remark from Donald Trump has heightened concerns in Britain about its military capacity after the US president seemed to dismiss the idea of helping one of America’s closest allies. Trump suggested the UK would not get his help in the event of a clash with Argentina over their rival claims to the Falkland Islands, where the two countries went to war in 1982. Trump has repeatedly linked the island dispute to the UK declining to send ships to help open the Strait of Hormuz. Bloomberg The president linked the issue to the Iran war by noting, as he has in the past, that former British prime minister Keir Starmer turned down his request for military support to help open the Strait of Hormuz. “Your country was not there to help me,” he told broadcaster GB News.



While Trump’s comments were brief and did not constitute a formal shift in foreign policy, they added to the debate in Britain over a potential conflict with Argentina, as its leader is becoming increasingly assertive about the territorial claim. Related Article FIFA World Cup ‘Build up the Royal Navy’: UK brawls over Falklands war after World Cup loss to Argentina Argentine President Javier Milei, one of Trump’s ideological allies and the beneficiary of generous White House support, this week declared the islands were a “sacred” claim for his country. When GB News asked Trump if he would back Britain in any dispute, the US president praised the UK for winning the 1982 war but cast doubt on whether he would help in another conflict. “I was there when they had the first war, that was a long time ago, and I watched it so carefully,” he said.



“And you comported yourselves very well. You took it back pretty strongly. “But it’s a long way away. That’s a big trip. It’s a long way. “So, your country’s not doing well. Don’t forget you get a big percentage of your oil from the Strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me. Your country was not there to help me.” British paratroopers march across East Falkland island during the 1982 war. Hulton Archive Trump made the complaint while also repeating his previous claim that the US did not need help from Britain in the war with Iran. He said he asked Starmer if the UK could send a “couple of ships” and was told the UK had none to spare.



The formal US policy on the conflict is to remain neutral on the rival claims. Under the Monroe Doctrine, declared two centuries ago, US administrations see the Americas as their own sphere of influence, not a domain for European powers. Related Article Middle East at war The US warship that spent too much time at sea finally gets a break Under Trump, the “Donroe Doctrine” dictates that America comes first. And the US president will only help those who give him what he wants – whether it is Greenland or a fleet of ships in the Persian Gulf. While the US said it was neutral in the 1982 war, it leaned toward Britain when Argentina’s military junta ordered an invasion of the islands. US president Ronald Reagan kept up supplies of military material to the UK when British prime minister, Margaret Thatcher, sent a fleet to the South Atlantic to reclaim the formal British territory. The British victory was followed by the crumbling of the Argentine military dictatorship, under which an estimated 30,000 people were murdered, and many others were targeted in human rights abuses over eight years.



The Royal Navy had almost 200 vessels at the time of the Falklands War, while it has about 70 today, including some that are being decommissioned. MPs have warned in a series of reports that the country needs a stronger military. Labour MP Tan Dhesi, the chair of the House of Commons defence committee, this week urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to spend more on defence – and he named concerns about the US as one of the reasons. Trump with Argentine President Javier Milei in January, who is seem as one of his major ideological allies. Bloomberg “The British people should be under no illusion that the nation faces a significantly increased threat level, especially from Russia, but also that we have a US leadership for whom European security is no longer a focus or a priority,” Dhesi told parliament. “That is why it is imperative that we invest in our armed forces in the here and now, rather than being sorry later.”



Related Article Analysis

UK politics Britain’s budget blues will end Burnham’s honeymoon Burnham’s office has issued a statement that repeats the British claim to the Falklands, which have been British territory since 1833 and were first sighted by an English captain in 1592. There were no indigenous inhabitants. The key unknown is whether Milei will seek to provoke Britain rather than merely repeat his rhetoric about Argentina’s claim to the islands. Would he really start a serious fight? That would be utterly irrational. Even so, the war of 1982 illustrates the key risk for Britain: some governments are quite capable of starting stupid wars. World.title: Missing out on Katseye was the best thing to happen to this rising pop star
World.content:
CultureMusicReview Missing out on Katseye was the best thing to happen to this rising pop star Robert Moran and Barry Divola September 4, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Adela’s debut album is essential pop. Adela, Prima ★★★★★ Failure can be a difficult stench to shake for aspiring pop stars. For Adela Jergova, the Slovak singer-songwriter who’s about to become your favourite new pop star, it could’ve proved terminal. Her public debut to most was on Netflix’s Pop Star Academy: Katseye, where she was one of the desperate hopefuls who didn’t make the cut for the global K-pop girl group Katseye. On that series she was an elder mentor of sorts at 18, a favourite among the industry experts for her strong singing and dancing skills but a complete bust among the fan votes. In the end she was the first contestant eliminated, her pop dreams dashed unbearably close to the dangling carrot.



Considering what’s happened to Katseye in their short history – just last month they lost their second member to a “health hiatus” – Jergova’s outcome on the show looks like a blessing. Almost four years on she has built an aesthetic identity on her own Eurotrash terms, and now a debut album that’s the best pop baptism since Addison. The Slovak singer-songwriter leans into her outsider status on Prima. On Prima, the cast-off narrative serves her persona well: she’s the rebellious pop outsider the corporate machine couldn’t control, a lone wolf with something to prove. (Never mind that she’s signed to Capitol Records, an imprint of the behemoth Universal Music Group; illusion is the language of pop.) Raucous opener KGB dives straight into her story, with dirty electro-pop that plays on her ethnic background. She’s the kid in post-communist Eastern Europe, plotting her pop future by studying Disney Channel stars and Y2K-era MTV videos ’til her eyes are “bloody”. “I was like eight, working the night shift to learn English,” she sings over glitchy handbag house – the hip production credits include 100 Gecs’ Dylan Brady and The Dare’s Harrison Patrick Smith – marrying her pop aspirations to the wider immigrant struggle.



Her songs showcase the exacting detail of her pop studies. Stellar lead single Ain’t in LA – with its loser reclamation, “I’d rather be a nobody than be like everyone!” – blends Miley’s We Can’t Stop with Salem’s chopped and screwed wooziness, while Nicole Kidman bizarrely borrows Kanye’s golden-era chiptune soul, a handful of tacky references to Our Nicole (“Moulin Rouge, my corset is so tight/Babygirl in control, I feel like Nicole”) and somehow makes it feel effortlessly fun. Boys and Fantasize, meanwhile, throw back to In the Zone-era Britney, all head voice and coquettish whispers. It’s enough to get you excited for Adela’s inevitable MTV VMAs performance (Jergova has trained in ballet since she was three), once you’re done doing your own hip thrusts and hair-whips in the kitchen. But it’s the personal indulgences that make Prima essential pop. On Therapy, a devastating stream of consciousness that takes Charli XCX’s tilt towards vulnerability to its extreme, she sings raspily about the sacrifices she’s made for her pop aspirations, such as leaving her family behind in Slovakia and not seeing her sister grow up, and the drive behind it all (“I wanna move my mum out here, but I don’t have that kinda money”). It’s definitely not the sort of thing you’d get to make being in a girl group for K-pop conglomerate Hybe. Adela’s infectious attitude on Prima reminds us you can’t spell failure without an “f” and “u”. Robert Moran



Dinosaur Jr’s new album is as consistent as death and taxes. Dinosaur Jr, There Near ★★★ As someone who has interviewed Dinosaur Jr main man J Mascis more than once, I can confidently say the man prefers to speak through his guitar. He has the demeanour of a sloth in conversation, and his wall of Marshall amps makes all the noise he needs to communicate. No wheels are reinvented on the 13th Dinosaur Jr album, which is fair enough, but at times it’s like, “Is this actually the same wheel?” Several Got Away has the familiarly fuzzy guitars, yawning vocals and teeth-rattling solo that have made songs like The Wagon so enduring, even if it is the sonic equivalent of a shrug. Everything is cranked to 11 – so far, so normal – until you get to Take Me With You and realise that Mascis’s amps must actually go to 12.



There’s not much point quoting lyrics. Mascis himself points out in the album bio, “I try not too hard to think about any of it”, and the lyric sheet backs this up. Bass player Lou Barlow gets his obligatory two songs, the mid-paced kiss-off Blowin’ Up and the pointed No One’s Ready, where the recurring line “no one’s ready for your war” leaves little doubt about his target. So yeah, it’s a “not bad” Dinosaur Jr album. Mascis probably wouldn’t say much more than that, so neither will I. Barry Divola

World.title: The critics have spoken: Add these books to the stack
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There are some big forces at work in this week’s new releases: oceans, technology, history, motherhood and the occasional supernatural presence. Our five novels range from a Hawaiian love story shaped by disaster to a wonderfully strange satire in which childbirth produces a rather alarming new mother. In non-fiction, Thomas Mayo considers fathers and sons, George Megalogenis takes Australia’s temperature, and Toby Walsh contemplates a future dominated by AI. Fiction Photo: Everything to the Sea by Alicia Upano (Bloomsbury, $35)

Hawaiian writer Alicia Upano delivers an impressively restrained love story from amid the epic ruin caused by a tsunami. Growing up in Hilo, Hawaii, Jane is an architecture student whose ambitions call her away to university. Summer holidays draw her back to Hilo, where she falls unexpectedly in love with Kenji – a family-oriented friend who works in construction. The summer fling gets serious, and Jane invites Kenji to live with her in Honolulu. Passion will soon turn to grief, when a tsunami devastates Hilo and Kenji rushes back to assist. A traumatised Jane can’t face the life that has been swept away, leading to an estrangement between them. Some of the novel’s most sensitive writing describes how Jane and Kenji tentatively re-establish contact years later and discover their true feelings about a love derailed. Everything to the Sea is a nuanced literary romance, with lively, well-observed characterisation, understated humour, and a narrative that draws force from the conflict of values between the lovers. Reconciliation is a vital theme, and it’s embedded within a piercing portrayal of the pain and struggle of community recovery in the aftermath of a catastrophic event. Photo: Mother Waters by Lisa Nan Joo (Affirm Press, $35)

A subgenre of feminist gothic cli-fi has emerged lately. Books in this vein feature a strong female protagonist (usually a scientist) embarking on a survival adventure; they tend to take place in extreme natural environments, with flickers of the numinous haunting the action. Where Charlotte McConaghy’s Wild Dark Shore did it with subantarctic islands, Lisa Nan Joo descends into the lightless depths of the ocean.



Mother Waters follows Charlie, a bioacoustic specialist who has lost herself in marriage. Walking out on her husband on their fifth wedding anniversary, she rededicates herself to a career exploring the sounds of life beneath the waves, even as she remains haunted by her father’s death. He was lost at sea when she was a girl, and his memory is one ghost lying in wait on a planned deep-sea expedition. Funded by a billionaire’s son, Dexter, who’s battling his own father’s difficult legacy, the mission will descend into the otherworldly refuge of an oceanic trench. It’s an unsettling odyssey, marrying psychological and political obstacles (especially those facing women in science) to the greater problems caused by our war against nature. Photo: The Wild Beneath by Kelly Anderson (Text Publishing, $35)

Another title in this subgeneric surge, Kelly Anderson’s The Wild Beneath makes more of a ripple than a splash – despite using another tsunami as a hook. On the Pacific Northwest coast, 20-year-old Annie MacLeod has always been deeply attuned to the sea, yet it will be the source of a disaster that strikes just as adulthood arrives. When a tsunami washes away her parents and much of her hometown, it leaves Annie and her childhood sweetheart, Evan, as survivors. But when Annie saves a strange, mute young man called Walker from the wrack and wreckage, a visceral bond forms between them. They seem bound by something as ancient as the waves, including a private language: Walker emits a hum that only Annie can hear. A predictable love triangle develops, and it’s the formulaic quality of The Wild Beneath that fails to satisfy. What should be a turbulent coming-of-age romance, awash with trauma and wonder, resorts to uninspired prose and superficial characterisation, and the book’s uneven pacing and tone can make its wildness seem rather tame. Photo: The Perfect Circle by Claudia Petrucci (Wakefield Press, $35)

Italian author Claudia Petrucci’s The Perfect Circle is a pleasingly patterned feminist ghost story. A real estate agent, Irene, is called upon for a hard sell. The “round house” on Via Saterna in Milan is known for its circular staircase and interiors, despite its square facade. It’s also haunted by a woman, Lidia, who’s reputed to have died there. Reports of her death may be exaggerated, and the novel unfolds in dual timelines – one moving towards death, one towards new life – as Irene begins to expose the secrets of the haunted house, and the twisted geometries of space and time combine to disorienting effect. The Perfect Circle creates an escalating sense of unease: the haunted house trope here is a vehicle for exploring gaps between the illusion and reality of women’s experience over everything from romantic love to motherhood. It’s a ghost story that also bears a fascinating resemblance to high-concept detective metafiction – to Borgesian labyrinths, say, or the existential architectural horror of Mark Z. Danielewski’s House of Leaves.



Photo: But Won’t I Miss Me by Tiffany Tsao (HarperVia, $35)

When it comes to satirising the social expectations of women regarding pregnancy and motherhood, no plot device could be too outrageous. Tiffany Tsao hits upon a sensational speculative trick. In the world of But Won’t I Miss Me, new mothers gain superhuman powers in the final stage of delivery – the “Rebirth” – in which they spawn a “fetal mother”. This doppelganger is identical to the mother, rapidly grows to adult size, and promptly cannibalises and replaces them with a new self – indestructible, ideally maternal, and with an endless (and renewable) supply of energy. All perfectly normal, except to Vivi, whose Rebirth goes awry, leaving her weakened by postpartum depression. To save herself and her child, Vivi must flee to an uncle and an underworld that society has left behind. She becomes an electrician to serve people who have gone off-grid, and dystopian answers loom to the question of what happened to Vivi during her pregnancy. Tsao’s idea is a brilliant one. True, the world-building isn’t always as well executed as this speculative feminist parable deserves, but it should attract a wide audience with its unflinching critique of the pressures of motherhood. Non-fiction Photo: Dear Son by Thomas Mayo (Hardie Grant, $35)

In 2021, when the first edition of this book was published, Thomas Mayo was confident that racism was on the wane. Travelling the country to take the Uluru Statement from the Heart to the wider community, he’d been struck by the positivity. Everything changed, however, when the Nationals and the Liberals announced they opposed the Voice referendum. A torrent of hatred was unleashed. Despite this dark event and the shadow of intergenerational trauma, these letters by Indigenous men to their fathers or their sons are suffused with love and compassion. At the same time, the history that shaped them and their fathers is never far from the surface. Stan Grant writes of the “deep well of pain” he saw in his father’s eyes. And how glad he is that life has been easier for his son. “Writing to you,” says Mayo to his son, “has been like an antidote for the vestiges of toxic masculinity learnt from father figures, peers and Western culture. I’m still unlearning.” These soul-searching letters are a soulful reckoning with what it means to be a First Nations father and son.



Photo: Three Shocks by George Megalogenis (Penguin, $37)

Alfred Deakin, our second prime minister, declared that he would “have no traffic with the unclean thing” of “coloured immigration”. When George Megalogenis was growing up in Melbourne in the 1960s and ’70s, this attitude lingered in the playground where he was called “dirty” because of his olive skin. Even as a boy, he sensed that this was an argument about belonging: “Australia’s perpetual agony of identity”. While most of Three Shocks is political and demographic analysis, this brief foray into memoir captures the origins of Megalogenis’ attunement to the changes in the make-up of our society in recent decades and his insights into how our politicians are lagging the electorate. Migrants and their children now constitute the majority of the Australian population – this is the first shock. The second is that professional women now outnumber blue-collar men in the workforce. The third concerns uncertainty in global alliances and Australians’ wariness of the US and China. Having drilled down into the data and surveyed shifts in the body politic, Megalogenis distils powerful trends that politicians would be wise to heed. Photo: Wild Hope by Claire Scobie (NewSouth, $37)

Claire Scobie calls it her “ecophony”. An epiphany of the ecological variety. Ordinary people can wait for governments to “do something” about the urgent crises of our times, she realised, or they can instigate change themselves. As a storyteller, Scobie set out to find the innovators who were showing how things can be done differently. The term that underpins all their stories is “regenerative thinking”. For farmers Dianne and Ian Haggerty, this means taking infertile land and creating a drought-resistant, chemical-free ecosystem for crops and top-grade wool. For Regen Melbourne, it’s about being the “engine” for the community collaboration behind the push to make the Yarra fit for swimming and for the creatures that live in it. Scobie’s own story binds these hopeful stories together as she moves with her husband, Gumbaynggirr man Aden Ridgeway, to his Country on the mid-north coast of NSW, and discovers what regeneration might mean in her own life. World.title: A quarter-billion-dollar mistake? Queensland’s diesel bus route slammed
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandElectric vehicles A quarter-billion-dollar mistake? Queensland’s diesel bus route slammed Cameron Atfield September 4, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A leading electric bus company has blasted the Queensland government’s purchase of 630 diesel buses, saying the decision could be a mistake that would eventually cost the state’s taxpayers a quarter of a billion dollars. Queensland Transport Minister Brent Mickelberg launched a procurement process for up to 630 new diesel-fuelled buses on Tuesday, at the same time blasting the former Labor government’s electric bus plan as “buying big, expensive paperweights to block local streets” due to a lack of associated charging infrastructure. Mickelberg defended the move on Thursday, arguing that immediate fleet upgrades were required for local depots that are not yet equipped for electric infrastructure. A Zenobe electric bus-charging system in Sydney. But Zenobe Energy’s Australia and New Zealand country director, Gareth Ridge, told this masthead Queensland’s decision to mandate diesel in its procurement program could prove costly.



The UK-based company entered the Australian market in 2023, on the back of a $1.7 billion capital-raise led by private equity giant KKR, building an electric bus depot at Leichhardt, in Sydney’s inner-west. Zenobe Australia-New Zealand country director Gareth Ridge. Oscar Colman “I would have thought that a tender like this would be technology-agnostic and would allow the market, whatever the technology that comes out, to decide,” Ridge said. “Putting aside the carbon [emissions] and whether it’s zero-emission or not, one thing that everyone should care about is the best value-for-money procurement option, and then that pulls away from the debates around climate. “You would probably see a clear winner on a financial case, and no one needs to debate whether it’s clean or green or not, because I think the winner will be both clean, green, and be cheaper as well.”



Energy Futures Foundation executive director Bruce Hardy said responsible economic management demanded an open tender, where all technologies could bid on an equal footing. Related Article Electric vehicles Soaring EV sales to shield Australia from fuel shortages “Not doing so is a betrayal of Queensland taxpayers and ratepayers, who miss out from seeing the best deals the market has to offer,” he said. Hardy said, at a time of increased fuel costs due to conflict in the Middle East, Queensland taxpayers should be furious that the government was “picking winners without properly comparing bids”. “If the government is so sure about electric bus technology, why wouldn’t they let electric bus companies bid for the tender?” he said.



“They simply don’t want to have to justify their decision to go with a more expensive diesel option in an open process if electric buses powered by Queensland sunshine come back cheaper and more reliable.” Mickelberg said the bus industry found the former Labor government’s electric buses plan “overly ambitious”. The Brisbane Metro bus system runs on electric/battery power. Courtney Kruk “This tender is for buses to be stored at facilities without either recharging or alternative fuelling facilities, but we remain technology-agnostic for future purchases and depot constructions,” he said. Addressing the minister’s concerns about depot infrastructure, Ridge said that while upfront costs for electric buses exceeded those of diesel, they proved far cheaper over the vehicle’s lifespan.



“Definitely, there’s a premium if you’re looking at it just purely on what you are buying today – the buses are maybe around 15 per cent more expensive and you’ve got all the depot upgrades, which for 600 buses would be in the order of $100 million,” he said. “There is a significant upfront premium that you pay, but looking at that in isolation is not quite accurate because you’re going to have all the operating costs that go with it. “You really need to look at this from a whole-of-life or a total-cost-of-ownership perspective to see how it really stacks up.” Ridge said, based on Zenobe’s dealings with governments across the Western world, Queensland was an outlier in its pursuit of diesel. “Sure, we’ve seen some small numbers to plug some gaps, but the scale of this procurement is nothing that we’ve seen,” he said.



The electric vehicle industry has lined up to condemn the Crisafulli government’s diesel policy. Australian Electric Vehicle Association Queensland branch director Nathan Gore-Brown took particular aim at Mickelberg’s “paperweight” comment, which he said was ill-informed. “This is not a risk his interstate counterparts seem worried about,” he said. Electric Vehicle Council chief executive Julie Delvecchio said the policy exposed Queenslanders to health risks. “Queensland communities will be paying for this decision – in asthma treatment, preventable hospitalisations and lung disease – for years to come,” she said.



“These diesel vehicles will still be on the road come the 2032 Olympics, spewing out pollution for decades to come, right when the eyes of the world will fall on the Sunshine State. “We urge the Queensland government to make the tender for these 630 buses open to all fuel types so that they can consider the best solution which is cheaper to run, cleaner electric buses.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Weather: Wind warning in place for Wellington, heavy rain for the South Island
World.content:
A strong wind warning is in place for the capital on Friday, while parts of the central and northern South Island are being drenched with heavy rain.

MetService said a front impacting parts of the South Island and the Tararua Range had hit on Friday and strong northwesterlies could reach a severe gale in eastern areas from Canterbury all the way up to Hawke's Bay.

A strong wind warning has been issued for Wellington and Wairarapa, excluding the Tararua District, from 4am on Friday through to 12pm.

Severe gales gusting up to 120km/h in exposed places were possible, the forecaster said. This could bring damage to trees, powerlines and unsecured structures and make driving difficult for high-sided vehicles and motorcycles.

Wellington was the windest place overnight - but the warmest at the same time.

MetService meteorologist Braydon White said gusts reached 137km/h at the Remutaka Summit around 7am.

Mount Kaukau followed closely at 136km/h gusts.

Urban areas also saw high winds, with the suburb of Kelburn getting gusts as high as 120km/h.

"We're well into the classic Spring westerlies," White said.

While he said these winds were normal for the start of Spring, it was warmer than average.

Both Wellington and New Plymouth were 14 degrees overnight.

Some areas quickly got warmer on Friday, like Napier rising from 7 degrees to 17 degrees within about an hour.

The strong wind dragging warm air will make its way across the country today, finishing in Auckland and Northland this evening.

"These fronts are continuing their march across the country, weakening as they do so."

Heavy rain warnings were also in place for the headwaters of the Canterbury Lakes and rivers until 8am on Friday, and the Tararua Range until 1pm.

The road into Milford Sound. (File pic) RNZ / Nate McKinnon

A road snowfall warning is also in place for Milford Rd (SH94) until 6pm on Friday, with the possibility of 2cm to 5cm of snow accumulating by the tunnel.

The weekend was looking more settled, according to MetService, with some rain. The North Island would see a few showers in the west on Saturday, but be mainly fine while the South Island could expect rain or showers in the west and south with possible heavy falls.

On Sunday, MetService said rain would be developing in the west with possible heavy falls for the North Island and rain the west and south with heavy falls for the South Island.

Wind threatens Auckland Harbour Bridge closure

Travel across the Auckland Harbour Bridge might be disrupted on Friday, transport officials have warned.

Gusts of up to 80km/h have been forecast between midday and 4pm.

"Motorists are advised to drive to the conditions and pay attention to electronic message boards on the motorway, which will advise if any lane closures and reduced speed limits are required," the New Zealand Transport Agency said in a statement on Thursday.

World.title: Uni student caught wearing smart glasses in exam
World.content:
Student caught using smart glasses in university test Morning Report Download MP3 3m

A University of Auckland student has been caught wearing smart glasses in a test, raising concerns about how the new tech could be used by students to cheat.

New products like Meta glasses have small built-in cameras which can be used to film what is in front of them, and have it answered by an outside helper or AI.

Exam supervisors would now have to check students wearing glasses to their exams to see if they could be using them to cheat.

Gone are the days of trying to smuggle pieces of paper into an exam or writing answers on a hand or water bottle label.

Technology has brought new ways for students to try to cheat their tests, as Computer Science Senior Lecturer at the University of Auckland Ulrich Speidel explained.

"You can go, for example, and record your questions, you can possibly send them to external helpers and most of those glasses also project stuff into the glasses that only the wearer can see."

A University of Auckland spokesperson said a student was seen wearing smart glasses during a test by an invigilator, after a pre-test announcement explicitly said no smart glasses or watches were allowed.

The student had the glasses taken off them, and was allowed to continue the test, they said.

The student was given a penalty over the incident, but the university would not say what it was.

Ulrich Speidel said exam invigilators would now be on the lookout for smart glasses.

"Generally what you can see is they've got rather broad hinge parts or large bridges, so we can ask our invigilators to go and look for those, and for example ask [or] offer masking tape to be put over them."

University of Auckland computer science lecturer and technology consultant Ulrich Speidel. RNZ/Luka Forman

Invigilators would tape over the cameras rather than taking the glasses, if students were using them as prescriptions.

Meta, the company that owned Instagram and Facebook, had two models of smart glasses made with brands Rayban and Oakley.

They retailed for between $350 and $750, depending on the model.

On the cheaper end, K-mart sold its own smart glasses for just $99 - which recorded videos and photos but did not have the AI features of the Meta ones.

Engineering student at AUT, Preston Williams, had a pair of the Meta glasses, which he used to make content for his business.

"I've got like a detailing business, so I do like POV [point of view] videos and stuff. But I don't use it for tests, because there's a massive white flashing light. So it's kind of hard to be inconspicuous."

However, that flashing light could be disabled through a relatively quick repair job.

US tech journalist Joanna Stern found in an investigation that dozens of services were available to do just that for about US$100 on Facebook marketplace.

However, those services did not appear to be available online in New Zealand.

Speidel said the university was keeping on top of cheating in exams, for now.

"I dread the day once smart glasses will be available as contact lenses. At that point I think it will be checkmate for us."

His department has moved to mostly pen and paper tests with randomised multi-choice questions, meaning each student had different tests to their peers.

World.title: Pacific Islands Forum winds up by condemning China nuclear test
World.content:
Leaders in the Pacific have registered their concern over a nuclear-capable missile test conducted by China in July, calling on all states to provide advance warning ahead of any testing.

Nauru - one of the 18 Pacific Island Forum (PIF) members - noted its dissent from the statement.

Partners to the forum will also be split into two tiers in future, and member states agreed to a declaration for urgent and inclusive climate action to keep 1.5 degrees of warming within reach.

The Pacifc Islands' Forum in Palau has concluded, with leaders taking part in a daylong meeting on Thursday to discuss various issues, releasing a joint statement outlining their conclusions.

The Pacific Islands Forum has been winding up discussions in Palau. Ohanna Rabo Galo/TMC Palau

Specifically, the forum noted an intercontinental ballistic missile test that had "overflew" a number of members "without adequate notice".

The members called on all states undertaking testing of intercontinental ballistic missiles to provide transparency and reassurance, including advance notification of at least 24 hours.

Palauan President Surangel Whipps Jr who read the statement concluded by saying: "I might note that the Republic of Nauru has dissented."

The forum has been overshadowed with the tensions between China and Taiwan.

One local told RNZ all he'd been hearing about was "China, Taiwan, and how the outside world, outside countries are ... making certain nations either afraid to talk or not standing up boldly."

"All I hear is about just drama, and that defeats the whole purpose."

He said he wanted to hear more about what other countries were going through, whether that matched up with the problems facing Palau - like outmigration, cost of living, and drugs - and see what could be done by working together.

New Zealand Prime Minister Chirstopher Luxon said on Thursday that China-Taiwan hadn't been a focus inside the PIF.

"It's a piece of a conversation, but it's not the dominant conversation."

But another geopolitical issue was the lingering desire by many in the forum to reach consensus on condemning the intercontinental ballistic missile test by China.

It's understood Nauru and Kiribati, both closely aligned with China, stood in the way of full consensus on a statement earlier in August.

Even as the meeting on Thursday was taking place, China's foreign ministry made accusations toward Palau, after the host of the forum urged the group to condemn China's launch.

"Palau has repeatedly raised this issue in an ill-intentioned attempt to hijack the position of other member states of the Pacific Islands Forum. It will not have its way," the ministry said.

Prime Minister Chistopher Luxon says it;s important to push back over nuclear missile tests that are not signalled in advance. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Luxon himself felt strongly about the matter, telling reporters later it was important to push back so the behaviour wasn't normalised.

"Given all the history in our part of the world with nuclear testing … that's just not something we want to see."

Luxon described Nauru as being "in the room", and wanting to be "disassociated with the statement".

"We said, look, that's great, but we're not going to not make a statement as a Pacific Island Forum because of the objection of one country, and you'd have to ask them as to what their rationale for that was.

"Suffice to say, everyone else was fully on board."

When pressed on whether Kiribati was also on board, Luxon said Kiribati had no representation in the room.

Even stranger was the delayed recognition during the closing ceremony of Kiribati's representative to the forum, David Teaboo, well after all the other leaders had received applause.

The forum also confirmed it would run a tiered system next year, splitting around 30 partners into two streams: one for strategic partners, and one for sector partners.

"Everyone's a partner, but we just need to make sure that we can manage it well going forward," said Luxon.

"We have to acknowledge that as we go forward, we can't treat them all the same or give the same sort of effort."

Foreign Minister Winston Peters at the forum. Supplied / screenshot

Taiwan remains a development partner, and while its foreign minister, Lin Chia-lung, was attending the forum this year after being invited by Palau, New Zealand's Foreign Minister indicated on Thursday that wouldn't be the case next year.

New Zealand adheres to the One China policy, which means it doesn't have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan.

That would prevent the foreign minister being invited - instead representation at a lower level would be likely at next year's forum.

Despite the geostrategic tensions at play throughout the forum, Luxon said PIF was at its "strongest."

Before setting off to Palau, Luxon denied PIF was being weakened as a mechanism for resolving region-wide difficulties.

"No, I think it's about strengthening it, though," Luxon said.

After his hours' long meeting on Thursday, he said he wanted to see PIF "continue to evolve and strengthen and move - it's the arc of progress that we're focused on".

World.title: Super at 68? Departing National MP calls for pension age to start rising in 2029
World.content:
Outgoing National MP Andrew Bayly is using his final days in Parliament to urge all parties to start raising the superannuation age from next term, warning further delay will make the eventual fix more painful.

In an interview with RNZ, Bayly said the age of eligibility should be increased by one month every year from 2029, climbing to 68 by 2065.

He also wanted the dollar amount of the payments to rise more slowly, and said some people should be able to access the pension earlier - but at a lower rate - if they had poor health, shorter life expectancies or physically demanding jobs.

Bayly's proposals were set out in a research paper published last month in the International Review of Public Administration, which he co-authored with economist Leonard Hong and data analyst Emmanuel Jo.

He told RNZ he had deliberatedly published in Asia to make it clear he was not speaking on National's behalf, but was instead setting out his own "considered view based on economic and demographic modelling".

Bayly said he had sent his paper to all party leaders in Parliament, arguing there was a "burning economic imperative" to act.

"This is the biggest economic issue facing New Zealand," he said. "The cost of superannuation is growing exponentially, and we can't just keep pushing it out for another day."

Could this be the future of superannuation? Nights Download MP3 14m

Under the current settings, Bayly and his co-authors estimated superannuation would consume almost 30 cents of every dollar of government tax revenue by 2065, up from about 19 cents today.

They said spending on super, health and education together would swallow nearly 80 percent of all tax revenue by then.

"This is a freight train coming down the line," Bayly said. "What we're advocating is a graduated approach now, rather than something being done in the middle of a crisis... we will have to be brutal if we delay it."

In 2023, National campaigned on gradually lifting the super age to 67. National initially said "very slow, staged" adjustments would begin in 2037, but later pushed the start date back to 2044.

Bayly said that plan was "worthwhile but insufficient", reducing super's share of tax revenue to 26.5 percent by 2065.

Starting the increases in 2029 would shrink it further, to about 25 percent.

"The approach is gradual, planned, and provides successive cohorts with greater certainty for retirement planning," the paper said.

Bayly and his co-authors estimate superannuation will consume almost 30 cents of every dollar of government tax revenue by 2065. 123RF

Bayly said significant savings could also be made by treating the pension the same as other welfare payments and indexing it to general inflation rather than wage growth.

He suggested a "moderated" approach with regular reviews to allow adjustments if pensioners fell too far behind the wider population.

The paper also proposed a limited early-access scheme for people who could no longer work because of reduced capacity, lower life expectancy or physically demanding jobs.

The authors said that would address one of the biggest objections to a later age of eligibility and make reform "more politically durable".

They also backed compulsory KiwiSaver contributions and continuing payments into the NZ Super Fund.

An RNZ-Reid Research poll in July found 58 percent of voters wanted the super age to remain at 65, compared with 35.3 percent who supported an increase to 67. Another 6.8 percent were unsure.

The poll found more support for means-testing the pension, with 46.6 percent in favour, 40.7 percent opposed and 12.7 percent undecided.

Bayly's paper discounted that option, arguing it would be "exceedingly difficult" to win support across Parliament for "such a radical change".

Treasury forecasts released in May showed the annual cost of super rising from $24.7 billion this financial year to $31.2 billion in 2029/30.

Labour and NZ First both support keeping the eligibility age at 65. RNZ

National has yet to set out the details of its policy for this year's election, but finance spokesperson Nicola Willis warned in May that parties ignoring the rising cost were robbing young people for "their own political expediency".

ACT campaigned in 2023 on rapidly increasing the super age to 67 by three months a year, starting almost immediately.

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters last week reiterated his party's long-held opposition to changing access to current entitlements.

Labour and the Greens also supported keeping the age at 65. Te Pāti Māori last year argued Māori should be able to receive super up to 10 years earlier because of their lower average life expectancy.

Bayly announced in June he would step down at the election, bringing his 12-year career at Parliament to an end.

World.title: 'About bloody time': Former student deplores years of inaction as Gloriavale school looks to be shut
World.content:
Lilia Tarawa on cancellation of Gloriavale school registration Morning Report Download MP3 7m

The possible closure of Gloriavle school came as a relief but feels like "the bare minimum", former student Lilia Tarawa says.

The Ministry of Education wants to cancel the school's registration, effectively closing it, after a special report by the Education Review Office (ERO) found it was not providing a physically and emotionally safe place for students.

It's the Ministry of Education's second move to cancel the school's registration in less than a year.

The school remains open after an attempt in December was challenged at the High Court by the school's board. On Thursday the ministry applied to the court to lift the orders preventing the school's closure, which has a roll of about 80 students.

Barrister Brian Henry. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Former Gloriavale Christian School student Lilia Tarawa, who is the granddaughter of the founder Hopeful Christian, fled with her family from Gloriavale in 2009.

She described her life there in her autobiography Daughter of Gloriavale, including shocking descriptions of her experiences as a student.

She told Morning Report she had seen a church leader come into her classroom, pull down the pants of his son and assault him with a leather belt.

"This type of behaviour is not OK and it's the government's duty to protect the children who are part of that organisation.

"My initial reaction [to the school closure] was about bloody time. We've been fighting for change and for safety for the kids in Gloriavale a very long time."

Many had been calling loudly for change, she said.

"It is a relief for a lot us but at the same time it feels like the bare minimum."

She criticised Social Development Minister Louise Upston's view there was no threat to children's safety.

Tarawa said there had been many reports from leavers about the abuse they had suffered, meanwhile, Gloriavale continued to enjoy tax benefits.

"The fact that it didn't lose its school licence years ago is just horrific to me. It's not good enough."

Gloriavale's leadership maintained it had changed but it was only two years ago that a leader Howard had stepped down because he was facing criiminal charges.

He had mentored leaders who had taken over, Tarawa said.

"It's really not good enough when you have the same men in power inside Gloriavale who stood aside and let this happen on their watch while they were supposed to be stewards of the children of those schools."

The Gloriavale Leavers Trust wanted a transitional facility to provide extra support for the current pupils and their families before they could be integrated into other schools.

Tarawa compared their situation to refugees.

"We really do have to provide them with some additional support around that."

Morning Report has invited the Minister to be interviewed on the programme.

Should have happened years ago

A barrister representing Gloriavale leavers says the Christian community's school should've been shut down decades ago.

Barrister Brian Henry, who has fought for Gloriavale leavers to be recognised as employees, backed the move, but simultaneously criticised the ministry for what he described as decades of inaction.

He said the ERO report revealed nothing new and that the school should have been closed 20 years ago.

"They have, as a historic department, not done their job. Finally someone's done it and I applaud them for that."

However, Henry said the fact that it had taken two attempts to cancel the registration was "appalling".

He said the ministry should have been ready to follow through with it in December but wasn't, meaning the school's closure got "bunged up" in litigation.

The ministry rejected Henry's criticism and said closing a registered school was a significant statutory decision that had to follow a robust process.

The Gloriavale compound on the West Coast. Jean Edwards

After Gloriavale filed court proceedings, the ministry and the school agreed to defer the decision until the legal process had finished, it said.

Henry wouldn't speculate on when the school would shut its doors, but said the students would need to be educated elsewhere.

"They just need to put on a school bus and shift them - like all country kids are shifted - to a public school."

Education services deputy secretary Geoff Short said the ministry would work with the school community to determine the most practical timing for the school's closure.

In a statement, the Gloriavale Christian School board said it was considering its options.

"The school strongly disagrees with the ministry's decision and is currently considering its options to challenge it. Given that the matter is ongoing, we will not be making any further comment at this time," the board said.

The ERO special review report said the school had failed to meet one of eight criteria - to provide a physically and emotionally safe place for students.

While the school met the other criteria, such as providing suitable premises, provision of tuition, and suitable staffing, and that there had been "some improvement", it said the improvement was "partial and, in key areas, not yet sustained".

World.title: Push for long-term solar energy plans that survive elections
World.content:
Push for cross-party plan on solar energy Morning Report Download MP3 5m

The Sustainable Energy Association is pushing for a cross-party government plan for solar energy that will last longer than an electoral cycle.

Solar energy has moved from the margins of mainstream political debate into a fully fledged election issue in 2026 - with Labour, National, the Greens and other parties making solar commitments.

The Sustainable Energy Association's CEO Gareth Williams hoped future governments could develop long-term solar plans that survived electoral cycles.

Williams told Morning Report, the association's annual conference on Friday, was being attended by all the political parties this year.

"Our theme last year was 'this is our time', and we were right I think... we're being aspirational but for good reason, I think, but it's probably exceeded out expectations these last 12 months."

Solar energy in homes had really taken off in February, Williams said, in large part due to the fuel and energy crisis caused by the Iran war.

A house with a new solar system. (File photo) Supplied by Lightforce Solar

"We saw a jump around March and that momentum has just continued and it's really taken off."

In the past, Williams said there had been policies from parties about solar energy, but this year every party now had an interest in it.

"It's painful out there for people and solar is by far the cheapest way of people having electricity into their homes."

There had been a lot of work installing solar in some areas of the country, Williams said, especially around Wānaka, but the number of homes with solar in Auckland remained surprisingly low, with less than 2 percent of homes with solar installed.

"Auckland is near the bottom for some reason and about to be overtaken by the West Coast of the South Island, which is ironic, really."

Williams feared too much government involvement in solar energy could be a hindrance and said it needed to be understood how significant solar energy would be to New Zealand's infrastructure.

"The growth is coming, what's really important is quality, we don't want to see what happened in Australia where every man and his dog suddenly became a solar installer and there were all sorts of issues."

Roughly 4 percent of homes in New Zealand have solar panels installed, whereas in Australia it was roughly 40 percent.
